sections.notes: Tabbed showcase (Featured, Popular, Sleep, Stress, Meditation) with cards — the Ebb AI companion and a Cocomelon partnership on display.

sections.name: FAQ
sections.notes: Nine expandable questions on basics, subscription and cancellation — objections handled inline without visual clutter.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Four columns (Get some Headspace, Our content, About us, Support) plus app badges and legal links.

principle.title: Open with an intent router, not a single funnel
principle.explanation: When your audience arrives with different problems, forcing one path loses the rest. A 'what do you need?' selector near the top lets each visitor route themselves, so the very next screen already feels personalized — higher relevance, higher conversion.
principle.howToApply: On a multi-audience landing page, add a set of need-based entry buttons just under the hero and wire each to a tailored section or page. Name them by the visitor's problem ('Sleep soundly'), not your feature ('Sleepcasts').

entries.tagline: Logo, one universal benefit line, one green button — a square that says everything a merchant needs in three beats.
entries.summary: Shopify's square banner is textbook restraint on a small canvas: a warm off-white ground, the green bag logo up top, a single sweeping benefit ('Everything you need to sell online'), and a rounded green 'Try it free today' button. There's no product screenshot to shrink into illegibility — at 300×250 the copy and CTA get all the room, and the free framing kills risk.
whatWorks: A single, all-encompassing promise ('Everything you need to sell online') does the work of a feature list in a space too small for one.
A warm off-white ground keeps the tiny unit calm and legible instead of shouting — contrast is spent on the button, not the background.
The rounded green 'Try it free today' button is the one saturated element and the clear focal point.
The bag-logo plus wordmark up top gives instant attribution without stealing space from the message.
'Free' in the CTA lowers the barrier — exactly the right ask for a top-of-funnel display impression.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The clean green Shopify bag mark on calm cream — brand-forward and uncluttered, it reads as trustworthy at a glance.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'Everything you need to sell online' — one benefit that contains the whole product, ideal for 300×250.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: No product shot; whitespace and the logo carry it, keeping the small unit uncrowded and readable.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: A rounded green 'Try it free today' pill — the single saturated element, risk-free framing, thumb-sized.

principle.title: On a small unit, sell the whole product in one line
principle.explanation: A 300×250 has no room for a feature list or a legible screenshot. One sweeping benefit that stands in for everything (plus a free CTA) converts better than three cramped selling points fighting for the same 250 pixels.
principle.howToApply: When designing small banners, write the single sentence that would make someone click if it were the only thing they read; drop the product shot if it can't be legible, and spend the saved space on whitespace and the button.

entries.tagline: The Constructivist who fused photography, type and geometry into 'production art' — design as a tool with a job, not a picture to admire.
entries.summary: Rodchenko abandoned painting to become an engineer of images: posters, book covers, ad graphics and photomontage built from photography, bold geometric shapes, diagonal dynamism and hard-working typography. With the poet Mayakovsky he ran the 'Reklam-Konstruktor' studio, treating advertising as a constructive craft. He also revolutionized photography with extreme angles (the 'Rodchenko perspective') to make the everyday newly legible.
whatWorks: Build with photography instead of illustration — real photographic fragments in montage read as modern, factual and immediate.
Use strong diagonals and geometric blocks to create movement and hierarchy on a flat page — energy from structure, not ornament.
Integrate type as a structural element (bars, arrows, size jumps) that directs the eye, not just labels the image.
Shoot from radical angles (worm's-eye, bird's-eye) to defamiliarize a subject and force fresh attention.
Treat design as 'production art' — every piece is a functional tool made for a task, judged by whether it works, not whether it's pretty.

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: From the communicative job to be done — what must this poster or cover make the viewer do or see? — then assembles from photographic and geometric parts, not a drawn composition.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Photomontage and construction: cut, scale and layer photographic fragments with geometric shapes and type into a dynamic, purposeful whole.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Aggressive diagonals plus the 'Rodchenko perspective' (extreme camera angles), and type set as bold structural bars and arrows.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Reject 'pure' art for utility — design serves a social/commercial function; a work succeeds if it communicates and mobilizes, and dynamism beats symmetry.

principle.title: Compose with real fragments and diagonals, not tidy symmetry
principle.explanation: Rodchenko got energy and credibility by building from photographic reality and driving the eye with diagonal structure. Montaged real elements feel factual and modern, and an off-axis, dynamic layout commands attention that centered symmetry can't.
principle.howToApply: For a bold editorial or campaign layout, assemble from real photographic pieces rather than stock illustration, and set a strong diagonal or angular grid to lead the eye; use type as structural bars and arrows that point, not just caption.

entries.tagline: A B2B homepage written like a straight-talking letter — the founder's voice, not a feature matrix, does the selling.
entries.summary: Basecamp's homepage is a masterclass in voice-led B2B. Instead of a slick feature grid, it leads with a plainspoken promise, then a conversational 'Tell me if this sounds about right' section where founder Jason Fried names the customer's pain in human language. Twenty years of trust are proved with a wall of real customer quotes and staggering 'big numbers', and even the support team is sold as people with names and tenure. The design is quiet and typographic on purpose — the copy is the product demo.
whatWorks: A founder's-voice value prop ('Tell me if this sounds about right') names the buyer's pain conversationally — empathy sells before features do.
A dense wall of short, attributed customer quotes across varied industries reads as breadth of trust at a glance.
'Big numbers. Highly-trusted' (84M accounts, 1.7B to-dos, 99.99% uptime) turns 20 years into hard, scannable proof.
Support sold as humans — 'Remember when companies cared about service?' with a named person and a 9-year average tenure — a differentiator most SaaS buries in a help center.
A deliberately quiet, typographic layout with generous whitespace keeps the opinionated copy the hero, not decoration.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: 'The refreshingly straightforward project management system…' plus a 3-minute walkthrough video over a real project screenshot — clarity over spectacle.

sections.name: Value proposition
sections.notes: 'Tell me if this sounds about right' — Jason Fried's personal letter naming the scattered-tools problem and Basecamp's 20-year answer.

sections.name: Social proof
sections.notes: 10+ short attributed customer quotes from marketing, nonprofits, universities and churches — diverse, human, scannable.

sections.name: Big numbers
sections.notes: 'Big numbers. Highly-trusted' — 84M accounts, 60M projects, 1.7B to-dos, 99.99% uptime as trust evidence.

sections.name: Service / culture
sections.notes: 'Remember when companies cared about service?' with a video of Chase, Head of Support, and a 9-year average tenure.

sections.name: Features
sections.notes: 'All these questions have the same answer: Yes!' — 21 capability questions answered in one move, linking to the full feature list.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Extensive links, company values, and cross-links to HEY and Fizzy.

principle.title: Sell in the founder's voice, not the feature matrix
principle.explanation: A distinctive, plainspoken voice that names the customer's pain builds trust and differentiation a spec grid never can — especially for a mature product whose edge is philosophy, not features. Copy becomes the demo.
principle.howToApply: On a value-prop section, write the pain in the customer's own words as if speaking one-to-one ('Tell me if this sounds about right…') before listing any capability. Keep the layout quiet and typographic so the voice carries.

entries.tagline: A dev-infra product made charming — a specific speed claim plus a flying-mail illustration turn deliverability into delight.
entries.summary: SendGrid takes a dry developer utility — email deliverability — and makes it likeable in a tall, narrow unit. A pale-blue sky, the Twilio SendGrid lockup, and a single concrete claim ('gets to the inbox in 2.6 seconds') sit above a playful illustration of a figure speeding through the clouds in a red car trailing envelopes. The oddly specific number does the persuading; the illustration carries the brand's warmth in a format that usually feels utilitarian.
whatWorks: An oddly specific claim ('2.6 seconds') reads as true and technical — precision is more persuasive than a round 'fast'.
A warm, whimsical illustration humanizes an infrastructure product and fills the awkward tall skyscraper shape without stretching a photo.
The sky-blue palette with a mail metaphor makes the abstract benefit (deliverability) instantly legible as a picture.
A clean top lockup gives Twilio/SendGrid attribution while the vertical space is used as a narrative (headline up top, journey below).
The AdChoices marker and full-bleed clickable creative show it's built as a real GDN unit, not a portfolio mock.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The pale-blue cloud sky and a red car mid-flight — an unexpected, friendly scene that stops the eye in a column of text.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'Email delivery service that gets to the inbox in 2.6 seconds.' — one concrete, quantified promise.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: A figure driving a red convertible through the clouds trailing envelopes — the deliverability benefit rendered as a single memorable picture, sized to fill the 160×600.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: No explicit button; the whole banner is the click target, with the specific speed claim carrying the persuasion — a reminder that a strong claim can be its own CTA.

principle.title: Use an oddly specific number as your proof
principle.explanation: A precise figure ('2.6 seconds') is far more believable than a vague superlative ('lightning fast') — specificity signals a real measurement stands behind the claim, which is exactly what a technical buyer trusts.
principle.howToApply: Replace generic speed/scale adjectives in headlines with the actual measured number wherever you have one; if you don't have it, go measure it. Precision reads as honesty.

entries.tagline: The studio that industrialized identity — turning brand design into a documented, repeatable process and one of Europe's largest independent firms.
entries.summary: MetaDesign, shaped by co-founder Erik Spiekermann (pictured) in Berlin, made its name building rigorous, systematic corporate identities (Berlin's BVG transit system, Deutsche Bank, Audi, Volkswagen, Adobe) and codifying them into exhaustive guidelines and custom typefaces. Its operating model treated identity not as a logo but as a complete, documented system a large organization could run for decades — process and consistency over one-off flair.
whatWorks: Design the system, not the logo — deliverables are complete identity toolkits (type, color, grid, usage rules) an organization can operate itself.
Commission or draw a custom typeface as the identity's backbone — proprietary type does more brand work than a mark alone (e.g. FF Meta, transit faces).
Document everything: exhaustive guidelines make consistency survive staff turnover and scale across a huge org.
Structure the studio around process and multidisciplinary teams so large, long-running programs are delivered repeatably, not heroically.
Solve real wayfinding/functional problems (transit maps, signage) as design — usefulness is the brief, decoration a by-product.

sections.name: How it's structured
sections.notes: A large, process-driven, multidisciplinary firm (Berlin-founded, later international) built to deliver big corporate-identity programs repeatably rather than depend on a single star's hand.

sections.name: How it takes on work
sections.notes: Engages major institutions and corporations needing a coherent system at scale — transit authorities, banks, carmakers, software — where consistency across thousands of touchpoints is the real problem.

sections.name: Signature method
sections.notes: Systematic identity: define a custom typeface, grid, color and usage logic, then capture it in comprehensive guidelines and asset systems the client can run for years.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Clarity and function first (Spiekermann's typographic rigor); an identity is judged by how consistently and usefully it performs in the wild, not by novelty.

principle.title: Ship the system and the manual, not just the mark
principle.explanation: A logo is a moment; a documented system is what actually holds a brand together across a large organization and many years. MetaDesign's edge was treating the guidelines, type and asset kit as the real deliverable — so consistency survived scale and staff turnover.
principle.howToApply: When you design an identity, even a small one, deliver a short but real system: a type scale, color tokens, spacing/grid rules, and a one-page usage guide. Hand over the rules, not just the artwork, so it stays coherent after you leave.

entries.title: Snap a two-column article to a baseline grid in InDesign
entries.skill: Baseline-grid alignment, paragraph styles, and killing widows/orphans so body text locks to a shared rhythm across columns.
entries.brief: Set the supplied headline and body copy in a two-column text frame, turn on a baseline grid, and lock every line of body text to it — then fix widows and orphans with tracking and hyphenation, never with extra returns.
steps: New Letter doc: 2 columns, 12mm gutter, 20mm margins. Set a baseline grid at 14pt increments (Preferences ▸ Grids), starting at the top margin.
Create a Body paragraph style at 9.5/14pt and enable 'Align to Grid: All Lines' so every baseline snaps to the grid.
Create a Heading style for the headline; set 'Space After' in whole grid increments (e.g. 28pt) so the body picks the grid back up cleanly below it.
Flow the body copy into both columns and confirm the baselines align rung-for-rung across the two columns.
Hunt widows/orphans: turn on Keep Options (2 lines at start/end), then fix any single-word last lines by tightening tracking (−10 to −20) or adjusting hyphenation — not by hitting Return.
Export a PNG/PDF and check: drop a ruler guide on any baseline in column 1 — it should hit the same baseline in column 2.

assets.label: Headline
assets.value: Form is the visible result of a rule

assets.label: Body copy
assets.value: Good design rarely begins with a picture of the finished thing. It begins with a rule — a proportion, a grid, a progression — and lets that rule decide where every element goes. When the system is honest, the layout feels inevitable rather than arranged, and it holds together at any size and in any medium. Ornament is what we add when we don't trust the structure. Strip it away and the discipline shows: consistent spacing, a clear hierarchy, type that sits on a shared rhythm. The reader never notices the grid, only the calm it produces. That quiet is the whole point of setting type well.

entries.successLooksLike: A ruler dropped on any body baseline lands on a baseline in the other column too; no line of body text floats off-grid, and there are no one-word widows or single-line orphans.
entries.stretch: Add a pull-quote that spans both columns and still returns the following body text to the baseline grid.

entries.tagline: A firehose of design news made navigable — every piece is filed on two axes (discipline AND topic) and hierarchy is built from scale and space, not boxes.
entries.summary: It's Nice That publishes at high volume, so the whole site is an exercise in making a lot of content feel curated rather than overwhelming. It leans on a disciplined two-axis taxonomy (14 disciplines plus an alphabetical tag list), an hourly-refreshed 'Nice Feed' that gives the page a living pulse, and clean colored discipline badges that act as a scannable legend across every card. Hierarchy comes almost entirely from typographic scale and whitespace rather than background panels, which keeps a dense page feeling calm and editorial.
whatWorks: Two-axis taxonomy: every article is classified by discipline (Photography, Animation…) AND by topic tag, so the archive can be entered from either direction
Colored discipline badges give each card a consistent, scannable legend — you read category before headline
'The Nice Feed' — hourly micro-updates (thumb + headline + source + timestamp) — adds a living pulse without stealing focus from featured stories
The full-width spotlight uses a big serif headline on plain white; hierarchy is scale + space, not a colored box
Lowercase, utilitarian tag typography keeps a dense taxonomy visually quiet
Accessibility is built in (Recite Me toggle) rather than bolted on

sections.name: Masthead & primary nav
sections.notes: Wordmark plus four broad category pairs ('Projects + Creatives', 'Insights + Opinion', 'Resources + Advice', 'Culture + Lifestyle') and search; a secondary row surfaces standing programs (Nicer Tuesdays, Ones to Watch, Visual Research Department). Grouping pairs of ideas per nav item keeps a broad remit to four choices.

sections.name: Discipline taxonomy menu
sections.notes: A 14-discipline menu (Advertising → Publication) plus an alphabetical, lowercase 'popular tags' list. This is the two-axis IA in the open: browse by medium or by subject.

sections.name: The Nice Feed
sections.notes: Hourly-refreshed stacked cards — small thumbnail, brief headline, publication, timestamp. Information density is deliberately high here; it reads as a live ticker of the design world.

sections.name: Category article grids
sections.notes: Four sections, each showing 3–4 featured articles in a clean grid with category tags, dates, and colored discipline badges. Consistent card anatomy makes scanning across sections effortless.

sections.name: Featured spotlight
sections.notes: A full-width lead story with a large serif headline and descriptive subtext; discipline/tag badges sit below. No background color — scale and spacing alone signal 'this is the big one'.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Multi-column, white sans on a dark ground: company info, category links, social icons, legal, plus a 'Network' block linking sister properties (Creative Lives in Progress, If You Could Jobs). The dark footer bookends the light editorial body.

principle.title: Give a firehose of content two ways in
principle.explanation: A high-volume archive drowns the reader unless each item is classified on more than one axis. It's Nice That tags every piece by discipline and by topic, so someone can enter by medium ('Photography') or by subject ('Branding') — and colored badges make the category legible before the headline.
principle.howToApply: On any content-heavy build (blog, docs, gallery, catalog), define two orthogonal taxonomies and expose both as filters; render one of them as consistent colored badges so category is scannable at a glance across the whole grid, and build hierarchy from type scale and whitespace instead of colored panels.

entries.tagline: Two matched two-word lines carry the whole pitch; a calm pink photograph carries the mood.
entries.summary: Klarna states 'buy now, pay later' in a single glance with a parallel headline — 'Shopping, done. Payments, later.' — then spends the rest of the unit on feeling, not features. A soft-pink monochrome palette ties the headline, the lifestyle photo, and the wordmark into one calm mood, and the hero is product-in-context: the phone in the scene is running Klarna's own app. The model's relaxed, eyes-closed posture literally performs the benefit (stress-free), and the CTA stays a quiet 'Try it now'.
whatWorks: Parallel two-word headline ('Shopping, done. Payments, later.') communicates the whole BNPL value prop pre-attentively
Exactly one benefit subline spells out the mechanic ('pay in 4 interest-free payments') — and then stops
Monochrome soft-pink palette unifies headline, photo, and logo into a single calm mood
Hero is product-in-context — the phone in the scene shows Klarna's own app, so the proof is inside the lifestyle shot
The relaxed, eyes-closed model performs the emotional benefit rather than describing it
A low-pressure 'Try it now' under the wordmark matches the brand's easygoing tone

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The wash of soft pink and a person visibly at ease stops the scroll on mood — it reads as calm before you read a word.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: Two symmetrical two-word fragments in bold black set the top of the unit; the parallel cadence makes the offer feel inevitable and is legible in under a second.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: A relaxed model reclining, phone-in-scene running the Klarna app — lifestyle and product proof folded into one image, all in the pink family.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: The Klarna wordmark sits low-centre with a quiet 'Try it now' beneath it — no loud button color, trusting the brand and low-friction verb to carry the click.

principle.title: Write the headline as two parallel beats
principle.explanation: 'Shopping, done. Payments, later.' uses matched two-word rhythm so the value proposition lands in a single glance. Parallel structure makes copy feel inevitable and memorable, and it survives being read in the sub-second window a display ad actually gets.
principle.howToApply: When drafting a display unit or hero headline, try shaping the promise as two symmetrical fragments of the same length and grammar; let the repetition do the persuading, keep the palette monochrome around it, and fold your proof into the hero image instead of adding a separate element.

entries.tagline: The hand-typesetter who broke the Swiss grid from the inside — the father of New Wave (Swiss Punk) typography.
entries.summary: Weingart trained as a metal-type compositor, then taught at the Schule für Gestaltung Basel from 1968 alongside his own teachers Emil Ruder and Armin Hofmann. Rather than reject Swiss typography, he interrogated it rule by rule — wide letterspacing, layering, stepped lines, reversed type, photomechanical collage — and built New Wave out of the pieces. His American students (April Greiman among them) carried the language back to the US, reshaping graphic design there.
whatWorks: Manipulate the real material, not a mockup of it — discover form by pushing the medium's actual constraints (lead spacing, film, photostats)
Build a personal vocabulary of ~20–30 reusable moves you can recombine, instead of reinventing each layout
Invert one inherited rule at a time (spacing, grid, weight, tone) as a generative prompt
Earn the right to break a system by first mastering it by hand
Turn the tooling itself (copier, film overlays, crumpled tissue) into a source of form
Keep legibility as the tension the experiment plays against — not an obstacle to ignore

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: At the composing stick, not the sketchbook. Every experiment started hands-on in metal type and photomechanical process — he manipulated the actual material (letterspacing with lead, film positives, photostats) rather than drawing an idea of a layout.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Systematic rule-breaking. He took each 'law' of Swiss style (tight setting, the strict grid, a single weight) and asked what happens if you invert it — wide-spacing letters, stepping lines, layering type over image — assembling a recombinable vocabulary of moves rather than one-off tricks.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Photomechanical collage — overlapping film positives, photocopying crumpled tissue for texture, reversing type out of tonal fields. He turned the darkroom and the copier into compositional tools decades before Photoshop made layering ordinary.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Master the craft before you subvert it — his freedom rested on a typesetter's apprenticeship. Break a rule to add meaning or emotion, never for novelty, and hold legibility as the counter-tension so the disruption still reads as typography.

principle.title: Master the grid by hand before you break it
principle.explanation: New Wave wasn't chaos: it was a trained compositor subverting rules he knew intimately. The discipline underneath is exactly what kept the disruption meaningful rather than merely messy — the breakage reads as intent because the underlying order is felt.
principle.howToApply: Before you deviate from a design system, rebuild its rules once yourself — set the type on the grid, hit every token. Then break exactly one rule at a time as a deliberate, legible move, so an 'expressive' layout still communicates. See [[april-greiman]] for how a student carried this into digital.

entries.tagline: A magazine that treats its homepage like a printed cover — one issue, two actions, and vast quiet space doing the luxury work.
entries.summary: Kinfolk applies print-magazine logic to the web: the landing is essentially the current issue's cover, centred on the page with only 'Buy' and 'Read' as choices, floating in an ocean of warm off-white. Below that calm hero, content arrives as restrained image-led article rows — tiny sans labels, letterspaced serif titles, honest editorial photography — punctuated by a single high-contrast black subscription bar and a greige 'free preview' block. Nothing shouts; the emptiness itself reads as premium. The one caveat is that the homepage keeps loading into a very long article feed, so the disciplined top gives way to a more ordinary scroll.
whatWorks: Extreme negative space as the primary material: the fold is ~70% empty, which signals calm and confidence more than any decoration could
Print-cover logic — lead with ONE object (the issue cover) and only two verbs, 'Buy' and 'Read', instead of a menu of CTAs
Classic editorial type pairing: a letterspaced old-style serif for the masthead/headlines against a small quiet sans for kickers and deks
Image-led article cards where honest, un-stylised portrait/landscape photography carries the mood; text stays a whisper beneath
One deliberate high-contrast interruption — the slim black 'Subscribe Now' bar — so the single conversion moment stands out against all the white
A warm near-white (not pure #fff) plus muted greige section blocks keep the whole page soft and gallery-like

sections.name: Masthead / nav
sections.notes: Just the letterspaced serif 'KINFOLK' wordmark top-left and a hamburger top-right — the chrome gets out of the way so the issue can be the page.

sections.name: Hero — current issue
sections.notes: 'ISSUE 60 / HISTORY SPECIAL' centred in serif caps above the cover image, with a 1/10 carousel and 'Buy' / 'Read' flanking it. The homepage IS the cover; symmetry + whitespace make it feel like a physical object.

sections.name: Subscription bar
sections.notes: A slim full-width black band ('Discover unlimited access to Kinfolk' + outlined 'Subscribe Now'). The only loud element on the page, so the one revenue ask can't be missed.

sections.name: Featured articles row
sections.notes: A horizontal run of cards (Tove Jansson home tour, Cosima Vahesar, Rebecca Solnit, a garden piece): small 'Arts & Culture, Issue 60' kicker, caps title, one-line dek. Photography leads; copy is deliberately minimal.

sections.name: Free preview
sections.notes: 'FREE PREVIEW — Take a look inside Issue Sixty' on a muted greige block with two large image cards (David Chipperfield, 'Finding Albion'). The tonal background gently separates it without a hard divider.

sections.name: Newsletter + footer
sections.notes: A single understated line, 'Never miss out—sign up for newsletters from Kinfolk', with underline-only inputs, resolving into a dark image-led footer band. Restraint held all the way to the bottom.

principle.title: Make whitespace the loudest thing on the page.
principle.explanation: Premium and calm are communicated by what you remove, not what you add. When the fold is mostly empty and there's only one object and one or two actions, the eye has nowhere to go but the thing that matters — and the restraint itself reads as taste and confidence.
principle.howToApply: On a hero, strip it to one focal object plus at most two verbs, and let 60–70% of the first screen be empty warm-white. Reserve exactly one high-contrast element (a dark bar or button) for the single most important action so the quiet has one deliberate exception.

entries.tagline: One flat field of brand-red and three product states that literally show the promise — play handheld, tabletop, or on the TV.
entries.summary: This unit sells the single core benefit of the Switch — that it plays anywhere — by showing the exact same console in its three modes across one frame: handheld, tabletop with detached Joy-Cons, and docked to a TV. A saturated flat Nintendo-red background isolates the hardware so nothing competes with it, the headline states the benefit in five words, and a single pill CTA closes. It's textbook display craft: one idea, one colour, one action.
whatWorks: The product IS the proof — showing three play modes in one row demonstrates 'anywhere' faster than any copy could claim it
A single flat brand-red fills the whole field so the hardware pops with zero background noise and the brand colour is unmissable
Five-word benefit headline ('Play Together Anytime, Anywhere') in bold caps — readable in the half-second a banner gets
One clear pill CTA ('Offers On Now') in white, the only enclosed shape on the frame, so the click target is obvious
Left-locked logo + centred headline + product baseline create a clean left-to-right read with a stable horizon

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The wall of saturated Nintendo-red stops the scroll on colour alone, then the trio of familiar consoles pulls the eye across the frame.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'PLAY TOGETHER ANYTIME, ANYWHERE' — bold white caps, two tight lines, benefit-first and instantly legible against the red.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: The same console shown in three modes (handheld, tabletop, docked-to-TV) is the whole argument; each state is spaced so it reads as a sequence, not clutter.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: A single white pill, 'OFFERS ON NOW', is the only outlined shape — low-key wording but unmistakable as the one thing to click.

principle.title: Let the product demonstrate the benefit instead of claiming it.
principle.explanation: A banner has a half-second to land one idea. Showing the product in the exact states that embody the promise (here, three ways to play) proves the claim visually and needs almost no reading — far stronger than an adjective-laden headline.
principle.howToApply: For a feature-led ad, stage the product itself performing the benefit (before/after, or the key modes side by side) on a single flat brand colour, add a five-word benefit line, and one enclosed CTA — nothing else.

entries.tagline: Turned magazine typography into image — building bespoke letterforms and a visual system that made 'The Face' feel like a movement.
entries.summary: Brody rose to fame art-directing The Face in the 1980s, where he treated type as expressive image rather than neutral information, drawing on Dada, Futurism and Rodchenko. He built custom typefaces and a recurring visual grammar for each publication, later co-founding FontShop and the experimental FUSE project. His lasting lesson is method, not style: design a system and its own alphabet, then evolve it issue to issue so the whole feels authored.
whatWorks: Design a repeatable visual system (grid, symbols, type treatments) for a project, then vary it rather than restarting each time — consistency through evolution
Treat typography as image: letterforms can be the hero, not just the label
When existing type won't carry the idea, draw your own — a bespoke typeface (like his 'Industria' for The Face) makes a brand unmistakable
Mine unlikely sources (Dada, Constructivism, street signage) and translate their energy into a modern layout
Ignore inherited 'rules' deliberately, but keep legibility as the non-negotiable floor — experiment on top of a readable base
Build recurring symbols/marks that let readers navigate and recognise the publication at a glance

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: Starts from the publication's attitude, not a template — asks what the thing should feel like, then invents a visual language (marks, type, grid) specific to it, borrowing energy from Dada, Futurism and Rodchenko.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Builds a system and then evolves it across issues: consistent underlying structure with deliberately changing type treatments, so the design feels authored and alive rather than fixed or generic.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Type-as-image — widely letterspaced words, type set on diagonals/curves, dramatic size contrast, and hand-built custom typefaces (Industria, Typeface Six) drawn when off-the-shelf fonts couldn't carry the idea.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: 'Design cannot remain neutral' — typography should express and provoke; break conventions on purpose, but never sacrifice the reader's ability to actually read it.

principle.title: Invent a system and its own alphabet — then evolve it, don't restart it.
principle.explanation: Brody's power came from authoring a visual language (grid + recurring marks + bespoke type) and then varying it issue to issue. That yields something that feels both consistent and alive, and makes a brand unmistakably its own instead of assembled from stock parts.
principle.howToApply: For a recurring project (newsletter, deck series, site sections), define a small kit — a grid, two type treatments, a couple of recurring symbols — and commit to remixing that same kit each time rather than redesigning; draw or heavily customise one signature type element so it can't be mistaken for anyone else's.

entries.tagline: A hardware storefront that sells speakers as design furniture — cinematic product film, editorial lifestyle photography, and one electric-blue used like a spotlight against an otherwise neutral page.
entries.summary: Bang & Olufsen treats its homepage like a design magazine that happens to sell speakers. The palette is almost entirely neutral — off-white grounds, charcoal type, and full-bleed lifestyle photography — so the single saturated electric-blue reads as an event every time it appears (a promo band, the footer). Products are shot in real rooms and on real people rather than floating on white, which is exactly the honest, in-context imagery that makes a $2,300 object feel lived-with rather than advertised. The page closes on an oversized vertical BANG & OLUFSEN wordmark that turns the logo into architecture.
whatWorks: One saturated brand color (electric blue) used only as periodic full-bleed punctuation, so it never dilutes and always signals 'pay attention here'
Products shot in context — a speaker on a real kitchen counter, headphones on John Legend — never isolated on sterile white
A horizontal 'Explore our bestsellers' rail with consistent name + price treatment lets luxury pricing sit calmly instead of shouting
Editorial two-up blocks pair an atmospheric lifestyle image with a short product line, so mood and merch share the frame
Generous whitespace and restrained chrome (thin nav, tiny cart) make restraint itself read as the luxury signal
An oversized vertical wordmark brackets the footer, using the logo as structural typography rather than a small lockup

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: A dark, cinematic autoplay film frames the new Beo Grace earphones shot through a car window onto a cityscape — 'Wireless sound. Connected to the moment.' A carousel pause control and a single outlined 'Learn more' button keep chrome minimal; the mood is film, not spec sheet.

sections.name: Promo band
sections.notes: A full-bleed electric-blue block interrupts the neutral flow with a complimentary-powerbank gift offer in large white text. The saturated color does the work of a graphic — no image needed — and marks a clear rhythm break between hero and catalog.

sections.name: Bestsellers rail
sections.notes: 'Explore our bestsellers' — a horizontal scroll of six products on white, each with a clean thumbnail, name, price, and a small 'New' tag. Prices ($299–$2,300) are stated plainly and quietly; the restraint is what makes them read as premium.

sections.name: Editorial lifestyle blocks
sections.notes: Alternating full-bleed and two-up sections: a Beosound 2 on a real kitchen counter, a portable speaker held against a brick wall, John Legend as brand ambassador in headphones. Copy is a single sentence; the photography carries the value.

sections.name: Newsletter — 'The House of Bang & Olufsen'
sections.notes: A calm sign-up block pairs an intimate lifestyle photo with a short benefits checklist (early products, events, personalized content). The ask is framed as joining a community, not subscribing to marketing.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: A striking electric-blue footer with tidy link columns (Customer Care, Policies, Company, Social) framed left and right by a giant vertical BANG & OLUFSEN wordmark — the logo scaled up into page architecture, a memorable last impression.

principle.title: Reserve one saturated color as punctuation, not paint
principle.explanation: A single vivid brand hue keeps its power only if the rest of the page stays neutral and photographic. Used as occasional full-bleed bands and the footer — never as everyday UI color — it marks rhythm and signals 'this matters' every time it appears, which is stronger than sprinkling the color everywhere.
principle.howToApply: Set the whole site in neutrals + honest photography, then deploy the brand color in just two or three deliberate full-bleed moments (a promo band, the footer). Keep buttons and body chrome neutral so the color never becomes wallpaper.

site.name: The New York Times — 300×250 medium-rectangle display ad

entries.tagline: A type-only subscription ad that sells a conviction, not a feature list.
entries.summary: This is a banner with no image at all, and that is the whole point. Against a plain white ground it runs the blackletter masthead as its logo, a bold three-line Cheltenham headline ('This is when journalism matters most.'), a single gold accent line ('Subscribe to The Times.'), and one black pill CTA. Every element is the brand's own editorial typography, so the unit feels like The Times rather than an ad for it. It proves that when a brand voice is strong enough, type alone can carry a paid unit that most advertisers would stuff with stock photography.
whatWorks: No imagery — the recognizable masthead and editorial serif ARE the brand asset, so the ad is unmistakably NYT at a glance
Sells a belief ('when journalism matters most'), not a price or a feature, matching a value-driven purchase
A single gold accent line is the only color, pulling the eye straight from headline to the subscribe promise
One high-contrast black CTA ('SEE MY OPTIONS') — soft-framed permission phrasing, not a hard 'BUY NOW'
Tight type hierarchy (masthead → headline → accent line → button) reads top-to-bottom in one pass
Massive restraint: white space does the framing, so the small unit never feels cramped

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The blackletter New York Times masthead at the top — instant, unmistakable brand recognition that stops the scroll on authority alone, no image required.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'This is when journalism matters most.' — a bold, three-line conviction statement in the Times' Cheltenham serif. It sells the mission, not a discount, so it reads as editorial voice rather than marketing.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: There is deliberately no photo. The typography itself is the visual: black headline weight against white, with a single gold line ('Subscribe to The Times.') as the only color and the pivot from belief to ask.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: A solid black rounded rectangle, 'SEE MY OPTIONS' in caps — high contrast, permission-framed (options, not a hard sell), and the single darkest mass on the unit so the eye lands on it last.

principle.title: When the voice is strong, make brand type the entire creative
principle.explanation: A distinctive masthead and editorial typeface can carry a paid unit with no image at all. Selling a conviction in the brand's own type feels like the brand speaking, not advertising it — and it sidesteps the generic stock photography that makes most display ads interchangeable.
principle.howToApply: For a brand with real typographic equity, try an image-free hero/banner: recognizable logotype, one belief-led headline in the brand serif, a single accent color, one high-contrast CTA. If it still reads as unmistakably you, the image was only decoration.

entries.tagline: The book-jacket designer who made the cover a visual haiku of the story — an invitation, never a summary.
entries.summary: Chip Kidd has been designing jackets at Alfred A. Knopf since 1986 and is the most recognizable book-cover designer of his generation (his 1993 Jurassic Park skeleton logo became the entire film franchise's mark). His method starts not with a visual style but with the manuscript: he reads deeply, then solves the book as a 'visual problem,' hunting for the one surprising image or typographic twist that captures its soul without spoiling it. Crucially, he refuses a signature look — believing a house style would limit the range of solutions — so his process, not his aesthetic, is the thing to steal.
whatWorks: Read the source before touching the tools — the concept comes from the content, not from a style you already own
Frame the job as a 'visual problem' with one right-feeling answer, and let it take as long as it takes (his solutions could take months)
Find a single surprising image or twist that intrigues rather than explains — the cover is an invitation, not a summary
Refuse a signature aesthetic on purpose, so each project gets the solution IT needs instead of your habit
Let type and image do one job together — often a witty, unexpected pairing that rewards a second look
Stay humble about your role: the cover serves the book, so 'first, do no harm' — never misrepresent what's inside

sections.name: How he begins
sections.notes: By reading the manuscript itself and talking to the author (who keeps final approval). Inspiration comes 'from whatever the book is' — never from a pre-decided look — so every cover starts from content, not from a template.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: He treats the jacket as a visual problem to be solved, gathering photographs, illustrations, and 'ephemeral detritus' until the right idea surfaces. He gives it real time — a solution can take up to six months — trusting the concept to arrive rather than forcing a style onto the page.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Conceptual wit: a single unexpected image or type move that captures the book's essence with a twist (the Jurassic Park T-rex skeleton, sly/creepy/smart covers). The image intrigues and rewards a second look instead of literally illustrating the plot.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: No signature style — 'the simplest and most effective solutions aren't dictated by style.' The cover must serve, not misrepresent, the book ('first, do no harm'), and he stays humble that it's 'only a small part' of whether a book connects.

principle.title: Design from the content, and reduce it to one surprising image
principle.explanation: Kidd's power comes from refusing a house style and instead deriving each solution from the material itself, then compressing it to a single idea that invites rather than explains. Intrigue beats completeness: a cover (or a hero) that says everything says nothing.
principle.howToApply: Before designing a landing hero or brand mark, read/absorb the actual product story, then force yourself to one surprising visual metaphor that makes someone want to look closer — and cut the urge to illustrate every feature. Resist reusing your last project's look; let this one's content dictate the form.

entries.tagline: A consumer-fintech homepage that makes fee transparency the hero — a working currency calculator with live rates sits above the fold, so you use the product before you sign up.
entries.summary: Wise's homepage (2023 Ragged Edge rebrand) turns the industry's dirty secret — hidden FX margins — into its whole pitch. Instead of stock photos of happy travellers, the hero is an operable rate calculator showing the real mid-market rate, the exact fee, and 'most arrive in under 20 seconds.' A bright-green / deep-forest-green system, a proprietary sans, and blunt, number-led copy carry a page that stays confident and uncluttered from calculator to Trustpilot proof to the dark footer.
whatWorks: The hero's centrepiece is a real, working tool (live currency calculator), not a screenshot or a promise — value is demonstrated, not described
A two-green system does the identity work: acid bright-green (#9fe870-ish) for action against deep forest-green (#163300), so CTAs never compete with themselves
Copy is number-first ('3.14% APY', 'under 20 seconds', '700,000 businesses') — specifics substitute for adjectives
Testimonials are flag-pair + short quote + 'View on Trustpilot' — proof is routed to a third party and made scannable at a glance
Value props are three tight cards (receive fast / save abroad / earn interest), each linking deeper rather than over-explaining on the homepage
Generous whitespace and left-aligned type give a dense fintech product an unhurried, app-like calm

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Centered headline + a live USD→EUR calculator showing the true mid-market rate, the fee, and arrival time. The product's core action is playable before signup; transparency IS the hook.

sections.name: Value props (3 cards)
sections.notes: Receive money fast / save on spending abroad / earn interest — each a card with one icon or the green card image and a bold benefit header, linking to a deeper page instead of expanding inline.

sections.name: Safe at every step
sections.notes: Trust block: short reassurances on regulation, safeguarded funds and anti-fraud, paired with simple icons and an atmospheric city photo — credibility without a wall of legalese.

sections.name: Social proof
sections.notes: Customer quotes tagged with sender/recipient flag pairs and 'View on Trustpilot' badges; ~140-char quotes keep it skimmable and outsource credibility to a named authority.

sections.name: Business + app
sections.notes: A 'Built for business too' band with a scale stat (700,000 businesses) and dual CTAs, then a QR + store badges for the app — secondary audiences handled without diluting the primary flow.

sections.name: Currency lists + footer
sections.notes: Expandable flag-led lists (send-to countries, account details, hold/convert currencies) give SEO and utility depth, closing on a dark charcoal footer with grouped links and fine-print regulatory identity.

principle.title: Put the working product in the hero, not a picture of it
principle.explanation: When the value is a number or a computation, a visitor believes the tool far more than the pitch. Letting them operate the real thing (with honest data) above the fold collapses 'learn about it' and 'try it' into one act, and pre-empts the skepticism a claim invites.
principle.howToApply: On any quote / pricing / estimate / calculator product, embed the live tool in the hero wired to real data — show the true number including fees. Conversion then becomes 'finish what you already started,' not 'trust us and sign up.'

site.name: Dropbox — square product-feature display unit (Dropbox Replay)

entries.tagline: The hook is a screenshot of the feature itself — the ad demonstrates the benefit instead of illustrating it.
entries.summary: A square Dropbox Replay banner splits into two clean zones: the top two-thirds is a real screenshot of the Replay review UI (a video with frame-anchored comments), the bottom third is a dark charcoal panel with the product wordmark, a benefit headline, and a CTA. Copy is nine words. A single orange accent lands on one word ('frame-accurate') and again on the outlined button, drawing a short line from the promise to the click.
whatWorks: The visual is the product doing its job — an actual Replay session — so the benefit is shown, not claimed
One accent colour used exactly twice (the key word + the CTA) builds a deliberate eye-path: hook → benefit → button
Nine-word headline names a specific, concrete capability ('frame-accurate feedback'), not a vague outcome
Two-zone layout (bright product shot over dark copy panel) gives instant hierarchy in a small square
Outlined ghost button keeps the CTA present without shouting over the one-colour system
Restraint: no logo wall, no feature list — one feature, one promise, one action

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: A screenshot of the Replay UI — a real video review with a comment pinned to a moment — stops the scroll by showing the tool in use rather than a lifestyle image.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'Keep collaborators aligned with frame-accurate feedback' — one concrete benefit, with 'frame-accurate' set in orange to spike the specific value word.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Bright product shot occupies the top two-thirds; the dark lower panel carries the Dropbox Replay wordmark so brand and message never fight the screenshot.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: An orange outlined 'See how it works' button reuses the exact accent from the highlighted word, so the colour itself points the eye to the click.

principle.title: Use one accent colour as a path to the button
principle.explanation: In a small unit the eye needs a route. Repeating a single accent on the most important word and again on the CTA creates a visual thread hook → benefit → action; everything else can stay neutral so the thread reads instantly.
principle.howToApply: Pick one accent and spend it only twice per banner (or hero): on the value word in the headline and on the CTA. Keep product shot and body chrome neutral so the accent always means 'look here / click here.'

entries.tagline: The type designer behind Gotham, Interstate, Whitney and Retina — a craft built almost entirely on invisible optical corrections.
entries.summary: Frere-Jones designed some of the most-used typefaces of the last thirty years (Interstate, Gotham, Whitney, Tungsten, Retina), first at Font Bureau, then at Hoefler & Frere-Jones, now at Frere-Jones Type. His method is unglamorous and deeply transferable: source letterforms from the real world, then bend them against the eye's own distortions until they simply *look* right. His public writing on 'typeface mechanics' makes the usually-hidden decisions teachable.
whatWorks: Mine the vernacular: Gotham was drawn from the plain 1950s lettering on New York's Port Authority terminal — start from a real, found source, not a blank page
Correct optically, not mathematically: round shapes overshoot the flat ones, joins are thinned, so equal-looking beats equal-measured
Design for the worst case: Retina was engineered for tiny stock-listing type on cheap newsprint — let the hardest use dictate the form
Judge by reading, not by ruler — print it, shrink it, squint, iterate against how it actually reads
Build the whole system: weights, widths and italics conceived as a family so the type works across every real context
Make the invisible explicit: name and document the optical tricks so they become repeatable craft, not intuition

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: Starts from a source and a function — a piece of found lettering (signage, old catalogues) plus a hard question: where will this be read, and under what abuse? The brief is a constraint, not a mood.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Draw, output at real size, and test relentlessly at the sizes and stocks it will actually face; refine against reading rather than against the on-screen outline. The eye, not the coordinate, is the instrument.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Deliberate optical corrections — overshoots on curves, adjusted stroke weights, ink traps, thinned junctions — distortions the reader never notices but which make letters feel even and clean.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Form is earned from function and context; a shape is 'right' when it disappears into effortless reading. Nothing is decorative-by-default — every curve answers to where the type has to survive.

principle.title: Correct for the eye, not the ruler
principle.explanation: Mathematically equal shapes look unequal; the eye distorts. Great craft is the set of deliberate, invisible corrections that make something *look* right rather than measure right — and the discipline of testing in the real, ugly conditions the work will face.
principle.howToApply: In UI, logo and layout work, adjust by eye: overshoot circles past the cap/baseline, optically centre (not mathematically), add size-specific tweaks, and always test type/marks at the smallest real size and worst real screen before calling it done.

entries.tagline: The Browser Company sells a browser the way a consumer brand sells a lifestyle — one electric-indigo world, product UI in every frame.
entries.summary: Arc's marketing page runs on a single saturated indigo that it splashs into full-bleed bands to pace a very long scroll. Instead of describing features it shows the actual product UI in browser-chrome mockups at every step, warmed by playful hand-drawn illustrations and hot-orange/pink gradient accents so a tech product still feels human. It closes on a wall of real user quotes and a single email-to-download conversion.
whatWorks: One saturated brand indigo used structurally — full-bleed color bands (hero, a Verge press quote, the sign-up) segment the page into chapters
Every feature claim is anchored to a real product screenshot inside browser chrome, not an abstract graphic
Warm orange/pink gradients play against the cool indigo so long stretches don't read monotone
Hand-drawn peace-sign and device doodles keep a software product feeling human and playful
Social-proof wall of cream quote cards with real handles, then a single clear CTA (email -> download link)

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Light band: 'Meet Dia, the next evolution of Arc', a black pill 'Try Dia' button with app icon, and a real product screenshot of the AI browser sidebar. Product-first, one CTA.

sections.name: Press-quote band
sections.notes: Full-bleed indigo block with an oversized pull quote ('Arc is the Chrome replacement I've been waiting for.' - The Verge) plus a press-logo strip. Color change alone signals a new chapter.

sections.name: Anticipation / bento
sections.notes: 'A browser that doesn't just meet your needs - it anticipates them.' A bento of real screenshots + photo tiles shows Spaces/organization concretely.

sections.name: Spaces & Profiles
sections.notes: Warm orange-gradient browser mock: 'Space for the different sides of you' - a feature shown as a lived-in UI, not a bullet list.

sections.name: Setup / themes
sections.notes: Pink-purple browser mocks for Split View & Themes, with a whimsical handheld-device illustration - personality between product shots.

sections.name: Social proof + CTA
sections.notes: Cream quote cards with real user handles, then 'Enter your new home on the internet' email capture with an orange 'Get Download Link' button.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Minimal utility footer, product/resource columns, 'The Browser Company, New York' sign-off.

principle.title: Segment a long page with full-bleed color bands, not just whitespace
principle.explanation: On a long marketing page, whitespace alone makes sections blur together. Pulling one or two key moments (a press quote, the sign-up) into full-bleed brand-color bands gives the scroll rhythm and makes each stretch feel like a distinct chapter.
principle.howToApply: Pick your 2-3 highest-value moments on a long landing page and render them as full-bleed brand-color bands between the light content sections; keep the accent gradients for variety so the color never reads flat.

site.name: Warby Parker - Meta feed ad (1:1 eyewear)

entries.tagline: A pair of sunglasses held to a summer sky - a paid unit dressed as an organic post.
entries.when: Meta feed, 2026 (pulled live from the Meta Ad Library)
entries.summary: A currently-running Warby Parker feed ad: one hand holds a pair of shades up against bright blue sky, sea horizon and green grass, sun flaring through the lens. It reads like a friend's vacation snap, not a studio ad - which is exactly why it slips past the scroller's ad-filter. The pun headline 'See summer better' ties benefit to season, and a soft 'Learn More' CTA plus free-shipping line lower the risk.
whatWorks: Single product held against huge negative space (sky) - one unmistakable focal point
UGC-style handheld shot in natural light and a real place - feels native to the feed
Benefit-driven pun headline ('See summer better') doing double duty as product + season
Low-friction top-funnel CTA ('Learn More') with a 'Free shipping on every order' risk-reducer
Seasonal hook ('summer styles ... a refreshed palette') gives a reason to act now

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: Sunglasses raised to a clear sky with sun-flare through the lens - an aspirational, scroll-stopping single image.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'See summer better' - a pun that reads as a product benefit and a seasonal invitation at once.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Handheld, natural-light, real-environment framing (sky/sea/grass). Deliberately un-studio so it blends into organic posts.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: Soft 'Learn More' button (top of funnel) plus 'Free shipping on every order' to remove hesitation.

principle.title: Make the paid creative look like an organic post
principle.explanation: Feed scrollers have a fast ad-filter; glossy studio creative trips it. A handheld, natural-light shot of one product in a real setting blends into the feed and gets read before it gets skipped.
principle.howToApply: Shoot feed creative in-hand, in real light, one product, lots of sky/negative space; skip the studio sweep and let it look like something a person would post.

entries.tagline: The designer who put graphics on buildings - and turned a whole Olympic city into a temporary brand.
entries.summary: Trained in the Eames Office, Sussman pioneered environmental graphic design: graphics that live in space, at architectural scale. With Sussman/Prejza she created the 'Festive Federalism' look of the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics - magenta, vermilion, chrome yellow and purple on columns, tents, sonotubes and scaffolding - branding an entire city on a modest budget through a recombinable kit of parts.
whatWorks: Design for the moving body in space, not a static page - wayfinding, scale, sequence
Build a kit of parts (bounded palette + modular shapes) so a huge program stays coherent across many hands
Use a tight, high-chroma palette as the unifier rather than a single logo
Hit architectural scale cheaply with modular, recombinable, temporary components
Let a strict system license exuberant, playful execution

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: Start from the site and the person moving through it - walk the space, study sightlines, scale and sequence. Design for the body, not the sheet.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Define a KIT OF PARTS: a bounded palette, a set of shapes (columns, tents, sonotubes) and modular components that many people can recombine cheaply at any scale.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Supergraphics - huge flat fields of high-chroma color and form applied to architecture and temporary structures, used systematically, never as decoration.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: It must read at building scale AND on a badge. Consistency lives in the system; that frees the execution to be joyful. From the Eameses: rigor plus play.

principle.title: Design a kit of parts, not a set of pages
principle.explanation: When work has to scale across many surfaces and be built by many hands, a bounded palette plus modular, recombinable components keeps it coherent. Consistency lives in the system; freedom lives in how the parts get assembled.
principle.howToApply: For any multi-surface project (site + ads + signage + social), first define the reusable kit - colors, shapes, type, components - then build every artifact by recombining it, instead of art-directing each piece from scratch.

entries.tagline: A monumental condensed wordmark, a full-bleed Night Watch, and a whisper-quiet interface that lets the art do everything.
entries.summary: The Rijksmuseum site opens with its wordmark set as ultra-condensed all-caps architecture spanning the full width, laid over a dark full-bleed photo of The Night Watch with a visitor in frame for human scale. Below, the page is a stack of edge-to-edge image tiles - each an exhibition or promo with only a tiny uppercase kicker and title lower-left. The chrome is reduced to almost nothing so wildly different imagery still reads as one calm, curated system.
whatWorks: A single ultra-condensed display wordmark used as a graphic device, not just a logo
Full-bleed artwork hero with a real visitor in frame - scale and emotion, not a flat reproduction
One consistent tile treatment (tiny uppercase kicker + title, bottom-left) unifies a Rembrandt, a Toy Story toy and a book mockup
Interface reduced to a whisper: no card borders or shadows, minimal type, edge-to-edge images
Utilitarian dark footer carries the real jobs - Book a ticket, Donate, Newsletter

sections.name: Masthead + hero
sections.notes: Giant condensed 'RIJKS MUSEUM' over a dark full-bleed Night Watch; small-caps 'OPEN TODAY / VISIT THE HIGHLIGHTS' label and partner logos sit quietly beneath.

sections.name: Promo tile - Disney
sections.notes: Full-bleed Toy Story image, kicker 'FREE FOR AGES 18 AND UNDER', title 'SUMMER BREAK WITH DISNEY'. Same overlay grammar as every other tile.

sections.name: Split tile - Ed van der Elsken
sections.notes: A B&W photo tile ('Up Close') paired with a book-mockup tile ('Book now available'), showing exhibition and shop in one consistent pattern.

sections.name: Gardens tile
sections.notes: Full-bleed museum-facade photo, kicker 'FREE ADMISSION', title 'CAREL VISSER - In the Rijksmuseum gardens'.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Dark utility footer: Visitor Information, opening hours, address, About/Press/Careers/Contact, Donate + Newsletter buttons, socials, partner logos, legal.

principle.title: When the content is the star, reduce the interface to a caption
principle.explanation: With imagery this strong, borders, cards and shadows only get in the way. Going edge-to-edge and stripping text down to a small kicker and title makes the work dominate and the whole page feel curated rather than templated.
principle.howToApply: On image-rich pages (museums, portfolios, editorial), go full-bleed, drop card chrome, and cap each tile's text at a small uppercase kicker + title so the imagery carries the page.

site.name: Casper - Meta feed / story ad (portrait, illustrated)

entries.tagline: A calm two-color illustration with the offer drawn right into the pixels.
entries.when: Meta feed, 2026 (pulled live from the Meta Ad Library)
entries.summary: A running Casper unit that skips photography entirely: navy line-art on cream, a sleeper on a mattress ringed by floating bedroom pieces and a little 'Zzz'. The strict two-color palette says 'calm/sleep' and is cheap to scale, while the headline and the offer are baked into the image - so the value prop survives even when the platform caption gets truncated.
whatWorks: Strict two-color palette (navy on cream) - calm, ownable, and cheap to produce at scale
Illustration instead of photography - whimsical, on-brand, no photoshoot needed
Staccato four-noun headline 'Mattress. Foundation. Pillow. Sheets.' communicating full range
The offer/CTA ('Build your bedroom refresh & save 25%') is drawn INTO the creative
Clean top-to-bottom hierarchy: wordmark -> headline -> illustration -> CTA pill

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: Cozy navy-on-cream line illustration with a sleeping figure and a 'Zzz' cloud - the calm palette itself signals 'sleep' and stops the scroll softly.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'Mattress. Foundation. Pillow. Sheets.' - four words that say 'we make the whole bed', reinforcing the bundle.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: A single two-color illustration of the mattress surrounded by floating bedroom items; ownable and warm, no stock photography.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: In-image navy pill: 'Build your bedroom refresh & save 25%' - action plus a specific offer, baked in rather than left to the caption.

principle.title: Bake the offer into the creative, not just the caption
principle.explanation: On feed and story ads the platform caption truncates and is easy to skip. Drawing the hook headline and the offer/CTA inside the image guarantees the whole value prop travels with the pixel wherever it's shown.
principle.howToApply: Put your hook line and the offer/CTA inside the image itself; treat the platform caption as a bonus, not the load-bearing part of the message.

entries.tagline: The identity designer who thinks by hand first - one running sketchbook since 1982.
entries.summary: A Pentagram partner in New York (after a decade with Vignelli), Bierut is as known for how he works as for what he's made. He has kept a single continuous, numbered sketchbook since 1982 - dozens filled - and starts every project in words and pencil before software. His work pairs a witty, one-sentence conceptual hook with the classical typographic discipline he learned from Vignelli.
whatWorks: Keep one running sketchbook - think by hand, in words, before opening software
Lead with a one-sentence idea/story; let form follow the narrative
Generate many rough directions fast and cheaply by hand
Pair a witty conceptual hook with strict typographic craft
Build taste over decades through a continuous personal archive

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: In a notebook, by hand, in words - write the problem and the idea before designing. He's kept a numbered sketchbook running since 1982; the story comes first, the form second.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Find the narrative - the single idea you can say in one sentence - then let it drive the form. Sketch many rough directions by hand to keep thinking loose and cheap.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Idea-led identity: a simple, often witty conceptual hook you can tell as a story, executed with Vignelli-grade typographic rigor.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: If you can't say the idea in a sentence, it isn't finished. Good design tells a story and rewards a second look; taste is built by looking constantly and keeping the record.

principle.title: Think by hand, in words, before you open the software
principle.explanation: An idea that survives as one sentence and a rough sketch is an idea worth building; form should follow that story. Starting in software too early locks you into shapes before you have a point.
principle.howToApply: Begin each project in a notebook: write the one-sentence idea, then sketch ~10 rough directions by hand before touching Figma. Keep the notebook running as your personal taste archive.

entries.tagline: Magazine-grade editorial grammar - kicker, serif headline, byline on every story - turned a watch blog into an authority.
entries.summary: Hodinkee runs like a print magazine online: a serif masthead, an 'In-Depth' lead story with a full-width hero photo, then a story grid where every card carries the same triad - an uppercase category kicker, a serif headline and an author. The kicker taxonomy ('Bring A Loupe', 'Reference Points', 'Hands-On') is both navigation and house voice. A dark 'Featured Videos' band separates media type by changing the background, not just the layout.
whatWorks: Every story labeled with the same triad: uppercase kicker + serif headline + byline
A named category system (Bring A Loupe, Reference Points, Hands-On...) that doubles as insider vocabulary
Serif display type for editorial authority against a restrained black/white/grey palette
A dark background band to separate 'Featured Videos' from articles - content type signalled by color, not just position
Rich, uncluttered product photography given room to breathe; a numbered 'Most Discussed' list for engagement

sections.name: Masthead + In-Depth hero
sections.notes: Centered serif 'HODINKEE' wordmark and slim nav; lead story with a full-width photo of two gold Patek Philippe pocket watches, kicker 'IN-DEPTH', serif headline, byline and dek.

sections.name: Story grid
sections.notes: 3-up then rows of cards, each with image + uppercase kicker + serif title + author. The kickers organize the firehose and set the voice.

sections.name: Featured Videos (dark band)
sections.notes: Background flips to near-black; a large video still beside a vertical list of thumbnail+kicker+title rows - a clear media-type switch by color.

sections.name: Latest
sections.notes: Back to light: a big lead card then 2-up and 2-up rows, same editorial card grammar throughout.

sections.name: Most Discussed + footer
sections.notes: A numbered ranked list as lightweight social proof, then the serif masthead repeated in the footer.

principle.title: Give every item the same three-part label - kicker, headline, byline
principle.explanation: A consistent kicker + headline + attribution triad signals editorial rigor and lets readers scan a dense index by section and voice. The named kicker set becomes both navigation and a recognizable house vocabulary.
principle.howToApply: Define 5-8 named content categories and set them as consistent uppercase kickers above every headline, with an attribution line; the taxonomy becomes scannable navigation and a brand voice at once.

site.name: Magic Spoon - Meta feed ad (appetite macro)

entries.category: Meta feed ad (product macro on brand color)
entries.tagline: One glossy spoonful frozen mid-drip on electric purple - the money shot as the whole ad.
entries.when: Meta feed, 2026 (pulled live from the Meta Ad Library)
entries.summary: A running Magic Spoon unit built on a single dramatic macro: a spoon lifting creamy oatmeal with a syrup drip caught mid-fall, set against a vivid purple-to-magenta gradient. The appetite-appeal texture and frozen drip create implied motion that stops the scroll, the off-food brand color makes the hero pop, and the differentiator (15g protein / 6g fiber / 1g sugar) rides in the caption.
whatWorks: Appetite-appeal macro - glossy texture and a syrup drip as the 'money shot'
A saturated, non-food brand color (purple->magenta) makes the food pop and screams brand recognition
One hero object, zero clutter - the whole frame is the product
The frozen drip creates implied motion inside a static image
Product differentiator (macros) carried cleanly in the caption, not crowding the visual

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: Extreme close-up of the spoonful with a syrup drip caught mid-fall - texture plus frozen motion stops the scroll on craving alone.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: Caption leads with the differentiator: 'reimagined with the macros you expect ... 15g protein. 6g fiber. 1g sugar.'

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: A single hero spoon on a saturated brand-purple gradient; the unexpected background color makes the food read instantly as Magic Spoon.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: Flavor availability ('Maple Brown Sugar, Apple Cinnamon, and Banana...') pulls the viewer toward the shop; the image sells the craving, the copy sells the reason.

principle.title: Freeze the 'money moment' - the pour, the drip, the melt
principle.explanation: A static food or product ad gains implied motion and craving when it captures the peak sensory instant. The mid-drip freeze does more work than a tidy styled bowl ever could.
principle.howToApply: For food/beverage/product creative, shoot the drip/pour/steam mid-action and drop it on a bold off-palette brand color so the hero pops in a busy feed.

entries.tagline: The studio named after a daycare - run as a playground and learning space, not a factory.
entries.summary: Founded by Eike Koenig in 1994 (originally 'Eikes Grafischer Hort', out of music-industry work), Hort takes its name from the German word for a nursery or sanctuary - and means it. The studio is run as a small, individual-led collective and a place to learn, deliberately balancing commercial work with self-initiated projects and teaching. Its output is hand-made, experimental and anti-template, treating every brief as a chance to try something new. (Image: Eike Koenig, centre, with Erik Kessels and Marian Bantjes.)
whatWorks: Run the studio as a learning environment, not a production factory
Protect time for self-initiated work - it becomes the R&D that feeds client work
Choose clients who allow experimentation over pure billing
Keep it small and individual-led - a collective, not a hierarchy
Hold it together with a shared culture of play and curiosity rather than a fixed house style

sections.name: How it's structured
sections.notes: A studio-as-playground/atelier: kept small, a group of designers working as individuals under one roof rather than a hierarchical agency. Framed explicitly as a place to learn and feel at home ('Hort' = nursery/sanctuary).

sections.name: How it takes on work
sections.notes: Selective; favors clients who allow experimentation, and balances paid work with self-initiated projects and teaching (Koenig is a professor). The personal work feeds the commercial work.

sections.name: Signature method
sections.notes: Hand-made, craft-forward, experimental image-making - collage, type, illustration and analog processes; idea-and-play first, every project a chance to try something new instead of reusing a formula.

sections.name: What holds it together
sections.notes: A culture, not a house style: curiosity, play, generosity and learning. The rule of thumb - enjoy the process, protect the freedom to experiment, and share what you learn.

principle.title: Protect self-initiated work - it's the R&D that powers the paid work
principle.explanation: Hort treats personal experiments and teaching as core, not extracurricular. The freedom to play is where new methods and images come from, and those discoveries flow into the client work.
principle.howToApply: Ring-fence regular time for self-directed experiments (a daily design study like this journal counts), let the discoveries feed real projects, and choose clients who reward experimentation.

entries.title: Build one button as a proper auto-layout component set
entries.skill: Auto layout + variants + hug/fill so a component resizes and re-states without manual edits
entries.brief: Rebuild a single button as an auto-layout component with Default / Hover / Pressed / Disabled variants, so it hugs its label and switches states cleanly - no manual resizing anywhere.
steps: Type the label, select it, press Shift+A for Auto Layout. Set padding 12 (top/bottom) x 20 (left/right), gap 8, width Hug, height Hug.
Add a 16px square as a leading icon placeholder to practice gap + vertical-centre alignment.
Convert to a Component (Ctrl/Cmd+Alt+K), then add a Variant property 'State' with values Default / Hover / Pressed / Disabled.
Style each state from the palette below: Default solid, Hover darker, Pressed darkest (nudge content down 1px), Disabled greyed with no interaction.
Set corner radius 8 and a 15/1.2 semibold text style; then swap the label to a very long string and a one-word string and confirm it still hugs correctly.
Drop 3 instances, override the labels, and verify you never had to resize a frame by hand.

assets.label: State recipe
assets.value: Default bg #4B3BFF / text #FFFFFF | Hover bg #3D2FE0 | Pressed bg #2E22B8 (content +1px down) | Disabled bg #E5E4F7 / text #A6A2C4

entries.successLooksLike: Changing the label text never forces a manual width edit, and all four states switch purely by flipping the 'State' variant property.
entries.stretch: Add a second variant property 'Size' (S/M/L) driven only by padding tokens, so one component covers three sizes and four states.

entries.tagline: A tight, on-brand public brand-assets page - it nails the logo system and usage rules, and shows exactly where a press kit stops short of a full brand guide.
entries.summary: Discord's branding page is a model of the public-facing slice of a brand system: logo lockups in three finishes, a symbol-only usage rule, clearspace and minimum-size diagrams, the core Blurple palette with exact values, press banners, and a legal/usage section with Do's and Don'ts - all wrapped in the playful Discord voice, plus a one-click 'View Brand Kit'. It's a great teaching case precisely because of what it deliberately leaves out: it's a press/asset kit, not the full internal guide, so it's missing typography, voice-and-tone rules, brand strategy, and application mockups.
whatWorks: Logo shown as a real system - full logo, symbol-only, and three finishes (color / black / white) - not a single lockup
Rules are shown, not just stated: a clearspace grid diagram and a 1/3 minimum-size marker make the constraints unmistakable
Color given as named, copy-ready values (Blurple #5865F2, Light Blurple #E0E3FF, Black #000000) with a usage note
Do's and Don'ts plus a plain-English legal/trademark section set the guardrails for outsiders
The page is itself on-brand - Blurple, rounded display type, 3D mascots - so it demonstrates the identity while documenting it
One obvious action ('View Brand Kit') routes people to downloadable, ready-to-use assets

sections.name: Hero / Brand Kit
sections.notes: 'BRAND ASSETS - make sure to get our good side' with a single 'View Brand Kit' CTA. Personality up front, one clear next step.

sections.name: Our logo
