sections.notes: The primary logo in color, black and white - establishes approved finishes before anyone improvises.

sections.name: Symbol
sections.notes: Mark-only usage, gated by a rule ('use only when the Discord brand is clearly visible or well established') - a condition, not just an asset.

sections.name: Clearspace & minimum size
sections.notes: A clearspace grid diagram plus a 1/3 min-size marker and 'do not edit, distort, recolor, or reconfigure' - the misuse rules made visual.

sections.name: Colors
sections.notes: Blurple #5865F2, Light Blurple #E0E3FF, Black #000000, each as a copy-ready chip with a light usage note.

sections.name: Banners & press assets
sections.notes: Ready-made illustrated banners 'for discussing Discord', with a link to how to use them.

sections.name: Legal brand guidelines + Do's/Don'ts
sections.notes: Plain-English trademark/permission terms and expandable Do's and Don'ts - the guardrails for third parties.

needs: Typography - no typeface, weights, scale or pairing is specified (a full guide must define type, fallbacks and licensing)
Voice & tone - the personality is shown but not codified into writing rules with do/don't examples
Brand strategy up front - mission, values, personality and audience that explain WHY the rules exist
Imagery & illustration direction - the mascots/banners appear but there's no art-direction spec for photography or illustration
Iconography and a layout/grid system for composing on- and off-brand materials
Real-world application mockups (web, social, product, merch, presentation) beyond press banners
Accessibility guidance - contrast pairings and minimum legibility rules for the palette and logo
Rationale alongside each rule - a great guide teaches the thinking, so people extend it correctly, not just obey it

principle.title: Separate the public brand-assets kit from the full brand guide - and make each complete for its job
principle.explanation: A press/asset page and an internal brand guide have different jobs: the kit protects the mark for outsiders (logo, clearspace, color, don'ts, downloads), while the full guide equips insiders to create (strategy, voice, type, imagery, layout, applications, rationale). Discord's page nails the first job and is honest about not being the second.
principle.howToApply: When you build brand docs, decide which artifact you're making: a public brand-assets kit (mark + usage + downloads, kept short and protective) or a full brand guide (strategy -> verbal -> visual -> applications -> governance, with the WHY next to every rule). Don't ship a half-built guide as if it were either.

entries.tagline: A brand hub that leads with law rather than layout - it tells you what you may not do with the Insignia before it shows you a single swatch.
entries.summary: The NASA Brand Center is a permissions and usage-rights gateway for 'partners, brands and vendors working with NASA', not a visual standards document. It routes to four approval tracks (Images & Media, Film & Documentary, Merchandise, Strategic Partnerships), then spends most of its length on plain-language legal sections: Restrictions, Linking to NASA Websites, NASA Contractors and Partners, and Non-Fungible Tokens. The actual visual system - the Insignia, Logotype (Worm) and Seal construction rules - sits behind a single 'Learn More' link under NASA Graphic Standards, so the page you land on is honestly thin on design specifics. What it does better than almost any corporate guide is accountability: the footer carries 'Page Last Updated: Sep 28, 2024', 'Page Editor: Karen Northon' and 'Responsible NASA Official: Abigail Bowman'.
whatWorks: States the single most misunderstood fact up front in a NOTE block: 'The NASA Insignia, Logotype, identifiers, and imagery are not in the public domain.'
Cites its actual authority rather than asserting taste - use of the Insignia, Seal and Logotype is governed by 'the Code of Federal Regulations 14 CFR 1221 and the NASA Space Act of 1958 as amended'
Splits usage into four self-selecting approval tracks with photo cards, so a merchandiser and a documentary producer never read each other's rules
Writes restrictions as concrete scenarios, not abstractions: no implied endorsement, no 'NASA approved' or 'official NASA' wording, no NASA identifiers as trade dress by contractors, no NFTs

Handles the awkward edge cases most guides skip - recognizable former astronauts (right of privacy/publicity), third-party music in NASA audiovisual material, incidental identifiers on vehicles and spacecraft
Names a human owner, an editor and a last-updated date in the footer, which makes the guide auditable and clearly living

sections.name: NASA Brand Center intro
sections.notes: Full-bleed hero over the Insignia with a one-line scope statement: 'Guidelines, best practices, and resources for partners, brands and vendors working with NASA.' Sets audience immediately, which is more than most guides do.

sections.name: NASA Merchandise and Media Guidelines
sections.notes: Four photo cards - Images & Media Usage, Film & Documentary, Merchandise Approvals, Strategic Partnerships - each with a one-sentence purpose and a link out. Good routing, but every card leaves the page, so nothing is answered in place.

sections.name: NASA Graphic Standards
sections.notes: The only visual-identity section, and it is a teaser: one paragraph about the Insignia and Logotype plus 'Learn More'. This is where clearspace, color and type actually live, and none of it is on this page.

sections.name: Additional Guidelines
sections.notes: A four-item accordion index (Additional Restrictions, NFTs, Linking to NASA websites, Contractors and Partners) that jumps to the long-form sections below. Simple and effective navigation for a legal wall of text.

sections.name: Restrictions
sections.notes: The substantive core. About a dozen numbered-in-spirit conditions covering endorsement, false copyright claims, indemnity, third-party copyright, and recognizable persons. Dense but genuinely readable prose, not boilerplate.

sections.name: Linking to NASA Websites
sections.notes: Permits linking without explicit permission but bars using NASA images as 'hot links' for commercial goods or services, and requires acknowledging NASA as the source. A rule most brand pages forget entirely.

sections.name: Contractors and Partners / NFTs
sections.notes: Two short, unambiguous prohibitions: identifiers may not be used as branding devices or trade dress by third parties, and NASA does not approve NFTs or merchandising involving them. Dated-feeling topic, but a good example of the guide answering a live question.

needs: Any visual evidence at all on the landing page - no clearspace diagram, no minimum size, no Insignia vs Logotype vs Seal comparison, no misuse examples
Exact color values for NASA Red, Insignia Blue and the Logotype, in HEX/RGB/CMYK/Pantone, copy-ready
Typography: no mention of a display or body typeface, licensing, or the type pairing used across NASA properties
Downloadable asset package - the page describes what you may do with the marks but never hands you a correctly built file
A do/don't image pair for the highest-risk cases the copy describes, especially implied endorsement and merchandise
A version number on the standards themselves, not just a last-edited date on the web page

principle.title: Put a named owner and a date on the guide
principle.explanation: A brand guide with no visible owner and no date is unenforceable and quietly rots - people stop trusting it, fork their own version, and nobody knows which is current. NASA's footer names a page editor and a responsible official, so a partner with an edge case knows exactly whose desk the question lands on.
principle.howToApply: Add a persistent footer block to the 35353 brand guide with three fields: version number, last-updated date, and a named owner with contact. Render it from a single source (a JSON or frontmatter field) so it cannot drift out of sync with the content.

entries.tagline: Almost every rule on the page is a captioned picture, and the six-panel logo don'ts grid is the cleanest misuse spread in this batch.
entries.summary: Asana calls this page 'Asana brand guidelines' but it behaves as a public assets and trademark kit: five visual sections (Logo, Clearspace, Color, Logo don'ts, Partnerships) followed by three blocks of legal copy, with the real document behind a 'Download brand guidelines' button. Within that narrow scope it is excellent - the layout is a strict two-up image grid where each panel carries its own caption, so you read the rule and see it in the same glance. The gap is the one thing a stranger most needs: there are no hex values anywhere, only the words 'coral', 'black', 'white' and 'light grey', so nobody can actually reproduce the palette from this page. Footer notes it was last updated June 25, 2025.
whatWorks: Shows the logo as a system, not a file: horizontal lockup declared primary 'for most communications', vertical lockup reserved for 'space or size constraints'
Clearspace given as two annotated diagrams with red measurement guides and a memorable rule - clear space 'is equal to the height of the symbol'

Six-panel Logo don'ts grid, each panel a real rendered violation with a red diagonal strike: past versions, recolored, drop shadows/effects, symbol alone, secondary color background, wordmark without the symbol
Color section is behavioral rather than decorative - one light panel and one black panel showing exactly how the wordmark flips to white while the symbol stays coral
Partnerships section handles co-branding with a spacing rule that references the brand's own asset: 'the space between the logos should be the width of Asana's three dots symbol'
Every caption is one or two sentences directly under its image, so no rule requires scrolling away from its example

sections.name: Header / Download brand guidelines
sections.notes: Short intro - 'Download this simple kit to learn more about using the Asana logo in conjunction with our trademark guidelines' - plus a single black CTA button. Honest framing: this page is the summary, the kit is the artifact.

sections.name: Logo
sections.notes: Two panels, horizontal and vertical lockup, with primary/secondary use stated in the captions. Complete for a press kit. No mark-only or favicon/app-icon variant shown, which matters because the symbol-alone use is explicitly banned later.

sections.name: Clearspace
sections.notes: Strongest section. Two measured diagrams, one per lockup, with the symbol-height rule and a nudge that 'in most cases, the logo should be given even more room'. This is show-don't-tell done right.

sections.name: Color
sections.notes: Weakest section relative to its importance. Demonstrates light-background and dark-background logo treatment well, but names colors only in words (coral, black, white, light grey) with zero HEX, RGB, CMYK or Pantone values.

sections.name: Logo don'ts
sections.notes: Six rendered violations in a 2x3 grid. Notably each don't maps back to a rule stated earlier, so the section reads as enforcement rather than a random list of prohibitions.

sections.name: Partnerships
sections.notes: Two co-branding lockups with Morningstar showing horizontal and stacked arrangements, plus rules on optical balance, equal size, and Asana positioned left of or above the partner mark.

sections.name: Trademark Guidelines / Brand Assets / How to use (and how to not use) Asana brand assets
sections.notes: Three dense legal blocks at the bottom - license scope, what counts as a Brand Asset (wordmark, both lockups, three-dot symbol, slogans, taglines), and permitted vs prohibited use. Thorough, and it ends with a contact route for questions.

needs: Exact color values - HEX at minimum - for Asana coral and the neutral greys; the page currently cannot be used to build anything
Minimum size for both lockups; clearspace is specified but reproduction floor is not
Favicon / app-icon and social avatar guidance, which is the real-world reason people reach for the symbol alone that the guide bans
Approved contrast pairings, especially coral on white and coral on black, given how much of the page is about background behavior
File formats and what is actually inside the downloadable kit, so the reader knows whether to click before clicking
A version number on the kit itself rather than only a 'Last Updated' date on the web page

principle.title: Render every don't as a picture, never a sentence
principle.explanation: Written prohibitions get skimmed and reinterpreted; a rendered violation with a strike through it is unarguable and takes half a second to absorb. Asana's six-panel grid also forces the guide's authors to be exhaustive, because you cannot draw a vague don't.
principle.howToApply: For the 35353 logo page, build a misuse grid as real markup: one card per violation, the actual mark rendered wrong inside it, a strike overlay, and a single-line caption. Generate it from the same component the correct logo uses so the violations stay accurate when the mark changes.

entries.tagline: The only guide in this batch that publishes its reasoning as by-lined editorial - every guideline card credits a named designer, so rules arrive with an author.
entries.summary: GEL is the BBC's standards manual for digital experiences, and the captured page is its portal rather than the standards themselves. The top nav splits the whole system into Home, Guidelines, Articles, Playbooks and About UX&D, with a separate 'BBC Staff' entry indicating internal-only material. Instead of opening on swatches, it opens on an introduction - 'Welcome to BBC UX&D. We do the layer between people and technology' - then leads with thinking: a Creative decision making playbook, Motion Design Principles, 'Cognitive biases - Thinking fast and slow', and 'How to write useful error messages'. The visual foundations are reached through an 'Essentials' rail (GEL Icons: Reith Suite, Spacing Units) rather than displayed inline, so as a capture this is a table of contents, not the manual - judge it as such.
whatWorks: Every guideline and article card carries an author and role - Andrew Nott, UX Creative Director on GEL Icons: Reith Suite; Sareh Heidari, Software Engineer on Spacing Units - which makes the system accountable and approachable

Cards are typed by content class in a small label under each one ('Guidelines: Foundations', 'Guidelines: How-tos', 'Playbooks', 'Motion Design Principles', 'Articles'), so you always know whether you are reading a rule or an opinion
Separates foundations from how-tos: 'GEL Icons: Reith Suite' and 'Spacing Units' sit as Foundations while 'How to design a voice experience' and 'How to design for children' sit as How-tos
Covers non-visual surfaces most brand guides ignore entirely - voice experience design, motion design principles, error message copy
Treats accessibility and inclusion as first-class content, not an appendix: a 'BBC for everyone' piece authored by a Principal Accessibility lead, plus 'How to design for children'
The site is itself on-brand - BBC three-box logo, Reith-style typography, saturated full-bleed color blocks, and a strict card grid that demonstrates the spacing discipline it teaches
Includes a Studio Culture collection about team process, acknowledging that consistent output depends on how the team works, not only on rules

sections.name: GEL top nav (Home, Guidelines, Articles, Playbooks, About UX&D, BBC Staff)
sections.notes: The information architecture in one bar, and the clearest thing on the page. Guidelines is a dropdown; the padlocked 'BBC Staff' item signals that some of the system is internal only.

sections.name: Welcome / introduction banner
sections.notes: Dismissible blue panel with an illustration and a plain-language positioning line about UX&D. Warm and unusual for a standards site, though it says what the team is rather than what the language is.

sections.name: Featured articles and playbooks
sections.notes: Seven-card grid led by 'The Futures Bazaar: A Public Imagination Toolkit', with Creative decision making playbook, Motion Design Principles and 'How to write useful error messages' alongside. Strong signal that GEL leads with reasoning.

sections.name: Studio Culture collection
sections.notes: Full-bleed dark-purple collection block about 'the approaches, processes and tools we use to create a positive team culture'. Good inclusion, but the summary text is duplicated verbatim on the later Story block, which reads as an editing slip.

sections.name: What we do
sections.notes: Four cards including 'What is UX&D?' and a 1:41 video 'What is GEL?'. Video-first onboarding for newcomers, with honest documentary-style photography rather than stock.

sections.name: Essentials
sections.notes: 'Some of the main tools we use to design digital experiences' - GEL Icons: Reith Suite, Spacing Units, How to design a voice experience, How to design for children. This is the closest the page gets to foundations, and it is only four links deep.

sections.name: We want you! / careers
sections.notes: Recruiting block routing to BBC Careers. Reasonable for a team-owned site, but it takes the terminal position on the page that a color or typography entry point should own.

needs: Foundations surfaced on the landing page - typography, colour and grid are the three things every reader arrives for and none appear in the capture
Copy-ready values: no HEX, no type scale, no spacing token names visible without navigating away
A logo section for the BBC blocks themselves, with clearspace and minimum size, rather than assuming the mark is known
A clear statement of which parts are public and which need the BBC Staff sign-in, so external readers know the boundary before hitting a wall
Version and last-reviewed dates on individual guidelines - several featured items reference 2021 and 2022 and read as stale in 2026
Downloadable assets: the Reith Suite icon set and Reith typefaces are named but no download or licensing route is visible from here

principle.title: Publish the reasoning as first-class content beside the rules
principle.explanation: Rules alone tell people what to obey; the reasoning tells them how to extend the system into cases the guide never anticipated. GEL gives principles, playbooks and articles the same visual weight as the guidelines and puts a named author on each, which turns a rulebook into a body of knowledge people actually cite.
principle.howToApply: Add a 'Thinking' section to the 35353 brand guide sitting at the same nav level as Logo and Color. Seed it with two short by-lined pieces - why the palette is built the way it is, and how to decide when a new component needs a new color role - and label every page with its content class so readers know rule from opinion.

entries.tagline: Written entirely in the brand's own voice - the misuse section is headed 'Please don't', and it lands harder than any 'Prohibited Uses' block would.
entries.summary: A short, deliberately protective press kit: Our name, Our logo, Our colors, The fine print, Download, then a Brand Assets FAQ. It opens on a Cavendish Yellow band with a sentence that sets the tone for everything after it - 'Thanks for your interest in Mailchimp. We have these guidelines for using our brand resources. Please take a moment to familiarize yourself with them.' The standout move is that the guide performs the identity while explaining it: friendly second person, 'Freddie's always winking because he has a great attitude', 'The fine print' as a heading, 'Please do' and 'Please don't' instead of usage and misuse. The trade-off is scope - two colors, one lockup, no typography, no clearspace measurement, so it is thin as a guide and complete as a kit.
whatWorks: Leads with the name before the mark - 'Mailchimp is one word, spelled with a big M and a little c' - plus a link to 'the times have changed', which catches the single most common brand error journalists make
Shows the logo on light and on dark, then puts a red-X and a green-check pair side by side so the reverse-version rule is settled in one glance
Palette is copy-ready and honestly ranked: Cavendish Yellow (#FFE01B) is named 'Mailchimp's hero color' and Peppercorn (#241C15) is explicitly 'for accents'
Reframes legal as brand voice - 'The fine print' introduced as 'a friendly legal reminder that these graphics are proprietary and protected under intellectual property laws'
The clearspace rule is phrased as behavior rather than geometry: 'Make them big, make them small, just give them the chance to breathe and not feel cluttered'
Ships assets immediately - EPS and PNG downloads with one condition attached, 'Please don't alter the Mailchimp logo'
The Brand Assets FAQ is a genuinely useful bonus: four plain-language answers on what brand assets are, how to develop them, how to protect a brand, and how to stand out

sections.name: Our name
sections.notes: Two sentences, and the most valuable content on the page. Capitalization is the rule most often broken and most easily fixed, so putting it first is a smart ordering choice.

sections.name: Our logo
sections.notes: Three panels: the Intuit Mailchimp lockup on light grey, the reverse version on black, then a strike/check pair. Covers the co-brand reality of the Intuit lockup, but only one configuration - no stacked, mark-only, or Freddie-alone variant.

sections.name: Our colors
sections.notes: Two large color circles with the hex printed inside each, plus a one-line usage ratio (hero vs accent). Minimal but actionable, and the roles are stated rather than implied.

sections.name: The fine print
sections.notes: One short paragraph asserting IP ownership, in brand voice. Far shorter than Asana's or NASA's legal copy and correspondingly easier to actually read.

sections.name: Please do
sections.notes: A single instruction about breathing room around the logo and Freddie. Charming and memorable, but it is a feeling where a diagram should be.

sections.name: Please don't
sections.notes: Four tight bullets: no altering files, no implying relationship or endorsement, no use in your own product or business name, no combining with other graphics without written consent. Each is a distinct failure mode, none overlap.

sections.name: Download / Brand Assets FAQ
sections.notes: EPS and PNG links, then four expanded FAQ answers. The FAQ is educational content about branding in general rather than about Mailchimp, which is generous and also slightly off-topic for a press kit.

needs: A measured clearspace diagram and a minimum size - 'give them room to breathe' is unenforceable and every other rule on the page is specific
Typography: no display or body typeface named, no fallback, no licensing note
Rendered misuse examples for the four 'Please don't' bullets; the logo section proves they know how to do strike/check pairs and then does not reuse the pattern
Contrast guidance for Cavendish Yellow, which fails as a text color on white and is the brand's hero color - the single most likely accessibility mistake here
More of the logo system: stacked lockup, Freddie mark alone, favicon and social avatar specs
A version number and last-reviewed date; the page carries neither, so there is no way to tell whether the Intuit lockup shown is current

principle.title: Write the guide in the brand's own voice
principle.explanation: A guide written in neutral corporate register teaches people the rules and nothing about the personality behind them. Mailchimp's headings - 'The fine print', 'Please do', 'Please don't' - mean the reader absorbs the tone of voice by reading the tone-of-voice-free sections, and the document doubles as the best available sample of how the brand talks.
principle.howToApply: Rewrite the 35353 guide's section headings and rule captions in the product's actual voice instead of default labels: replace 'Misuse' and 'Prohibited' with phrasing a real 35353 page would use, and add one voice sample per section so the guide demonstrates the verbal identity even though it is a visual document.

entries.tagline: It defines the brand layer as a set of swappable styles rather than fixed values - the opening line is that these 'can be customized by changing your Material theme'.
entries.summary: Material Design 3's Styles index is the brand layer of a design system, and it declares that intent in its first sentence: 'Styles are the visual aspects of a UI that give it a distinct look and feel. They can be customized by changing your Material theme.' Structurally it is a card index into the individual style domains, with Color and Elevation the first two, sitting inside a persistent left rail that separates Get started, Develop, Foundations, Styles and Components. Two caveats on this capture: the page is JavaScript-rendered so WebFetch returned only the page title, and the screenshot is short (about 125 KB) covering the hero and the first card row - so the assessment below is based on the visible index and navigation, not on the individual style pages behind it.
whatWorks: Frames the visual layer as parameterized rather than prescribed, which is the inversion that lets one system carry many brands - the opposite stance from every press kit in this batch
Separates Foundations, Styles and Components as sibling nav items, so 'how it looks', 'why it behaves that way' and 'what you build with' never blur together
Each style card leads with a purpose sentence, not a value: Color is 'used to express style and communicate meaning', Elevation is 'the relative distance between two surfaces along the z-axis'

Names dynamic color explicitly on the index - Material 'puts personal color preferences and individual needs at the forefront of systematic color application' - so personalization is presented as a system property, not a feature
Elevation is treated as a first-class style with the promise that 'all surfaces and components have elevation values', which is a token commitment rather than a visual suggestion
The page ships two persistent viewer controls in the lower-left rail, a motion toggle and a light/dark toggle, so the documentation practices the accessibility and theming it documents
Abstract color-blob artwork per card gives each style domain a recognizable identity without pretending to be a product screenshot

sections.name: Left nav rail (Home, Get started, Develop, Foundations, Styles, Components, Blog)
sections.notes: Persistent icon-plus-label rail with Styles active. Clean separation of audience tracks - Develop for engineers, Foundations for principles, Styles for the brand layer. Search sits at the top of the rail.

sections.name: Styles overview
sections.notes: Dark hero card with a large 'Styles' heading and a three-line scope statement ending on theme customization. Concise and correctly scoped: it defines the category before listing its members.

sections.name: Color
sections.notes: First card. Purpose-led description covering expression, meaning, and dynamic color. The index entry is strong; everything actionable - roles, tonal palettes, schemes - is one click away and not visible in this capture.

sections.name: Elevation
sections.notes: Second card, defined geometrically as z-axis distance between surfaces with a values commitment. Notable because most brand guides omit elevation entirely or reduce it to a shadow preset.

sections.name: Remaining style cards
sections.notes: A further row begins below the fold with the same card treatment; the capture cuts off before their titles, so the full Styles set is not verifiable from this screenshot.

sections.name: Viewer controls (motion and theme toggles)
sections.notes: Two floating circular buttons pinned lower-left. Small but meaningful - the docs let you see the system in the mode you ship in, which is exactly what a themeable brand layer should let you do.

needs: Any logo or wordmark guidance - this is a brand layer with no brand mark, so it cannot stand alone as a brand guide for a product built on it
Verbal identity: no voice, tone, or content-mechanics entry point anywhere in the Styles nav
Values on the index itself; every card is a purpose statement, so nothing is copy-ready without navigating one level deeper
An explicit contrast and accessibility statement on the Styles landing page rather than only inside Foundations
A visible version indicator - Material 3 versus Material 3 Expressive is a real distinction and the page does not date itself
Application mockups on the index showing a themed product in context, so the reader can see what customizing the theme actually produces

principle.title: Express the brand layer as tokens so it can be re-themed
principle.explanation: When color, elevation and type are stated as named roles rather than fixed values, one system can carry several brands, a dark mode, a high-contrast mode and a partner skin without forking. Material puts that first: the styles are the theme's parameters, and the theme is the thing you change.
principle.howToApply: Restate the 35353 brand guide's visual sections as role names bound to values - surface, surface-raised, text-primary, accent, accent-pressed - and publish the value table per theme (light, dark) rather than as a single flat swatch list. Then have the guide read its swatches from the same token file the app imports, so the document cannot drift from the build.

entries.tagline: Three named voice principles get a per-channel volume dial, so 'be witty' never leaks into a fraud alert.
entries.summary: Monzo's public writing-principles page covers one slice of the brand - verbal identity - and covers it unusually deeply: three principles (Straightforward Kindness, Everyday Magic, Warm Wit), each broken into concrete sub-rules with real example wording. The capture is a very tall mint-green page with playful spot illustrations and do/don't cards that themselves demonstrate the voice. As a verbal guide it is close to complete; it just floats free of the rest of the brand system, with no visual-identity links, no downloads, and no version or date.
whatWorks: The 'How we sound across channels' matrix sets each principle to a level per context - operational comms get Straightforward Kindness 'Maxed out' and Warm Wit 'None', organic social gets Warm Wit 'Maxed out'
Rules come with exact replacement wording: say 'We're sorry' not 'We'd like to apologise', use 'blocklist' instead of 'blacklist'
Cites real research next to rules - Boroditsky's 2009 framing experiment, Flammer's 2010 study where judges preferred plain-English arguments 66% to 34%, Pinker's 'curse of knowledge'
Anti-rules are as specific as the rules: 'Don't make literal references to magic' (no 'hey presto'), no puns you've heard ten times before ('Eggcellent' at Easter is called out by name)
A 'brief history of professional English' section explains why formal Latin-rooted business language reads cold, so writers understand the reasoning behind the word swaps
The page's own copy and illustrations perform the three principles while teaching them

sections.name: Monzo Writing Principles (intro)
sections.notes: Frames the stakes - banking via phone means every word matters - and names the three principles up front.

sections.name: Our principles in brief
sections.notes: Quick-reference card row summarizing when each principle applies; good skim layer before the deep dive.

sections.name: Straightforward Kindness
sections.notes: Nine sub-rules covering reader focus, inclusive language, jargon, active voice, and sincere apologies, each with examples and research citations. The strongest section.

sections.name: Everyday Magic
sections.notes: Eight sub-rules on delight: vivid word choice ('tame' your bills), relatable money moments, handling money stress with care, and which cultural references are fair game (Barbie, Olympics - not politics).

sections.name: Warm Wit
sections.notes: Five sub-rules on humour: punch-up-only, 'a pinch of humour, not a dollop', smart asides over cheap puns, confident but never arrogant.

sections.name: How we sound across channels
sections.notes: Channel-by-channel matrix from operational comms to organic social with explicit intensity levels for all three principles. The most reusable artifact on the page.

needs: Any bridge to the visual identity - no logo, color, or typography links, so the verbal system floats disconnected from the rest of the brand
Messaging pillars, tagline, and boilerplate - principles are covered but the actual core messages are not
Content mechanics: naming conventions, capitalization, number and currency formatting rules a writer needs daily
A version number, date, or owner - no way to know if this is current
Downloadable or copyable artifacts (checklist, examples library) so writers can act without re-reading the whole page
Voice examples for hard moments beyond apologies - declined payments, account closures - where tone matters most

principle.title: Give every voice principle a volume dial per channel
principle.explanation: A single voice description fails at the edges: the same brand must be plain in a fraud alert and playful on TikTok. Monzo solves this with an explicit matrix - each principle gets an intensity level per channel - so writers never have to guess how much personality a context can carry.
principle.howToApply: When writing voice guidance for a future build (35353 included), end with a channel matrix: rows for contexts (transactional email, error states, marketing pages, social), columns for each voice trait, cells set to none/low/medium/high. Wire error-state copy reviews to that row, not to the general voice page.

entries.tagline: A one-line ethos ('Build Bonds') on top, a wall of downloadable starter kits underneath - philosophy and tooling on the same page.
entries.summary: The IBM Design Language homepage is the brand layer that sits above Carbon: a left rail runs Philosophy through Typography, Color, 2x Grid, IBM logos, Iconography, Illustration, Photography, Data visualization, Infographics, Layout, and Animation. The page states the ethos in three sentences ('Build Bonds... every experience Designed by IBM'), then routes straight to tools: Plex releases, color specifications, icon and pictogram resources, illustration starter kits, Carbon design kits. Judged as a hub it is excellent and visibly maintained (footer: 'Last updated 16 July 2026'); the live site blocked WebFetch (403), so this entry is based on the capture, which shows the homepage only.
whatWorks: The nav doubles as a completeness checklist - twelve foundation areas including ones most guides skip entirely: Data visualization, Infographics, Animation

'Tools, templates and assets' is a first-class section, not a footer link: IBM Plex typeface latest release, IBM color specifications, 2x Grid for video, UI icon resources, Pictogram resources, Illustration starter kits, Carbon design kits
A 'What's new' feed with dated releases (IBM Plex Sans Chinese SC - December 2024, IBM Plex Math - September 2024) proves the language is alive, not archived
Governance is concrete: footer gives 'Last updated 16 July 2026', a Slack channel (#ibm-brand) for internal users, and an inquiry form for everyone else

Entry tiles preview each foundation in its own medium - a construction-drawing Q for Typeface, a swatch grid of greens/teals/blues for Color, nested rectangles for the 2x Grid - so the index itself is on-brand
Sequential 'Next: Philosophy - Point of view' footer link turns a reference site into a guided read

sections.name: Gallery hero
sections.notes: Full-width video/photo banner with Philosophy and Gallery entry points layered over IBM Q hardware imagery; sets a technical, confident register immediately.

sections.name: Philosophy statement ('Build Bonds')
sections.notes: Three sentences naming the guiding ethos behind everything 'Designed by IBM'. Present and prominent, though the homepage gives only the headline of the why - the reasoning lives a click deeper.

sections.name: Foundation tiles (Typeface, Philosophy, Color, Photography, Illustration, 2x Grid)
sections.notes: Six visual entry cards, each rendered in the style of its subject. Strong wayfinding, deliberately unequal sizes.

sections.name: Tools, templates and assets
sections.notes: Eight-item download/link grid including Plex releases, color specs, icon and pictogram resources, and Carbon design kits. The bridge from rules to action.

sections.name: What's new
sections.notes: Three dated release cards for Plex font expansions. Doubles as proof of maintenance.

sections.name: Footer governance
sections.notes: 'Last updated 16 July 2026', copyright, Slack #ibm-brand for internal questions, inquiry form for external - a real support path, not a dead mailto.

needs: Verbal identity - no voice, tone, or writing guidance appears anywhere in the twelve-section nav
Accessibility surfaced at the top level - no contrast or WCAG mention on the homepage despite Color being a pillar
Do/don't examples at the hub level - the homepage shows zero misuse guidance; a stranger must dig for the rules
Application mockups (social specs, email, print) - the language covers foundations deeply but the homepage shows nothing about where they land
Strategy beyond the ethos line - audience, positioning, and personality attributes are absent or buried
A public path for the 403 problem - the guide is publicly linked but the server blocks non-browser access, which hurts tool integrations

principle.title: Ship starter kits beside the rules
principle.explanation: A guide that only describes correct usage forces every reader to rebuild assets from prose, and every rebuild drifts. IBM puts downloadable kits - fonts, color specs, icon sets, illustration starters, design kits - on the same page as the philosophy, so the fastest path to compliance is also the easiest one.
principle.howToApply: For the 35353 brand guide, pair every foundation page with a grab-and-go artifact: the color page links the token file, the logo page links the SVG package, the type page links the font files with licensing. Rule of thumb - no section ships until its kit does.

entries.tagline: Spells out the exact four circumstances in which the Shopping Bag may stand alone - most kits leave symbol-only use to guesswork.
entries.summary: A tight, protective public assets kit: one page running Primary logo, Monotone logos, The Shopping Bag, Clear space, Minimum size, Best practices, and Trademark Usage Guidelines, with a download button per section plus a master 'Download all brand assets'. Within its logo-protection job it is nearly airtight - clearspace in the mark's own units, split digital/print minimums, nine pictured don'ts. But it is logo-only: no color values, no typography, and it ends in a 'Start your 3-day free trial today!' sales CTA that does not belong in a brand kit.
whatWorks: 'The Shopping Bag' section lists the exact conditions for symbol-only use: when logo legibility is compromised, when a full-color logo is nearby, when the brand is already established, and when space is extremely limited (square/circle slots)
Clearspace is defined in the mark's own anatomy - 'X = the x-height of the wordmark' for the logo, half an S for the bag - so it scales with any reproduction size
Minimum size is split by medium with real numbers: 80px wide digital, 28mm wide print

Nine don'ts rendered as actual broken logos with red-X captions: don't use the old logo, don't use the wordmark alone, don't stretch or squeeze it, don't rotate it, don't use busy backgrounds, don't use against low-contrast, don't use gradients or shadows, don't stack the logo, don't create your own version
Catches the subtle rule a stranger would get wrong: 'the S on The Shopping Bag is always white, regardless of background color'
Monotone section explains when to downgrade from full color (single-color printing budgets, patterned or low-contrast backgrounds), not just that monotone versions exist

sections.name: Using our brand (intro)
sections.notes: One-line purpose, master 'Download all brand assets' button, and an acceptance clause - using the assets means accepting the Trademark Usage Guidelines.

sections.name: Primary logo
sections.notes: Full-color and inverted versions side by side with usage notes and a dedicated 'Download primary logos' button. Clean and unambiguous.

sections.name: Monotone logos
sections.notes: Black and white variants with the conditions that trigger them; notes the monotone bag has a gap the full-color one lacks.

sections.name: The Shopping Bag
sections.notes: Standalone-mark rules with four explicit qualifying circumstances and its own download. The standout section.

sections.name: Clear space
sections.notes: Measured diagrams for both lockup and bag, defined relative to the mark itself (X = x-height, 1/2 S).

sections.name: Minimum size
sections.notes: Digital 80px / print 28mm, each shown as a rendered specimen rather than just a number.

sections.name: Best practices
sections.notes: Nine-cell grid of pictured misuses, every cell a red-X caption starting with 'Don't'. Comprehensive for logo abuse.

sections.name: Trademark Usage Guidelines
sections.notes: Plain-English legal terms: written authorization required, no implied sponsorship, goodwill accrues to Shopify, no illicit or deceptive contexts.

needs: Color values - the Shopify green is never specified anywhere on the page; a partner cannot reproduce it without eyedropping the logo
Typography - no typeface is named even for partner co-branding contexts
Co-branding and partner lockup rules, the single most common real-world request against a public kit
In-context application examples (app icon, favicon, social avatar crops) showing the bag in the square/circle slots the copy mentions
A version number or last-updated date - 'don't use the old logo' implies history, but nothing tells you this page is current
An on-artifact ending - the closing 'Start your 3-day free trial today!' funnel CTA undermines the kit's authority as a reference document

principle.title: Write explicit conditions for when the symbol stands alone
principle.explanation: Symbol-only use is where most third-party logo abuse actually happens, and most kits either forbid it outright or stay silent. Shopify enumerates the four qualifying circumstances, which turns the fuzziest judgment call in logo usage into a checklist anyone can apply.
principle.howToApply: When the 35353 mark gets a symbol/monogram variant, publish a numbered 'when the mark may appear alone' list (small sizes, adjacent full lockup, established context, constrained slots) with a pictured example of each - and pair it with the minimum size at which the full lockup must return.

entries.tagline: States its entire job in one sentence - 'Make government services look and feel like GOV.UK' - then defends it with concrete prohibitions.
entries.summary: The capture is thin - just the Styles index page (157 KB), a short intro plus a link list - so this entry judges the hub, not the subpages behind it. Even so, the page does two things brilliantly: it compresses the mission into one sentence and immediately fences the edges ('do not assign new meanings to colours, do not change the style of buttons or adjust the thickness of borders on form inputs'). The index maps a styles layer of Page structure, Typography (seven subpages), and Visual elements (Colour, Images), and the Colour subpage confirms depth: colours ship as Sass functions with explicit WCAG 2.2 AA requirements.
whatWorks: The one-sentence job description - 'Make government services look and feel like GOV.UK.' - is the entire strategy section, and it is enough for this artifact
Prohibitions are specific behaviors, not vibes: 'do not assign new meanings to colours, do not change the style of buttons or adjust the thickness of borders on form inputs'
Routes readers to the Prototype Kit and GOV.UK Frontend first, so most teams never hand-copy styles at all - compliance is the default path
The Colour subpage forbids copying hex values ('use govuk-functional-colour("brand") rather than #1d70b8') so services inherit palette updates automatically
Accessibility is a hard requirement with a named standard: contrast must meet WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 level AA
Footer governance is real: 'Contact the team', accessibility statement, and everything published under the Open Government Licence v3.0

sections.name: Styles intro
sections.notes: Mission sentence, tooling route (Prototype Kit / Frontend), and the do-not-deviate conventions paragraph. Three short paragraphs doing the work of a strategy chapter.

sections.name: Page structure
sections.notes: Index links to Page template, Layout, Spacing, and Section break - the skeleton before any styling.

sections.name: Typography
sections.notes: Seven subpages listed: Typeface, Type scale, Headings, Paragraphs, Links, Lists, Font override classes. Granular, engineering-ready decomposition.

sections.name: Visual elements
sections.notes: Just Colour and Images at this level; the Colour subpage delivers functional colours as Sass functions with a full web palette and WCAG 2.2 AA rules.

sections.name: Footer governance
sections.notes: Accessibility statement, sitemap, 'Contact the team', built-by attribution, OGL v3.0 licence, Crown copyright. Ownership is unambiguous.

needs: The index page itself shows no visual examples - zero swatches, specimens, or diagrams before the click-through; the capture is honest about how bare the hub is
Logo and crest usage rules - the GOV.UK identity mark and Crown are used in the header but never explained at this level
Imagery and art direction beyond a bare 'Images' link - no photography or illustration stance
Voice and tone - verbal identity lives in a separate GOV.UK content style guide and is not even cross-linked from Styles
A version number or last-updated date on the page (releases are versioned in Frontend, but the guide page itself is undated)
Motion principles - no animation or transition guidance anywhere in the styles map

principle.title: Open with the one-sentence job
principle.explanation: Every downstream rule in a guide is easier to interpret, extend, and arbitrate when the artifact declares its single purpose up front. GOV.UK's whole styles layer hangs off one sentence, which lets even the prohibitions read as protecting a goal rather than enforcing taste.
principle.howToApply: Start the 35353 brand guide (and each major section) with one sentence naming what the section exists to make true - e.g. 'Make every 35353 surface instantly recognizable as 35353' - and reject any rule that cannot be traced back to that sentence.

entries.tagline: The homepage is organized around 'I would like to ...' reader tasks instead of the usual asset taxonomy.
entries.summary: Stanford's Identity Guide homepage is a wayfinding layer for a genuinely full institutional guide - the nav runs Brand (Brand Statement, Voice and Tone, Messaging), Visual Identity, Design Elements (Color, Typography, Photography, Graphic Elements, Iconography), Digital, Print, and Resources. Its signature move is a six-card 'I would like to ...' grid that routes people by intent: order business cards, align my website, generate a department logo package. The footer is unusually candid about governance: the creative elements 'are not mandates, but tools to aid strong, cohesive communications.' As a homepage it is excellent wayfinding; no actual specs (hex, typefaces) surface at this level.
whatWorks: The 'I would like to ...' grid names six real jobs - order business cards, learn primary brand elements, align my website, develop a mobile app, create a unit's social profile, generate a department logo package - and routes each in one click
Self-service tooling built into the guide: a logo generator that outputs a department logo file package, and pre-approved iOS/Android templates for app teams
Two contact routes split by question type: DesignIdentity@stanford.edu for visual brand identity, trademark_licensing@stanford.edu for branded merchandise
Full-pillar coverage in the nav, including verbal identity (Brand Statement, Voice and Tone, Messaging) that most university guides skip
Honest governance stance stated in the footer: elements 'are not mandates, but tools' - it tells decentralized schools and units exactly what kind of authority the guide claims
The rolling green-and-blue foothills graphic between content and footer quietly performs the brand's sense of place instead of using a stock divider

sections.name: Hero + quick links
sections.notes: Campus photography under 'Identity guidelines & best practices that inspire and align Stanford communications', with five icon shortcuts: Colors, Typography, Stanford Logos, Web Design, Templates.

sections.name: I would like to ... (task grid)
sections.notes: Six intent-based cards with icons, descriptions, and Learn more links. The page's structural idea and its best feature.

sections.name: Main navigation (Brand / Visual Identity / Design Elements / Digital / Print / Resources)
sections.notes: Deep dropdowns confirm a complete guide behind the homepage: voice and messaging under Brand, photography and iconography under Design Elements, email signatures and social under Digital, swag and stationery under Print.

sections.name: Other helpful resources
sections.notes: Cards for University Communications and the Communicator Resources site - the guide places itself inside a larger comms ecosystem rather than pretending to be the whole of it.

sections.name: About the Identity Guide (footer)
sections.notes: Origin story ('informed by many conversations, research, and workshops'), the not-mandates stance, two named contact emails, and ownership by the Office of University Communications.

needs: Any actual spec on the homepage - not a single hex value, typeface name, or logo rule is visible before a click; the quick links are icons only
A version number or last-updated date anywhere on the page
A clear line between what is optional and what is required - 'not mandates' is honest, but trademark and logo rules ARE enforced, and the homepage never says which is which
Accessibility guidance surfaced at the top level (color contrast, web standards) given that 'align my website' is a headline task
Do/don't examples on the entry page - misuse guidance presumably lives deeper, but nothing here previews it
A downloads hub - assets are scattered behind tasks (logo generator, app templates) with no single 'get all assets' path like Shopify's

principle.title: Organize the entry page around reader tasks, not asset taxonomy
principle.explanation: Most people arrive at a brand guide with a job, not a category - they think 'I need business cards', not 'I need the print stationery subsection'. Stanford's 'I would like to ...' grid meets that intent directly, which shortens the path to compliance more than any amount of better taxonomy would.
principle.howToApply: For the 35353 brand guide's landing page, list the top five or six real requests (grab the logo package, check ad sizes, style a new page, write an announcement) as first-person task cards above the section nav, and route each to the exact page plus its downloadable asset.

entries.tagline: A third-party integration rulebook where nearly every brand rule comes with a checkable number.
entries.summary: Spotify's developer-facing design and branding guidelines govern how external apps display Spotify content, logos, and links. It is not a full brand guide but a compliance manual for integrators, and at that job it is excellent: rules are scenario-driven (attribution, browsing, linking, playing) and unusually measurable. The long left-nav page walks from Introduction through Fonts with illustrated mock-UI examples in the brand's green throughout.
whatWorks: Rules are numeric and testable: artwork corners rounded 4px on small/medium devices and 8px on large, logo minimum 70px digital / 20mm print, max 20 items per browsed content set
Layout 'Considerations' give exact character counts to design for, e.g. 'Playlist/album name: 25 characters'
Attribution rule is unambiguous: full logo (icon + wordmark) in partner integrations, icon-only allowed solely as an app icon on a device screen
Content-type specifics: podcasts need episode title + podcast name (two-line layout recommended), audiobooks need title + author + chapter if sharing
Competitive-adjacency rule stated plainly: Spotify content should never sit next to content from similar services
Every section opens with 'When does this apply?', so integrators can skip what is not theirs

sections.name: Introduction
sections.notes: Frames the doc as brand plus legal/licensing guidance; accepting Developer Terms of Service is the entry condition

sections.name: Attribution
sections.notes: Strongest section - blue-grey hero collage of mock UIs, 'When does this apply?', full-logo vs icon-only rules tied to licensing

sections.name: Using our content
sections.notes: Artwork must stay unmodified (no crops, overlays, or text on artwork), corner-radius specs, metadata display rules per content type with character counts

sections.name: Browsing / Linking / Playing views
sections.notes: Display caps (20 items), deep-link CTAs with exact button wording ('GET SPOTIFY FREE', 'PLAY ON SPOTIFY'), play/pause-only controls and disabled states for Spotify Free

sections.name: Using our logo
sections.notes: Green-on-black/white primary colorway, monochrome elsewhere, 70px/20mm minimums; misuse covered in text

sections.name: Using our colors
sections.notes: 'Spotify Green is our resting color'; high-contrast pairings urged; no palette values printed on the page

sections.name: Logos and naming restrictions + Fonts
sections.notes: No 'Spotify' in app names, no brand pairing; fonts are pragmatic - platform sans-serif, then Helvetica Neue/Helvetica/Arial

needs: Exact color values - Spotify Green is named as the resting color but no HEX/RGB appears in the guidelines
Clearspace diagram for the logo - minimum size is specified but spacing rules are not drawn
Visual do/don't pairs for logo and artwork misuse - the prohibitions are prose lists, not pictures
Accessibility guidance beyond 'high contrast' - no approved text/background pairings
A version number or last-updated date - compliance docs change and integrators need to know when
A single downloadable asset bundle linked from the page rather than assets scattered per section

principle.title: Give every rule a number
principle.explanation: Vague brand rules ('keep it legible', 'don't crowd the logo') get argued about; numeric rules (4px radius, 70px minimum, 20-item cap, 25-character name field) get checked. Spotify's guide works because a third-party developer can self-audit without ever talking to Spotify.
principle.howToApply: When writing brand or integration rules for 35353 or any client, convert each qualitative rule into a measurable spec: minimum sizes in px and mm, radii, item caps, character counts. If a rule cannot be given a number or a testable condition, rewrite it until it can.

entries.tagline: A foundations hub where every brand ingredient gets a one-sentence job description and its own illustrated card.
entries.summary: The Foundations landing page of the Atlassian Design System, captured as a single dark-theme viewport - so this study covers the hub, not the deep pages behind it. It indexes the brand layer as Design tokens, then Guidelines (Accessibility, Content), then Styles (Spacing, Grid, Color, Typography, Iconography, Illustrations, Logos, Elevation, Border, Radius). As a map it is exemplary: each foundation has a hexagon icon, a card, and a single sentence saying what it is for, with 'Beta' badges marking maturity.
whatWorks: Tokens are positioned first and defined as 'the single source of truth to name and store decisions about the user interface'
Every foundation card carries a one-line purpose statement, e.g. Color 'distinguishes our brand and reinforces experiences across apps'
Beta badges on Border and Radius honestly signal which foundations are still settling
Accessibility is a top-level Guideline peer to Content, not a footnote
The docs are themable (Theme toggle in the header) and captured here in a true dark mode, demonstrating the system on itself
Custom hexagon icon set gives each abstract foundation a recognizable visual handle

sections.name: Design tokens
sections.notes: Single card with the green/purple/orange cube mark; sets tokens up as the source of truth before any style is discussed

sections.name: Guidelines - Accessibility
sections.notes: Card promising design 'people of all abilities' can interact with, understand, and navigate; depth lives behind the link

sections.name: Guidelines - Content
sections.notes: UX-writing guidance: 'clear, concise, and conversational language to get teams where they need to go'

sections.name: Styles - Spacing / Grid / Color / Typography
sections.notes: Core visual foundations, each with an icon card and one-line definition; sidebar shows Motion here too

sections.name: Styles - Iconography / Illustrations / Logos
sections.notes: Brand-expression trio present as first-class foundations, including logos as 'the visual representation of a brand or app'

sections.name: Styles - Elevation / Border / Radius
sections.notes: Surface-detail foundations; Border and Radius flagged Beta in both sidebar and cards

needs: The hub shows no actual values - not one hex code, type size, or spacing step is visible without clicking through
Brand strategy and personality - Content covers UX writing, but nothing states what the Atlassian brand stands for or sounds like
Logo usage rules (clearspace, minimum size, misuse) are not previewed; 'Logos' is just a nav entry here
Photography and art-direction guidance is absent; Illustrations is the only imagery foundation
Application examples - no marketing, social, or print mockups anywhere in the foundations layer
This capture is hub-only, so the study cannot confirm depth or quality of the underlying pages

principle.title: Define every section's job in one line
principle.explanation: Atlassian's hub works because each foundation must justify itself in a single sentence before any detail appears. That forces clarity about why a section exists, and readers can navigate a large system by purpose instead of by guessing from titles.
principle.howToApply: When structuring the 35353 brand guide or any docs hub, write the one-sentence job description for each section first - 'Color distinguishes our brand' style - and put it on the index card. If a section's job cannot be stated in one line, it is probably two sections or none.

entries.tagline: A trademark-protection page organized entirely by the asker's real-world scenario - and written like a human, not a lawyer.
entries.summary: Dropbox's public branding page is pure prose: eight scenario-based sections telling outsiders what they may and may not do with Dropbox names and logos, with brand@dropbox.com as the escalation path. As legal guidance it is unusually readable and well organized. But it is honestly thin as a brand-assets kit: there is not a single visual in the body - no logo lockup, no diagram, no color value, no download - so it protects the mark in words while giving you nothing to use correctly.
whatWorks: Sections map to the reader's actual situation: Advertising, Education and Instruction, Products/Websites/Names/Logos, Functional Uses (UIs/Buttons), Linking to Dropbox, Merchandise
The misuse rule is one exhaustive verb list: don't 'edit, change, distort, recolor, rotate, deconstruct, stretch, reconfigure, or otherwise modify' the logos
Precise word-mark grammar: always use marks 'as proper (i.e., capitalized) adjectives, not a noun or a verb', never plural or possessive
Human warmth inside legal copy: it's ok to say 'works with Dropbox' or 'compatible with Dropbox' - '(as long as it's true!)'
Gives publishers the exact disclaimer sentence to reprint: '(Title) is not affiliated with or otherwise sponsored by Dropbox, Inc.'
Routes API developers onward to dedicated Developer Brand Guidelines instead of overloading this page

sections.name: Introduction
sections.notes: States trademarks are IP owned by Dropbox, that use implies acceptance of the guidelines, and names a real contact: brand@dropbox.com

sections.name: Trademarks and Brand Usage
sections.notes: Core rules - no implied sponsorship, your brand must be more prominent than Dropbox's, word-mark grammar, the full logo-modification ban

sections.name: Advertising, Promotional, and Sales Materials
sections.notes: Check-with-us-first policy, plus the approved 'works with Dropbox' compatibility phrasing

sections.name: Education and Instruction
sections.notes: Permits editorial/instructional use, bans logos on book covers, supplies the required non-affiliation disclaimer

sections.name: Products, Websites, Names, and Logos
sections.notes: No 'Dropbox' in company, product, or domain names; no incorporating the logo into yours

sections.name: Functional Uses (UIs/Buttons) + Linking to Dropbox
sections.notes: Hands API cases to the Developer Brand Guidelines; allows the logo as a link with example phrasings

sections.name: Merchandise
sections.notes: Blanket no for third-party merch bearing brand materials, delivered with a light touch about their own t-shirts

needs: The logo itself - a branding page that never shows the logo it is protecting cannot prevent the most common errors
Clearspace and minimum-size diagrams; 'don't modify' is stated but correct usage is never drawn
Color values - Dropbox blue appears in the page chrome but is never specified in HEX/RGB/Pantone
Downloadable approved assets, so people stop screenshotting logos from the website
Visual do/don't examples for the misuse verb list
A version or last-updated date - the text says guidelines 'may be updated periodically' but never says when they last were

principle.title: Organize usage rules by the asker's scenario
principle.explanation: Nobody arrives at a branding page wondering about 'trademark taxonomy'; they arrive with a situation - I'm making a course, an ad, a t-shirt, an integration. Dropbox's headings answer the question the reader actually brought, so the right rule is found in one scan and compliance goes up.
principle.howToApply: For any 35353 usage or partner page, list the five or six real situations people will show up with, make each one a heading, and put the yes/no and the exact approved wording under it - rather than organizing by asset type or legal category.

entries.tagline: A brand layer that ships as a version-pinned npm package, with the logo itself delivered as a coded component.
entries.summary: Protocol is the design system behind mozilla.org and Firefox marketing sites, and its docs homepage - captured here as a single viewport - treats the system as software first: an 'npm v22.0.0' badge sits directly under the title, a GitHub link in the header, and 'Built on: Oct 3, 2025' in the sidebar footer. Fundamentals (Design Principles, Brand Themes, Typography, Color, Design Tokens) sit beside a 50-plus component library that includes Branding as a component. The homepage itself is spartan - three paragraphs and a nav - so the capture is thin on visual evidence.
whatWorks: Version-pinned distribution: the npm v22.0.0 badge means any site can state exactly which brand system release it runs
Brand marks ship as code - a 'Branding' component provides logo, wordmark, and zap variants, so nobody rebuilds the logo by hand
Radically honest scoping: 'Protocol is still an evolving project', currently 'used primarily by the Mozilla Marketing Websites team'
Open participation paths named right on the homepage: #protocol-design-system on Slack, Matrix for the public, and 'file an issue on GitHub'
Build-date stamp in the sidebar ('Built on: Oct 3, 2025') tells readers how fresh the docs are
Fundamentals nav puts Design Principles and Brand Themes ahead of components, so the why precedes the parts

sections.name: Documentation - Fundamentals
sections.notes: Design Principles, Brand Themes, Typography, Color, and Design Tokens; the brand layer proper, one click below this capture

sections.name: Documentation - Usage / Contributing
sections.notes: CSS framework docs plus naming conventions and a CSS guide - governance for code, which most brand guides lack

sections.name: Components
sections.notes: Long alphabetical sidebar from Basic Elements through Billboard, Branding, Callout, Card, Picto, Split, Sticky Promo to Video; marketing-page building blocks rather than app UI

sections.name: Homepage introduction
sections.notes: Three plain paragraphs defining Protocol as 'a common design language' with 'reusable coded components' and guidelines for content and accessibility

sections.name: Information / meta
sections.notes: npm version badge, GitHub icon, and build date - small elements doing the living-document work

needs: Any visual preview - the homepage shows zero color, type, or component imagery, so the system's look is invisible from its own front door
Brand strategy and voice - accessibility and content get 'high level guidelines' but nothing states Mozilla's personality or tone here
Photography and illustration direction beyond the Picto component
Application mockups showing composed pages, since Protocol exists precisely to build marketing pages
Accessibility specifics (contrast pairings) surfaced at hub level rather than implied
This capture covers only the docs homepage, so the depth of Fundamentals pages is unverified

principle.title: Ship the guide as installable code
principle.explanation: When the brand layer is an npm package, adoption is one install command, updates propagate by version bump, and drift between 'the guide' and 'the site' becomes impossible - the guide is the site's dependency. Mozilla's v22.0.0 badge is a stronger governance statement than any PDF version page.
principle.howToApply: For 35353, publish the brand CSS/components as a private package the site imports, with the docs generated from the same source. When the brand evolves, cut a release; every consuming project states its brand version in package.json.

entries.tagline: A redesign presented as a century of continuity - a 1913-1957 rings timeline earns the new system before a single new element is shown.
entries.summary: The IOC's 'Olympic Brand - Evolution of the Olympic Identity' page presents the Hulse & Durrell-designed system: custom typefaces, an extended palette, illustrations, and graphic devices, all framed as heritage evolved rather than replaced. It is a beautifully argued showcase with real substance (clearspace diagrams, named typefaces, credited designers), but it is the story about the guide, not the guide - the operative rules live in the separately linked Olympic Brand Book, and the page ends by reminding you the properties are IP-protected.
whatWorks: History as foundation: a timeline of the rings - 1913 introduction, 1914 flag, 1920 Games debut, 1957 definition - grounds the new work in 100+ years of lineage

Named, purposeful typefaces: Olympic Headline (bold athletic display 'for short and punchy titles'), Olympic Sans (Swiss Neo-grotesque body), Olympic Serif ('a touch of tradition'), credited to Fabian Harb and Seb McLauchlan (Dinamo) and Julien Hebert (Principal)
A real clearspace construction diagram on the IOC lockup, gridded in half-x units

Colour logic stated as strategy: the symbol's blue/yellow/black/green/red/white 'remain at the foundation', extended shades plus gold/silver/bronze medal colours added 'for digital interfaces, infographics and illustrations'
Endorsement with a face: pull-quote from May Guerraoui, Head of Brand - IOC, on 'communicating the brand values with emotion'
Full credits block naming client, agency (Hulse & Durrell), creative and art direction, illustrators (Francesco Ciccolella, Abbey Lossing, Karan Singh), and typeface designers

sections.name: Brand identity over the years + The Olympic Brand Book
sections.notes: Hero film of the evolved rings motif, narrative intro, and a CTA to the actual brand book - the page's rules live elsewhere

sections.name: History of the Olympic rings
sections.notes: Four-date interactive timeline with archival imagery, including Coubertin-era hand-drawn rings; the strongest section

sections.name: The new design system at a glance
sections.notes: Head of Brand quote plus a summary naming the ingredients: three custom typefaces, graphic devices, illustrations, colour-to-grid guidelines

sections.name: Logo system
sections.notes: Clearspace diagram in 1/2x units on the IOC lockup; copy explains one system so 'programmes, products and events share the same visual language'

sections.name: Typography + Colours
sections.notes: TYPOG card showing drawing-board bezier outlines; swatch sheet pairing each colour family with HEX/RGB/CMYK values, readable as an image only

sections.name: Illustrations + Graphic devices
sections.notes: 17 illustrations by three international artists; geometric patterns built from ring and track geometry in the six Olympic colours

sections.name: Credits + Olympic Properties
sections.notes: Full attribution block, press contact, then a reminder the properties are protected by registered designs, copyright, and trademarks

needs: The rules themselves - clearspace appears but minimum sizes, misuse don'ts, and co-branding rules are all deferred to the gated Brand Book
Copy-ready colour values - the swatch sheet is a static image; nothing on the page lets you copy a hex code
Verbal identity - no voice, tone, or messaging despite 'brand values with emotion' being the stated goal
Accessibility guidance for a palette that leans on saturated primaries
Downloadable assets or templates - understandable given IP protection, but even press use requires emailing pressoffice@olympic.org
A version or date for the system itself; the page narrates 'the evolution begins' without anchoring when

principle.title: Anchor a redesign in the brand's own history
principle.explanation: The IOC spends a third of the page proving the new system descends from 1913 before showing anything new, so the redesign reads as inheritance rather than reinvention. For institutions whose equity is continuity, a documented lineage disarms the 'why change it' objection better than any rationale paragraph.
principle.howToApply: When restyling an established brand (or presenting the 35353 V2 bold/dark direction against V1), open with a short timeline of the identity's real history and show which elements carry forward unchanged - then present what is new as the next dated entry in that same timeline.

entries.tagline: A one-screen press kit that bets everything on a single purple Download button and one perfectly judged joke.
entries.summary: Twitch's brand page is radically minimal: a 'Brand Assets' headline, the line 'Thank you for finding our correct brand assets instead of downloading fanart from 2017', and one Download button that serves a Twitch-Brand.zip. The page itself is on-brand (Twitch purple footer, Glitch mark, rounded pill button, light/dark toggle), but every actual rule - logos, colors, clearspace - lives inside the zip, so the visible guide is deliberately thin. As a capture it is honest but shallow: nothing on the page can be referenced without downloading.
whatWorks: One unmissable action: a single purple 'Download' pill in the center of the page, zero competing CTAs
The intro line names the real-world problem ('downloading fanart from 2017') in one sentence, which motivates outsiders to use official assets
The page demonstrates the identity while you read it: black outlined wordmark, Twitch-purple footer with the white Glitch mark, rounded geometry
Includes a light/dark toggle (sun icon, top right), acknowledging the mark must work on both surfaces
Zero navigation cost - a journalist or partner gets the correct files in one click

sections.name: Brand Assets hero
sections.notes: Large headline plus the two-line witty intro; sets tone and purpose in under 25 words

sections.name: Download CTA
sections.notes: Single purple pill 'Download' delivering Twitch-Brand.zip - the entire kit is this one action

sections.name: Site navigation
sections.notes: About / Stream / Watch / Company / Blog / Twitch.tv plus a theme toggle; routes to the wider brand world but adds no guideline content

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Full-bleed Twitch purple with the white Glitch mark and six link columns (Communities, Company, Newsroom, Products, Resources, Connect); the strongest on-page demonstration of the palette

needs: Logo system shown on the page: variations, clearspace and minimum-size diagrams are all hidden inside the zip
Copy-ready color values (hex/RGB) - the signature purple is shown but never specified on the page
Any visible don'ts or misuse examples to protect the mark before someone downloads
Typography guidance - the distinctive display face is used but never named or licensed
Plain legal/usage terms on the page (who may use the assets, and how)
Referenceable web content - nothing on this page can be linked to or cited; everything requires opening a zip

principle.title: If the kit is one page, make the download the hero
principle.explanation: A public assets kit succeeds when outsiders grab correct files fast. Twitch collapses the whole journey to one centered CTA with witty copy that explains why it matters - but shows how the trade-off costs you on-page reference value.
principle.howToApply: For a 35353 press-kit page: one primary download button above the fold delivering a complete zip, but keep the two or three most-abused rules (logo clearspace, the exact brand hex) visible on the page itself so they work without the download.

entries.tagline: A brand portal that treats translation as a first-class feature - the guide ships in 18 languages because the movement does.
entries.summary: The Wikimedia Brand portal on Meta-Wiki is the front door to the movement's identity: an overview explaining why 'thousands of volunteers from all over the world' need one visual identity, six color-blocked illustrated section tiles (Logo, Typography, Colours, Imagery, Attribution, Create), and a Resources list of eight deeper documents. It is a hub rather than the guide itself - no specimen, value, or rule appears on this page - but the governance story is unusually strong: maintained by a named department, tied to a Trademark policy, CC BY-SA licensed, and dated ('last edited on 10 May 2026').
whatWorks: States the why up front: decentralised volunteers make it 'all the more important for Wikimedia to be recognisable as one Movement'
Section tiles double as a palette demo - Logo on yellow, Typography on blue, Colours on pink, Imagery on cream, Create on orange, Attribution on green, each with hand-drawn line illustration
An 'Other languages' bar lists 18 translations with completeness indicators plus a 'Translate the missing messages' call to contribute
Clear ownership and rights: 'maintained by the Wikimedia Foundation Communications Department', with the Trademark policy linked for who can use the marks

Resources list routes to the specialist layers: Visual identity guidelines, trademark list, developer app guidelines, logo history, localised logos, affiliate logo rules, and Codex (the UX design system)
Includes an Attribution section - crediting content is a brand behavior unique to this institution, and the guide treats it as core

sections.name: Overview
sections.notes: Three-paragraph rationale for a common visual identity, ownership statement, and trademark-policy pointer; concise and genuinely strategic

sections.name: Anchor navigation
sections.notes: Overview / Logo / Typography / Colours / Imagery / Attribution / Create as an in-page row; the whole IA visible at a glance

sections.name: Section tiles
sections.notes: Six illustrated color-block cards linking into each topic; charming and on-brand, though the tiles carry no actual rules

sections.name: Languages bar
sections.notes: 18 translations with per-language completeness dots and an invitation to translate missing messages - localization as participation

sections.name: Resources
sections.notes: Eight-link list to the deeper documents, including Codex and affiliate/developer logo guidelines

sections.name: Licensing footer
sections.notes: CC BY-SA license, last-edited date (10 May 2026), and standard Meta-Wiki governance links

needs: Any actual specimen on the portal page - not one logo, hex value, or typeface is shown before you click through
A verbal identity section - voice, tone, and messaging are absent from the six-part IA entirely
Do/don't examples surfaced at portal level to protect the marks before readers dive deeper
Accessibility guidance (contrast pairings) anywhere in the visible structure
Application mockups - social, presentation, and print usage are implied under Create but not previewed
A friendlier reading surface - the MediaWiki chrome (edit tabs, sidebar, search) competes with the guide content

principle.title: Ship the guide in every language the brand speaks
principle.explanation: A global or multilingual brand cannot stay consistent if its rules only exist in English. Wikimedia treats translation as part of the guide's structure - with visible completeness states and an open invitation to contribute - so consistency scales with the community.
principle.howToApply: If a future build serves a bilingual audience, structure guideline copy as translatable strings from day one and show translation status on the page, rather than bolting on a second-language PDF later.

entries.tagline: A brand hub organized by what the reader is trying to make - identity, writing, illustration, marketing - not by design discipline.
entries.summary: Duolingo's brand site opens on a flat green hero with ghosted greetings ('hola', Japanese script, 'bonjour', 'jambo') and a welcome that ties the guide to the product: 'Language never stands still - and neither do we.' Below, five color-coded cards route readers by job: identity ('core brand elements and rules for usage'), writing ('produce content in the spirit of Duolingo'), illustration ('artwork that feels right at home in the expanding Duolingo universe'), marketing, and resources ('logos, fact sheets, images, and all the other downloadables'). The hub is complete for a full guide's scope - visual, verbal, art direction, applications, assets - though the landing page itself carries no specs, and a stray 'All good.' status line sits oddly in the captured footer area.
whatWorks: IA organized by reader job: a copywriter goes to writing, an artist to illustration, a marketer to marketing - nobody parses a designer's taxonomy to find their rules
Verbal identity is a top-level peer of visual identity, not a subsection - rare and correct for a brand whose voice is the product
Each hub card is a different brand color (green, blue, purple, yellow, coral) with a character illustration, so the landing page performs the palette and art style before you read a rule
Quick Links (Press Kit, Brand Colors, Illustration Colors, Duolingo.com) give returning users a shortcut past the hub
The welcome copy is in-voice and ends with an escape hatch: 'If you can't find what you need, please contact us'
Ghosted multilingual greetings in the hero tie the guide's look directly to the product's purpose

sections.name: Welcome hero
sections.notes: Green field, oversized translucent greetings in four languages, warm two-sentence welcome plus contact route; instantly recognizable as Duolingo

sections.name: Quick Links
