sections.notes: Press Kit, Brand Colors, Illustration Colors, Duolingo.com - the four most-fetched destinations pulled up to the hero

sections.name: Identity guide
sections.notes: Green card: 'Successfully represent Duolingo with core brand elements and rules for usage' - logo, color, type live here

sections.name: Writing guide
sections.notes: Blue card: content 'in the spirit of Duolingo' with consistency 'across all mediums' - full verbal-identity layer

sections.name: Illustration guide
sections.notes: Purple card: artwork for 'the expanding Duolingo universe' - the character system gets its own discipline-level guide

sections.name: Marketing guide + Resources
sections.notes: Yellow marketing card for applying the visual identity to materials; coral resources card for logos, fact sheets, and downloadables

needs: Any spec at hub level - no hex values, type names, or logo rules are visible until you enter a guide
Accessibility guidance (contrast pairings for that saturated palette) surfaced anywhere in the visible structure
Versioning or a changelog - nothing on the page says when guidance last changed
Co-branding and partnership rules - not hinted at in the five-card IA
Motion principles - a brand this animated in product shows no motion section at hub level
Governance beyond 'contact us' - no named owner, approval process, or usage-review path

principle.title: Split the guide by reader job, not by design discipline
principle.explanation: People arrive at a brand guide mid-task. Duolingo's five doors (identity, writing, illustration, marketing, resources) map to what someone is making, so each reader finds their rules in one hop instead of decoding a designer's category tree.
principle.howToApply: When structuring a 35353 brand guide, name top-level sections after the tasks collaborators actually do (build a page, write a listing, make an ad) and let logo/color/type live inside those journeys, with quick links for repeat visitors.

entries.tagline: A design system whose front door offers the same thing three ways: principles to think with, resources to design with, code to ship with.
entries.summary: Spectrum's homepage states its job in one line - 'Spectrum provides components and tools to help product teams work more efficiently, and to make Adobe's applications more cohesive' - then splits into exactly three columns: Principles ('foundational thinking'), Resources (download the XD plugin, UI kits, fonts, icons), and Implementations (Spectrum CSS, React Spectrum, Spectrum Web Components). The dark sidebar exposes the full IA (Foundation, Content, Components, Patterns, Tools and resources, Support) plus a Preview Spectrum 2 link. It is a product-UI system, not a brand guide - Adobe's logo, voice, and marketing identity live elsewhere - and the front-door footer still reads 'Copyright 2024 Adobe' in a 2026 capture, a small staleness tell.
whatWorks: The three-column front door mirrors the three audiences: thinkers get Principles, designers get downloads (XD plugin, UI kits, fonts, icons), engineers get Explore links to CSS, React, and Web Components
One-sentence mission with two measurable aims - team efficiency and cross-application cohesion - so every guideline has a test
Sidebar IA separates Foundation (visual language) from Content (writing) from Components and Patterns, keeping rules, words, and parts distinct
Implementations are 'open-source... in partnership with the detailed usage guidelines here' - the rules and the code that obeys them are cross-linked, not parallel universes
Preview Spectrum 2 is exposed in the nav: the next version is public while the current one remains canonical
Search sits at the top of the sidebar - the system assumes lookup, not linear reading

sections.name: Homepage intro
sections.notes: 'Spectrum, Adobe's design system' plus the efficiency/cohesion mission statement; abstract illustrated hero of UI parts on Spectrum blue

sections.name: Sidebar IA
sections.notes: Foundation, Content, Components, Patterns, Tools and resources, Support - a complete, discipline-separated table of contents always in view

sections.name: Principles
sections.notes: 'Get to know our foundational thinking and how we put it into action' - a thin teaser here, one click from the actual principles

sections.name: Resources
sections.notes: Four direct downloads: Adobe XD plugin, UI kits, fonts, icons - designers can act immediately from the homepage

sections.name: Implementations
sections.notes: Spectrum CSS, React Spectrum, Spectrum Web Components, plus Preview Spectrum 2 - three maintained code targets tied back to usage guidance

needs: A brand layer proper - no logo system, brand color rationale, or voice/personality content is visible; this is product UI only
Imagery and art-direction guidance - the illustration style is demonstrated in the hero but never specified
Visible versioning on the front door - no version number or last-updated date, and the footer copyright still says 2024
Application examples - no screenshots of Spectrum living inside actual Adobe apps to prove the cohesion claim
Accessibility surfaced at homepage level - contrast and inclusive-design standards exist deeper but get no front-door billing
Token documentation exposure - design tokens are not visible in the top-level IA of this capture

principle.title: Ship the rules with code that obeys them
principle.explanation: Guidelines drift the moment implementation is someone else's repo. Spectrum's front door pairs every usage guideline with maintained open-source implementations (CSS, React, Web Components), so following the rules is the path of least resistance for engineers.
principle.howToApply: For the 35353 design-system layer, publish the small CSS/component implementation alongside the written rules and link them both ways - a color or spacing rule should never exist only as prose.

entries.tagline: A design system that ships accessibility as working tools - Focus Order annotator, contrast checker - instead of leaving it as prose.
entries.summary: Fluent 2's dark homepage opens 'WELCOME TO Fluent 2 - Let the creativity flow' (the middle word rotates: work, ideas, imagination) over iridescent glass cubes, then forks into Design ('Dive into our Figma UI kits') and Develop ('Find installation guides and tooling tips'). Components are split per platform in giant type - Web, iOS, Android, Windows - and a Resources block ships four working tools: 'A11y - Focus Order', 'A11y - Color Contrast Checker', Content Reel, and Icon Scaling Tool. A Newsworthy section proves adoption with Teams, an emoji update, and 'A modern Outlook'. It is confident and current, but it is a product-UI system with an 'Employee sign-in' in the header - brand-level guidance (logo, voice, imagery) is not part of this artifact.
whatWorks: Accessibility ships as usable tooling: 'A11y - Focus Order' for annotating tab order and a Color Contrast Checker 'adhering to Web Content Accessibility Guideline standards' - rules turned into plugins
Platform honesty: Web, iOS, Android, Windows each get their own component library instead of one averaged spec, and the homepage says so in display-size type
Two-door entry (Design vs Develop) routes the two audiences to Figma kits or installation guides in one click
Newsworthy section proves the system with shipped products - 'Teams leverages Fluent 2 to boost performance and reduce complexity', emoji, and Outlook - adoption as evidence
The sidebar exposes 'Working with AI' and 'Web tokens' as first-class nav items, keeping the system current with how teams actually build
The hero's rotating verb ('Let the creativity flow') makes even the headline behave like a component with variants

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: 'WELCOME TO Fluent 2' with animated rotating tagline over 3D glass-cube art; dark, cinematic, unmistakably current Microsoft design

sections.name: Design / Develop entry cards
sections.notes: Two cards splitting the audience: Figma UI kits for designers, installation and tooling guidance for engineers

sections.name: Sidebar navigation
sections.notes: Get started, Design language, UX frameworks and guidelines, Working with AI, Web tokens, Web > Components - the system's real depth, always visible

sections.name: Components by platform
sections.notes: Web / iOS / Android / Windows in enormous type, each linking to a dedicated component library - per-platform fidelity over lowest-common-denominator specs

sections.name: Newsworthy
sections.notes: Three case tiles (a new era of Teams, Emoji update, a modern Outlook) demonstrating the system in shipped Microsoft products

sections.name: Resources
sections.notes: Four tools: A11y Focus Order, A11y Color Contrast Checker, Content Reel (pull text/images/icons from one palette), Icon Scaling Tool

needs: Brand identity content - no Microsoft logo rules, brand color story, or voice guidance; the 'Design language' section covers product UI, not the corporate mark
Open access throughout - an 'Employee sign-in' in the header signals part of the system is gated from outside readers
Downloadable brand assets - nothing equivalent to a press kit or asset zip is visible
Visible versioning - beyond a 'Check out what's new' button, no version number or dated changelog appears on the homepage
Imagery and illustration direction - the 3D art style is striking but nowhere specified for reuse
Motion principles surfaced in the IA - the hero animates, but motion has no visible top-level section

principle.title: Turn accessibility rules into tools
principle.explanation: Written contrast ratios and focus-order rules get skipped under deadline; a checker or annotator embedded in the design workflow gets used. Fluent 2 ships accessibility as plugins on the homepage, making compliance the convenient path.
principle.howToApply: For 35353, encode the accessibility bar as executable checks - a contrast-pair validator for the palette tokens and a lint step in the build - and link them from the brand guide instead of only writing WCAG numbers in prose.

entries.tagline: A one-screen gated front door that still manages to feel unmistakably Netflix before you read a single rule.
entries.summary: The public face of Netflix's brand portal is a single hero: 'Welcome to the Netflix Brand Site' in huge white Netflix Sans over a cinematic red-to-black gradient, with three entry buttons - BRAND LOGOS, SIGN IN, ACCOUNT REQUEST - and the red N monogram signing off bottom-right. Nearly everything of substance sits behind the sign-in / account-request gate, so as a public artifact this capture is thin: it routes you rather than teaches you. What is public (the Brand Logos path) protects the mark; the rest is deliberately insider-only.
whatWorks: The landing page is itself on-brand: the red-to-black vertical gradient reads like projector light in a dark theater, demonstrating the brand's cinematic identity with zero copy
Massive left-aligned white headline in the brand typeface shows the type system in action instead of describing it
Three clearly-labeled doors - BRAND LOGOS, SIGN IN, ACCOUNT REQUEST - split outsiders (who only need logos) from insiders (who need the full guide) in one glance
Keeps the highest-risk asset public: the logo path requires no account, so third parties have no excuse to redraw the N
The lone red N mark in the corner acts as a quiet specimen of the symbol on a dark surface

sections.name: Welcome hero
sections.notes: Full-viewport gradient with 'Welcome to the Netflix Brand Site' headline; confident, minimal, on-brand

sections.name: Brand Logos entry
sections.notes: Public button routing to logo assets and usage - the only substantive content reachable without an account

sections.name: Sign in / Account request
sections.notes: Gate for the full internal guide; access is by request, signalling a governed, partner-facing system

sections.name: N monogram sign-off
sections.notes: The red N symbol placed bottom-right on black - a small live specimen of the mark

needs: Public color values - the famous Netflix Red is nowhere stated as a hex on the open page
Clearspace and minimum-size diagrams visible without an account
Any public don'ts or misuse examples to protect the mark for press and partners
A public typography note (Netflix Sans is shown but never named or specced)
Application examples or downloadable press assets on the open layer
A version number, date, or contact path visible before the gate

principle.title: Gate the guide, not the logo
principle.explanation: Outsiders misuse marks because the rules are locked away. A gated portal is fine for strategy and campaign work, but the assets outsiders will grab anyway - logo, primary color, clearspace - must stay public or the gate itself causes the misuse.
principle.howToApply: When building a brand portal for 35353, split it into a no-login assets layer (logo files, hex values, clearspace, three don'ts) and a gated full guide; never put the logo download behind the account-request form.

entries.tagline: Every section is a color-blocked specimen of the asset it describes - the Snoo chapter treats the mascot as seriously as the logo.
entries.summary: A public brand overview page that walks through the identity in full-bleed color bands: OrangeRed hero ('Reddit aspires to be the heart of the internet'), a white logo chapter, an OrangeRed Snoo chapter, a lime Reddit Sans chapter, then a Brand resources card grid and a licensing call-to-action. It excels at rationale - the logo copy explains the Snoo-head-in-speech-bubble construction and names OrangeRed #FF4500 inline - but it is an overview that links out to the real guidelines rather than stating rules itself.
whatWorks: Names the exact brand color in running copy - 'contained within an OrangeRed (#FF4500) conversation bubble' - so the value travels with the reasoning
Gives the mascot a full section with rationale: 'Why Snoo? Because everyone has needed to see a friendly face at some point in their life' - character treated as a governed asset, not decoration
Reddit Sans chapter doubles as a live specimen: Light through ExtraBold weights shown in a card, with functional reasoning (large x-height, disambiguated letterforms, humanist characteristics)
Each section sits on a different brand color (OrangeRed, white, lime, black footer), so the page demonstrates the palette in use instead of swatching it
Brand resources card grid names the five subsystems - Brand guidelines, Logo assets, Reddit Sans, Traits & values ('Inherently eclectic'), Snoo - a clear map of the full system
Licensing section gives a concrete action path: contact licensing@reddit.com for commercial use

sections.name: The Reddit brand (hero)
sections.notes: Positioning statement - 'heart of the internet... people, conversations, and interests' - with 3D Snoo and a Brand resources CTA; strategy in two sentences

sections.name: The Reddit logo
sections.notes: Explains construction (stylized Snoo head in an OrangeRed #FF4500 speech bubble paired with the wordmark) and when the icon should appear; no clearspace or size diagrams on this page

sections.name: Snoo
sections.notes: Dedicated mascot chapter with personality rationale and 3D renders; strong, but rules for posing/usage live elsewhere

sections.name: Reddit Sans
sections.notes: Weight specimen (Light, Regular, SemiBold, Bold, ExtraBold) plus design rationale - accessible letterforms, large x-height, built for the internet

sections.name: Brand resources
sections.notes: Five-card grid linking to Brand guidelines, Logo assets, Reddit Sans, Traits & values, and Snoo - the page is a hub, the depth is one click away

sections.name: Licensing the Reddit brand
sections.notes: Plain-language commercial licensing path via licensing@reddit.com with a Contact licensing button

needs: Clearspace and minimum-size diagrams on the page itself - the logo chapter describes construction but shows no measurement rules
Misuse / don't examples for both the logo and Snoo
The palette beyond OrangeRed - the lime, teal, and pink used on this very page are never named or given values
Type scale and hierarchy rules for Reddit Sans (weights are shown, usage is not)
Application examples with specs (social avatars, covers, ads)
A version or last-updated date on the brand hub

principle.title: Codify the mascot like a logo
principle.explanation: Characters carry more emotional load than wordmarks, and they get misdrawn, off-model, and off-tone faster. Giving the mascot its own chapter - with a why, a personality, and eventually rules - protects the most human part of the brand.
principle.howToApply: If a future build has any recurring character or illustrated figure, write it a dedicated guide section: what it means, why it exists, approved poses/renders, and don'ts - same rigor as the logo system.

entries.tagline: A one-page kit that proves every mark on both dark and light tiles and names its neutrals like products.
entries.summary: A compact, dark, single-page assets kit: Naming, Usage (with an inline IP/legal notice), Wordmark, Logo, Icon, and Colors, opened by a single 'Download Brand Assets' button. It is disciplined and itself perfectly on-brand - every asset is shown twice, on a near-black and a near-white tile - but it is minimal to a fault: no typography section at all, and the Colors section describes a 'subtle desaturated blue' primary that is never actually swatched or given a value.
whatWorks: Every mark is proven on both surfaces: wordmark, logomark, and icon each get a side-by-side dark tile and light tile, so contrast behavior is shown, not described
Naming rules are verbal-identity done cheaply and well: 'Linear' single word, capital L, releases as proper nouns ('Linear Method'), never 'Linear app'
Named neutrals with full values - Mercury White (RGB 244,245,248 / #F4F5F8) and Nordic Gray (RGB 35,35,38 / #222326) - memorable and copy-ready
Legal/IP boundary stated inline in the Usage section (no alteration, no implied affiliation or endorsement) instead of buried in a separate terms page
One 'Download Brand Assets' CTA at the top - the reader can act before reading
Guidance includes judgment, not just rules: use the logomark 'for tight layouts or logo-only grids... as the Linear wordmark has stronger brand recognition'

sections.name: Naming
sections.notes: Capitalization and naming conventions with examples; small but rare to see in a public kit

sections.name: Usage
sections.notes: Breathing-room rule ('give them room to breathe') plus a boxed IP/legal notice; clearspace is described, never diagrammed

sections.name: Linear wordmark
sections.notes: Preferred mark, monochrome-first, shown on dark and light tiles

sections.name: Linear logo
sections.notes: Circular striped logomark for tight layouts, again on both surfaces, with a when-to-use caveat

sections.name: Linear icon
sections.notes: Chip-style app icon with corner-radius allowance for social contexts

sections.name: Colors
sections.notes: Two named neutrals with RGB+HEX; the primary 'subtle desaturated blue' is described in prose but has no swatch or value

needs: The actual brand color - the text says the primary is a subtle desaturated blue, but only the two neutrals get swatches and hex values
Any typography section: typeface names, weights, licensing, hierarchy - all absent
Clearspace and minimum-size diagrams (the 'room to breathe' rule is words only)
Pictured misuse / don't examples
Application mockups (product, social, deck) showing the marks in context
A version number or date; the closing note admits 'the Linear brand is dynamic and ever-evolving' but gives no changelog

principle.title: Prove every asset on light and dark
principle.explanation: A mark that has only been specified on one background will eventually be placed on the other one, badly. Showing each asset twice - dark tile, light tile - settles contrast, monochrome, and inversion questions before they are asked.
principle.howToApply: In the 35353 brand layer, render every logo variant, icon, and color pairing in a two-tile dark/light matrix (matching the V2 bold-dark default and V1 light option) and ship that matrix as part of the guide.

entries.tagline: Teaches the system by annotating live UI with highlighted spec labels - font names and pixel values sit right on the examples.
entries.summary: 'A guide to digital design at the Guardian' (dated 26/07/18) opens on a full-bleed yellow hero - 'Thinking outside the news in boxes' set in Guardian Headline - and walks through how the site is actually constructed: fronts, containers, story cards, article types, thrashers, then grids and spacing. Its signature move is yellow-highlighted annotations pinned to real examples ('Kicker - Guardian Headline Bold', 'Wide - 1300px'). The capture is partial, though: the page's media-heavy demo areas rendered as long blank stretches, the content repeats about three times in the scroll capture, and the colour palette the hero button jumps to never appears in the visible output.
whatWorks: Spec-as-annotation: highlighted labels on live card examples name the exact type roles - Kicker in Guardian Headline Bold, Headline in Guardian Headline Medium, Standfirst in Guardian Text Egyptian, Meta in Guardian Text Sans

Grid rules given as real numbers: desktop columns of 60px with 20px gutters; four fixed sizes (Wide 1300px, LeftCol 1140px, Desktop 980px, Tablet 740px) plus fluid mobile tweak points (Phablet 740px, MobileLandscape 480px, MobileMedium 375px)
Explains the system's vocabulary before its rules: fronts are made of containers, containers of modular story cards - a stranger learns the architecture, not just the styling
Ties digital back to heritage: 'Spacing is intentionally used to echo the placement of the typography in print'
The hero is itself a specimen - Guardian Headline at poster scale on the brand yellow, with a blue 'Jump to the colour palette' roundel as live UI
Card sizes are justified editorially: different sizes 'create hierarchy and pace... allow the reader to quickly gauge a story's importance'

sections.name: Hero / title
sections.notes: 'Thinking outside the news in boxes' on Guardian yellow, standfirst 'A guide to digital design at the Guardian' with a visible date (26/07/18) and an anchor button to the colour palette

sections.name: Introduction
sections.notes: Defines the page architecture - fronts, containers, modular story cards - with annotated live examples; the demo media itself failed to render in this capture

sections.name: Cards and card types
sections.notes: Anatomy (image, kicker, headline, standfirst, meta) with font-role annotations; card sizes explained as editorial pacing

sections.name: Article types and thrashers
sections.notes: Articles 'follow the design language of the cards' with distinct flavour per type; thrashers defined as custom containers promoting a single article or series

sections.name: Grids & spacing
sections.notes: Column/gutter values, four fixed grid sizes, fluid mobile tweak points, and the print-echo spacing rationale - the most copy-ready section

needs: The colour palette itself - the hero promises a jump link, but no named colours or values appear anywhere in the captured page
A typography chapter proper: the four Guardian typefaces are named only via inline annotations, with no scale, weights, or licensing
Logo/masthead rules - the wordmark appears as page furniture but gets no usage guidance
Accessibility guidance (contrast pairings for the yellow/blue/red editorial colours)
Downloadable assets or tokens for the values it does state
Resilience without media: whole sections go blank when the demo images/videos fail, because the prose was written to caption visuals rather than stand alone

principle.title: Annotate live examples with exact specs
principle.explanation: A rule pinned to the real thing ('Headline - Guardian Headline Medium', 'Wide - 1300px') is unambiguous and instantly copyable, where an abstract table forces the reader to map spec to reality themselves. The annotation also proves the rule is actually in use.
principle.howToApply: In the 35353 guide, screenshot real components from the site and overlay highlighted labels naming the token, font role, and pixel value on each part - make the annotated screenshot the rule, not an illustration of it.

entries.tagline: A versioned, WCAG-audited public design system where even the update path is documented as first-class content.
entries.summary: The design-system hub of the NHS digital service manual: a plainly-written landing page ('Build consistent, accessible NHS services for the public and staff') with a sidebar taxonomy - Design principles; Setup (Prototyping, Production code); Design (Styles, Components, Patterns); Update guides - and two headline update notices, 'Updating to v10' and 'Changes to meet WCAG 2.2' level AA. The capture is only the hub page (a cookie banner eats the top), so the actual styles and components are one click deeper, but the governance layer visible here is exemplary: versioned, licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0, and maintained by a named team with a get-in-touch path.
whatWorks: Explicit versioning with a migration path: 'We've updated the design system to version 10. Follow our guide to update your service or prototype'
Accessibility treated as a release, not a footnote: a dedicated 'Changes to meet WCAG 2.2' guide listing changes made to hit level AA
Clean three-part taxonomy under Design - Styles, Components, Patterns - plus Setup paths for both prototyping and production code
Purpose stated in one sentence aimed at its real users: consistent, accessible services for the public and staff, learning from other NHS digital teams
Open governance in the footer: content under the Open Government Licence v3.0, maintained by the service manual team at NHS England, with a feedback contact
Design system framed inside a larger service manual (NHS service standard, Content guide, Accessibility, Community and contribution) so visual rules sit next to verbal and process standards

sections.name: Service manual navigation
sections.notes: NHS service standard, Design system, Content guide, Accessibility, Community and contribution - the brand layer is one pillar of a whole operating manual

sections.name: Design system intro
sections.notes: One-paragraph purpose plus the promise that examples 'come with code' for prototypes and live services

sections.name: Principles / Setup / Design (sidebar)
sections.notes: Design principles, Prototyping, Production code, then Styles, Components, Patterns - a complete, shallow, predictable hierarchy

sections.name: Updating to v10
sections.notes: Version announcement with a step-by-step update guide for existing services

sections.name: Changes to meet WCAG 2.2
sections.notes: Level-AA compliance release with a full list of what changed and why

sections.name: Footer governance
sections.notes: Open Government Licence v3.0, named maintaining team, feedback route, accessibility statement

needs: The brand-identity layer itself: NHS logo rules, NHS Blue values, and identity heritage live on a separate NHS identity site and are not linked or summarized here
Imagery and art-direction guidance (photography, illustration) - absent from the design-system taxonomy
Voice and tone on this page - the Content guide exists but the design-system hub does not connect visual and verbal rules
Application examples beyond service UI (print, signage, campaign) for a brand this physical
On-page preview of what Styles covers (colour, typography, icons) - the hub gives no scent of what is inside
The capture itself is thin: hub page only, with a cookie banner consuming the top of the frame

principle.title: Ship a migration guide with every version
principle.explanation: A design system earns trust when change is survivable. Announcing v10 alongside 'follow our guide to update your service' and a WCAG 2.2 change list means downstream teams upgrade instead of forking - the update path is what keeps a living system alive.
principle.howToApply: When the 35353 tokens or components change (e.g. the bold-dark default evolves), publish a short 'updating to vN' note listing exactly what changed and the find-replace steps, next to the system itself - not in a commit message.

entries.tagline: A city brand hub that treats data visualization as a first-class identity discipline alongside marketing and visual identity.
entries.summary: This is the front door to Helsinki's brand: a hub page on hel.fi that routes to three guideline tracks - 'Brandi- ja markkinointilinjaukset' (brand and marketing), 'Visuaalisen ilmeen ohjeisto' (visual identity), and 'Tiedon visualisointi' (data visualization). The page itself demonstrates the identity: the framed Helsinki wordmark, wave-cut 'koro' edges in orange and blue, bright yellow content cards, and credited documentary photography. One honest caveat: the English URL (brand.hel.fi/en) 301-redirects to the Finnish-language page, so the capture and current entry point are Finnish-only, and the hub carries no specs itself - it is a router, not the rulebook.
whatWorks: Dedicated 'Tiedon visualisointi' (data visualization) track sits beside the visual identity guide - rare, and exactly right for a city that publishes statistics
The hub is itself on-brand: framed Helsinki bubble wordmark, orange/blue koro wave shapes, yellow cards, and a black footer with a wave-cut top edge
Real photography with visible credit ('Kuva: Juha Valkeakoski') models the honest, people-first image style the guide asks for
Each of the three cards states its job in one paragraph (who the guidelines steer: city organization, residents, visitors, businesses) before you click through
The data-viz card shows an actual printed spread of the 'Tietoa Helsingista' statistics booklet with charts, not an abstract illustration

sections.name: Hero intro (Helsingin brandi ja visuaalinen ilme)
sections.notes: Yellow band stating the brand concept's job - building Helsinki's image and making the strategy visible - over a night-lights city photo. Clear framing, no specs.

sections.name: Brandi- ja markkinointilinjaukset (brand and marketing guidelines)
sections.notes: Card linking to the strategy layer: how the whole city organization uses the brand, grounded in differentiating factors from the brand concept.

sections.name: Visuaalisen ilmeen ohjeisto (visual identity guidelines)
sections.notes: Card fronted by the framed Helsinki wordmark over an orange/blue koro wave graphic; promises the elements, when to use them, and the boundary conditions for on-brand solutions.

sections.name: Tiedon visualisointi (data visualization)
sections.notes: Card with a photographed spread of the city's statistics booklet - bar charts, donut charts, big figures - linking to guidance for clear, on-brand visualizations.

sections.name: Footer / contact (Ota yhteytta)
sections.notes: Black koro-edged footer with feedback prompt and contact routes; governance is implied via the city organization rather than a named brand owner.

needs: An English version at the English URL - brand.hel.fi/en currently 301s to the Finnish page, which shuts out international partners and vendors
Quick-reference specs on the hub itself: the palette values, the Helsinki Grotesk type story, and logo rules all sit behind the three doors
Visible download links for logo files and templates from the entry page
A version number and last-updated date for the guideline set
Accessibility guidance (contrast pairings for the yellow/orange/blue palette) surfaced as a named section

principle.title: Give data visualization its own chapter
principle.explanation: Charts are where most organizations quietly go off-brand - default Excel colors, random chart types - because the brand guide never claimed that territory. Helsinki treats data visualization as one of only three top-level guideline tracks, equal to marketing and visual identity.
principle.howToApply: On the next brand or design-system build, add a 'Data visualization' section with brand-derived chart palettes, chart-type do/don'ts, and one fully worked example (like Helsinki's statistics spread) so dashboards and reports inherit the identity automatically.

entries.tagline: A design system that stamps its release on the front page - 'Summer '26 v3.0, Styleguide updated 12 days ago' - and keeps its predecessor one click away.
entries.summary: SLDS 2 is the brand-and-UI layer for the Salesforce platform, pitched on the homepage as 'Bring your brand to life.' The capture shows the shell rather than the depths: a hero with explicit versioning, a 'Welcome to SLDS 2' intro video, and a left nav running Get Started, AI and SLDS 2, Foundations, Develop, Components, Patterns, Accessibility, Tools, with a live outbound link to SLDS 1. The site is JS-rendered so the text fetch returned nothing; this entry is honest about being a homepage-level read of a very deep system whose real brand layer (theming and styling hooks under Foundations) sits behind the nav.
whatWorks: Release identity right in the hero: 'Summer '26 v3.0' plus 'Styleguide updated 12 days ago' - freshness is legible before you scroll
The brand promise is one sentence - 'Bring your brand to life.' - which frames the whole system as a re-brandable layer, not a fixed skin
'SLDS 1' stays in the nav as an external link, so teams mid-migration always have the old system one click away
'Accessibility' is a top-level nav section, peer to Components and Patterns rather than an appendix
'AI and SLDS 2' as a dedicated section shows the system versioning its guidance for new surface types, not just new components
Onboarding by video ('Welcome to SLDS 2') lowers the entry cost for admins and partners who are not designers

sections.name: Get Started
sections.notes: First nav entry; paired with the welcome video on the homepage. Contents not visible in this capture.

sections.name: AI and SLDS 2
sections.notes: Dedicated top-level section for AI-era guidance - unusually forward-placed, second in the nav.

sections.name: Foundations
sections.notes: Where the brand layer (color, type, theming/styling hooks) lives in a design system of this shape; behind the nav in this capture.

sections.name: Tools + SLDS 1 link
sections.notes: Tooling section plus an external escape hatch to the previous system for teams that have not migrated.

needs: A visible brand-strategy or voice layer - this is product-UI territory; Salesforce's verbal identity and logo rules live elsewhere and are not linked here
Homepage-level quick reference: no palette, type sample, or token excerpt is visible before entering the nav
Imagery and illustration direction surfaced as a named foundation (not evident from the entry page)
Non-JS fallback or crawlable content - the page returns an empty shell to text fetchers, which also hurts search and AI-agent consumption
A stated owner or feedback channel on the homepage to go with the excellent version stamp

principle.title: Keep the previous system one click away
principle.explanation: Big redesigns fail at the seam: teams stuck on the old system lose their documentation the day the new site ships. SLDS 2 leaves 'SLDS 1' permanently in its own nav, which respects real migration timelines and keeps trust with every team mid-transition.
principle.howToApply: When shipping a v2 of any guide, site, or design system, keep the v1 docs live at a stable URL and link them from the v2 nav with a clear label - plus a migration page explaining what changed - instead of deleting or silently redirecting the old material.

entries.tagline: Sells the refreshed identity in three words - Optimized, Bold, Unified - with real merch, poster, and vehicle mockups before you ever hit a rule.
entries.summary: MIT's brand guide fronts a full system: Brand Architecture, Logos & Marks (down to the MIT Seal and Tim the Beaver), Color, Typography, Applying the Brand (Gallery, Do/Don't, Templates, Branded Merchandise, Photos & Videos), plus Downloads, FAQ, History, and Contact. The homepage is a pitch as much as an index - an animated cluster of the five brand-color circles (maroon, red, black, silver, white), then three claims ('Optimized' logo, 'Bold' color, 'Unified' architecture), each paired with photographic application mockups honestly labeled 'Conceptual designs.' Downloads carry a lock icon, so files appear gated behind MIT login while the rules themselves stay public.
whatWorks: Homepage argues the redesign in three one-word sections - 'Optimized', 'Bold', 'Unified' - each with one paragraph and a CTA into the relevant chapter

Applications shown as real-world objects up front: black tee and maroon hoodie with the modernized MIT mark, alphabet poster and confetti tote, 'mind and hand' pin, event poster templates, and a full red van livery
Mockups are captioned 'Conceptual designs' - honest labeling of what is aspiration versus shipped work
Deep logo governance in the nav: MIT Logo, Logo Lock-Ups, Social Media Logos, MIT Seal, and mascot 'Tim the Beaver' each get their own page
'Applying the Brand' includes a Gallery, Do/Don't, Templates, Branded Merchandise, and Photos & Videos - the show-don't-tell layer is structural, not an afterthought
Governance surface is complete: Downloads, FAQ, History, and Contact (mit-brand@mit.edu, contact form) in the persistent sidebar

sections.name: Brand Architecture
sections.notes: First nav item; homepage's 'Unified' section claims a simplified architecture so schools and units tell one story. Strategy-adjacent, but the deepest 'why' layer the guide shows.

sections.name: Logos & Marks
sections.notes: Expandable section covering MIT Logo, Logo Lock-Ups, Social Media Logos, MIT Seal, and Tim the Beaver - a real mark taxonomy, teased by the 'Optimized' story of the modernized logo.

sections.name: Color
sections.notes: 'Bold' section promises 'more vibrant core colors and an exciting secondary palette'; the hero's five circles preview maroon, red, black, silver, white. Exact values live inside the chapter, not on the homepage.

sections.name: Typography
sections.notes: Present as a top-level chapter; no typeface names or samples are exposed on the homepage itself.

sections.name: Applying the Brand
sections.notes: The strongest limb: Gallery, Do/Don't, Templates, Branded Merchandise, Photos & Videos, echoed by the homepage's merch, poster, and vehicle mockups.

sections.name: Downloads / FAQ / History / Contact
sections.notes: Full service layer; Downloads shows a lock icon (community login), History gives the identity a timeline, Contact routes to mit-brand@mit.edu.

needs: A verbal identity chapter - voice and tone, messaging pillars, boilerplate - nothing in the nav covers how MIT sounds
An explicit brand-strategy page (mission, audience, the idea in one sentence) rather than strategy implied through 'Optimized/Bold/Unified' marketing copy
Color values and typeface names surfaced earlier - the homepage shows swatch circles but no HEX/PMS or font naming
Motion guidelines - the hero animates, but no stated principles for how the brand moves
A public asset path for external vendors and press, since Downloads appears locked to MIT accounts
A visible version number or last-updated date (History covers the past, not the current revision)

principle.title: Open the rules, gate only the files
principle.explanation: MIT leaves every rule, mockup, and rationale public while putting a lock only on Downloads. Outsiders can learn and evaluate the brand; only the production assets require belonging. That maximizes education while keeping the mark controlled - the opposite failure modes are fully-gated guides nobody reads and open kits nobody governs.
principle.howToApply: When building a brand site for 35353 or a client, publish the entire rulebook publicly and put authentication only on the asset bundle (logo files, templates), with a request path for vendors - never gate the knowledge itself.

entries.tagline: Organizes every rule by who is asking - businesses, partners, press - instead of by asset type.
entries.summary: The Yelp Brand Center is a single long page - 'A guide for Yelp assets and content' - built for outsiders who touch Yelp's brand: businesses, resellers, and journalists. Its spine is audience-first: 'For businesses on Yelp', 'For strategic business partners and resellers', 'For press and media', then 'Additional terms.' It is strongest on content usage (reviews, photos, star ratings, attribution formats) and logo licensing, with a one-click download of .EPS/.PNG/.SVG logos. It is deliberately not a visual system: no palette values, no typography, no clearspace diagrams - protection and permission, mostly in prose.
whatWorks: Audience-segmented structure: businesses, strategic partners/resellers, and press each get their own section with only the rules relevant to them
The mark gets a story, not just a spec: the 'burst' is 'an homage to the symbol that pops up over the head of a cartoon character during a moment of discovery'
Review-usage rules are unusually concrete: numbered requirements including only 'Recommended Reviews', reviewer first name and date, and attribution 'via Yelp' with a follow link
Attribution formats are given as literal copy-paste strings - 'Photo by Jane D. via Yelp' and for press 'Photo by Jane D., 3/18/23, via Yelp'
Named logo taxonomy for third parties: 'Find us on Yelp', 'Yelp for business', 'Yelp for Restaurants', the favicon, and 'Yelp Advertising Partner' / 'Premier Partner' lockups
Clear escalation routes per concern: trademarks@yelp.com for branding questions, press@yelp.com for media, plus a sticker request form

sections.name: The Yelp Brand and our Guidelines
sections.notes: Brand story (community, trust, the 'burst') beside the Yelp and 'yelp for business' logos, with a 'Download logos' button covering .EPS, .PNG, .SVG. Good framing; no clearspace or sizing diagrams.

sections.name: For businesses on Yelp
sections.notes: The workhorse: which logos businesses may use, the favicon, five numbered rules for quoting reviews, photo/video attribution, star-rating rules (use dynamic 'Review Badges', never static star imagery), and a bulleted list of additional restrictions.

sections.name: For strategic business partners and resellers
sections.notes: Short section tying partner logo use ('Yelp Advertising Partner' / 'Premier Partner') to contract terms and eligibility.

sections.name: For press and media
sections.notes: Conditions for embedding Yelp content in stories - no use in negative stories about Yelp, follow-link required, dated attribution format - plus a logo download link and press@yelp.com.

sections.name: Additional terms
sections.notes: The legal floor: 'Yelp Creative Assets' license (non-transferable, royalty-free, revocable), governed by California law. Dense but honest about what the license is.

needs: Color specs - Yelp red is everywhere on the page but never given as HEX/RGB/PMS values
Typography - no typeface names, hierarchy, or usage rules at all
Clearspace and minimum-size diagrams for the logo family; sizing is only addressed as 'preserving the original proportions' in prose
Visual examples of misuse - the many don'ts (distortion, implying endorsement, comparative advertising) are text-only bullets
Per-variant asset downloads - one bundle exists, but the named variants ('Find us on Yelp', partner lockups) are not individually downloadable from their sections
A version number or last-updated date; only the footer's copyright range (2004-2026) hints at currency

principle.title: Structure external brand rules by audience, not by asset
principle.explanation: Outsiders arrive with a role ('I run a restaurant', 'I'm writing an article'), not an asset question. Yelp's sections mirror those roles, so each reader gets a short, complete rule set instead of scanning a full spec for the three rules that apply to them - which is how rules actually get followed.
principle.howToApply: For any partner-facing brand page, define the two to four audiences first and give each a self-contained section with only their permissions, their named assets, their attribution strings, and their contact route - and let the legal terms sit once at the end.

entries.tagline: An identity site shot like a campaign - every element of the system is shown living on real community imagery, never on a blank artboard.
entries.summary: Instagram's brand site walks the whole identity - custom typeface, gradient color, glyph, layout, motion - as a single cinematic scroll over full-bleed community photography, with an 'Explore' deep link per chapter carrying the actual specs. It is unusually complete for a public guide and doubles as proof of the identity in use: billboards, station posters and social frames appear as photographed applications, not mockups. The trade-off is that the index page itself carries almost no copyable values; everything specific lives one click deeper.
whatWorks: Every identity element gets a chapter with a giant demonstration and an 'Explore type / gradient / layout' deep link to the spec
A custom typeface (Instagram Sans) is presented 'created for global scale' with the glyph construction shown in blueprint style
The gradient is treated as a codified core asset with its own section, not a decorative effect
Applications are photographed in the real world - OOH billboards, transit posters, Reels frames - proving the system at street scale
The whole guide is art-directed with real community imagery, so it demonstrates the brand voice ('Yours to make') while documenting it

sections.name: Hero / glyph
sections.notes: The outlined glyph floats over a full-bleed community portrait - identity and audience in one frame before a single rule is stated.

sections.name: Brand identity intro
sections.notes: 'Instagram's brand identity' set in the brand's own type with the word 'brand' in gradient - typographic self-demonstration.

sections.name: Type
sections.notes: 'A custom typeface created for global scale' with a blueprint-style glyph card and an 'Explore type' link to the full spec.

sections.name: Color / gradient
sections.notes: 'Color designed to illuminate and inspire' with the signature gradient swatch as a first-class asset and an 'Explore gradient' link.

sections.name: Layout
sections.notes: 'Layouts built to showcase our community' - the glyph-on-grid system, with 'Explore layout' deep link.

sections.name: Applications & motion
sections.notes: Photographed real-world uses (billboards, station posters, tri-frame motion strip) rather than sterile mockups.

sections.name: Footer / governance links
sections.notes: Routes to About Instagram and Meta's Brand Resource Center for permissions and downloads.

needs: Copyable values on the surface - no hex codes, type scales or clearspace numbers are visible without clicking into each 'Explore' page
Voice & tone rules - the attitude is demonstrated ('Yours to make') but writing guidance is never codified
Do/don't misuse examples for glyph, gradient and type
Accessibility guidance - gradient-over-photo and white-on-photo text pairs are shown without contrast rules
Versioning and an update trail so users know which identity generation they are reading
Downloadable asset kit on the page itself rather than routed through Meta's separate resource center

principle.title: Shoot the brand in the wild, not on a blank artboard
principle.explanation: Instagram proves every element - type, gradient, glyph, layout - on photographed real-world surfaces and community imagery, which shows the system surviving reality instead of an idealized artboard, and teaches applications by example.
principle.howToApply: When documenting an identity, photograph or realistically mock each core element deployed in its real environment (a poster on a wall, a post in the feed, a sign on a building) and use those as the guide's illustrations instead of flat swatches on white.

entries.tagline: A third-party marketing rulebook that hands businesses pre-approved CTA lockups and even polices the exact phrases they may use.
entries.summary: A single long page aimed at businesses promoting their presence on Pinterest - 'These guidelines are for businesses promoting their presence on Pinterest' - covering in-store signage, packaging, digital media and broadcast. It is unusually deep on usage mechanics (lockup templates, acceptable phrasing, product depiction) and unusually shallow on raw specs: no hex values, no clearspace or minimum-size diagrams, no typography. As a protective outsider-facing kit it does its narrow job well.
whatWorks: Opens with 'The basics' - a three-column TLDR (Pinterest logo / Product screens / Language) before the full guidelines, so skimmers get the critical rules first
One blunt logo rule that removes ambiguity: 'Only use the Pinterest badge (please don't use our wordmark)', with just two approved treatments - primary red and secondary black or white
Four concrete logo don'ts, each shown as a crossed-out image: do not outline, do not add filters or effects, do not remove the P from the circle, do not alter the logo color

Ships ready-made call-to-action lockup templates (no container / gray container over white / white container, centered CTA, left-aligned CTA, account-URL variants) instead of trusting outsiders to compose their own
A real verbal-usage section: acceptable phrases like 'Follow us on Pinterest' vs unacceptable ones like 'Trending on Pinterest', plus conditions for saying 'Popular on Pinterest'
Product depiction rule that most kits forget: the interface shown must match the device - mobile UI on mobile mockups, desktop UI on desktop

sections.name: The basics
sections.notes: Quick three-column summary of logo, product-screen and language rules; a genuinely useful executive layer before the detail.

sections.name: Our logo
sections.notes: Badge-only policy with primary red and secondary black/white examples; clear but gives no color values or size specs.

sections.name: Things to avoid when using our logo
sections.notes: Four pictured don'ts (outline, filters/effects, removing the P, recoloring) - concrete and hard to misread.

sections.name: Call to action lockups
sections.notes: The standout: downloadable interactive lockup templates plus static lockup guidance for CTA and account-URL combinations.

sections.name: Language
sections.notes: Acceptable vs unacceptable phrases, when 'Popular on Pinterest' is allowed, and naming rules for third-party apps and services.

sections.name: Product depictions
sections.notes: Interface-must-match-device rule for showing Pinterest in marketing; short but specific.

sections.name: Press assets
sections.notes: Product screens, footage of product and Pinners, office/employee footage and leadership photos, plus press-inquiry contacts.

needs: Exact color values - the famous Pinterest red is never given as HEX/RGB/Pantone anywhere on the page
Clearspace and minimum-size diagrams for the badge; the guide describes usage but never dimensions it
Any typography guidance - the static CTA section says to use your own typeface, but Pinterest's own type is absent
A single downloadable brand-kit bundle; assets are scattered across per-section 'view' links
Accessibility guidance such as approved contrast pairings for the badge on backgrounds
A version number or last-updated date so marketers know the rules are current

principle.title: Ship pre-approved lockups, not raw logos
principle.explanation: Pinterest's CTA lockup templates show that the safest way to protect a mark used by thousands of outsiders is to do the composition for them - every rule you encode as a template is a rule nobody can break.
principle.howToApply: For 35353's partner or press page, publish assembled lockups (logo + CTA + URL in approved arrangements) as downloadable files, rather than a bare logo plus prose rules about how to combine it with text.

entries.tagline: A dark, searchable brand site whose sidebar taxonomy - Brand identity, Foundations, Graphic elements, Brand in action, Motion identity - is itself a lesson in how to structure a guide.
entries.summary: GitHub's 'Guidelines and principles to help design and write in GitHub's brand voice', fronted by a 3D render of Mona the mascot and a green Getting started button. The landing page is a router: five entry cards (Logo, Typography, Color, Illustration, Mascots) plus links out to the Primer Marketing UI and Primer Product UI design systems. The taxonomy is exemplary and the coverage broad - voice and tone, co-branding, accessibility, motion - though the overview itself surfaces no concrete values, so everything lives one click deeper.
whatWorks: The sidebar reads as an altitude map: Guides > Brand identity (Brand attributes, Co-branding, Copilot, Voice and tone) > Foundations (Accessibility, Color, Logo, Typography) > Graphic elements (Diagrams, Iconography, Illustration, Layouts, Mascots, Product UI, Textures) > Brand in action (eBooks, Experiential, Presentations, Social, Swag, Web) > Motion identity
Accessibility is a Foundation, listed as a peer of Color, Logo and Typography rather than buried in an appendix

Explicitly bridges brand and product: a dedicated section links Primer Marketing UI ('GitHub's design system for creating marketing websites') and Primer Product UI, so the brand layer and the shipping UI stay one hop apart
'Brand in action' gives real application surfaces - eBooks, Experiential, Presentations, Social, Swag, Web - not abstract swatches
A persistent 'Search Brand Toolkit' field in the header; almost no brand guide is searchable
An 'Edit this page' footer link and a light/dark toggle - the guide behaves like living, open documentation, on brand for GitHub

sections.name: Getting started
sections.notes: Hero with the Mona mascot render and one-line mission; a single green CTA routes new users into the guide.

sections.name: Brand identity
sections.notes: Brand attributes, Co-branding, Copilot and Voice and tone - strategy and verbal identity get their own top-level group, including a page for the Copilot sub-brand.

sections.name: Foundations
sections.notes: Accessibility, Color, Logo, Typography; the Typography card promises 'GitHub's own expressive typeface' plus typographic scales.

sections.name: Graphic elements
sections.notes: Seven pages (Diagrams, Iconography, Illustration, Layouts, Mascots, Product UI, Textures) - unusually granular; illustration is framed as 'the transformative power of collaboration'.

sections.name: Brand in action
sections.notes: Application gallery across eBooks, Experiential, Presentations, Social, Swag and Web.

sections.name: Motion identity
sections.notes: Events and logo-animation guidance - motion treated as a first-class identity layer.

sections.name: Primer design systems
sections.notes: Outbound cards to Primer Marketing UI and Primer Product UI connect the brand guide to the component/token layer.

needs: Concrete specs on the overview - no hex values, typeface names or logo rules are visible without clicking through; a values cheat-sheet on the landing page would make it usable in seconds
Photography and art direction for real imagery - Graphic elements covers illustration, icons and textures but no photo style, and Brand in action leans illustrated
A prominent all-in-one asset download; the landing page routes to guidance but never to a logo/color/type bundle
Messaging pillars, tagline and boilerplate to round out the verbal layer beyond Voice and tone
Public usage/legal terms for third parties who want to reference GitHub - nothing on the landing page addresses outsiders
A visible version number or changelog, despite the living 'Edit this page' mechanism

principle.title: Stage the guide from foundations to brand in action
principle.explanation: GitHub's sidebar teaches the system's logic before you read a single rule: identity first, then foundations, then the elements built on them, then proof in application, then motion. A reader always knows what level they are on and where a new rule belongs.
principle.howToApply: Structure the 35353 brand guide's nav in the same altitude order - strategy/voice, foundations (color/type/logo/accessibility), graphic elements, applications, motion - and make every new page slot into exactly one of those levels.

entries.tagline: A lawyer-forward trademark kit that uses its own masthead to announce a program shutdown - the hub doubles as the brand's channel of record.
entries.summary: A one-page hub - 'If you're looking to talk about LinkedIn for your business, or use LinkedIn branding, here's a helpful guide to show you how' - with four Guidance cards ([in] Logo, LinkedIn Logo, Badges & Other Programs, Business/Books & Other Media Usage) followed by a Legal section that occupies roughly half the page. Visually it is thin: the hub itself shows no color values, clearspace diagrams or don'ts, deferring everything to the four sub-pages. It is honest about what it is - a trademark-protection kit, not a design resource.
whatWorks: A red notice banner at the very top - 'The LinkedIn Local program has been discontinued as of January 1, 2026' - uses the brand hub itself to broadcast a program change, with a 'Learn what this means for you' link
Cleanly splits the mark into two artifacts with separate pages: the [in] badge and the full 'LinkedIn' wordmark-plus-badge lockup, each with its own card and rules
Covers genuinely awkward edge cases most kits ignore: certification badges, and using the brand in 'Business, Books & Other Media Usage'

The Legal section is plain-language and specific, e.g. usage must not 'create the impression that your use is sponsored by LinkedIn' and 'Any logos or images found elsewhere on the web are not approved for use'
Spells out consequences - violations can mean 'suspension or termination of your LinkedIn account' - so the rules have visible teeth
A clarifying footnote under a rendered badge - 'LinkedIn's use of the [in] Logo refers to the logo above' - removes ambiguity about which mark the text governs

sections.name: Notice banner
sections.notes: Site-wide program-discontinuation announcement dated January 1, 2026; the guide acting as a live communications channel.

sections.name: Guidance
sections.notes: Four-card index: [in] Logo, LinkedIn Logo, Badges & Other Programs, and Business/Books & Other Media Usage; thumbnails preview each artifact.

sections.name: [in] Logo / LinkedIn Logo
sections.notes: Separate sub-pages for badge vs full lockup; the hub itself shows the marks but no specs.

sections.name: Badges & Other Programs
sections.notes: Covers certification-style badges (a Certified Marketing Expert seal is pictured) and program marks.

sections.name: Legal
sections.notes: Six dense but readable paragraphs on trademark ownership, permission, prohibited confusion, enforcement and the instruction not to 'copy or imitate the LinkedIn platform's overall look and feel'.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Standard corporate links including Accessibility; (c) LinkedIn Corporation 2026.

needs: Any visual specification on the hub itself - no LinkedIn Blue value, no clearspace or minimum-size diagram, no misuse examples are visible before clicking through
Typography guidance - the brand's typeface is never mentioned
Pictured do/don't examples; the Legal prose carries all the weight that visuals should share
A downloadable asset kit with formats listed; the hub offers guidance links but no obvious download path
Voice/verbal identity - acceptable and unacceptable phrasing for talking about LinkedIn, which its peers (e.g. Pinterest) do provide
Accessibility guidance for the mark, such as approved contrast pairings on light and dark backgrounds

principle.title: Make the brand hub the channel of record
principle.explanation: LinkedIn's discontinuation banner shows the guide working as infrastructure: when a program dies or a rule changes, the people who need to know are exactly the people already using the brand hub. Announcing changes anywhere else guarantees stale usage in the wild.
principle.howToApply: Give the 35353 brand guide a persistent announcement slot at the top of the page and commit to posting every identity change there first - logo revisions, deprecated assets, renamed programs - each with a dated banner and a link to migration guidance.

entries.tagline: A federated university's brand hub that leads with permission - 'Who can use our brand' is the hero image caption, before a single visual rule appears.
entries.summary: The 'Our brand' hub for a university 'built of many unique parts ranging from academic departments and research centres to museums and hospitals'. Its nav runs The University logo / Guidelines / Content principles / Brand protection / Merchandise / Resources A-Z, and a six-card index routes to logo use, guidelines, photography, templates, content style and the Cambridge Web Platform. Strong on governance and tooling for a sprawling institution; the hub itself stays at the routing level, with no palette values or type specimens visible.
whatWorks: Permission comes first: the hero image is captioned 'Who can use our brand', and the logo card leads with 'Find out who can use the logo' - the right priority for a federated institution
A named, reachable owner in the sidebar: 'Get help' gives brand@admin.cam.ac.uk plus the Office of External Affairs and Communications with a full postal address
A dedicated 'Report unauthorised use' path with its own email route - enforcement is designed in, not implied
Photography style stated as one memorable sentence: 'Our photographic style centres around people. It is candid and captures real moments.'
Extends the guide into working tools: branded templates for presentations and documents, and the Cambridge Web Platform card for building compliant University websites
'Write clear content' makes the verbal layer a first-class card, pointing to content principles and a style guide for 'accessible, user-focused content'

sections.name: The University logo
sections.notes: Who may use it, downloads, and correct application; the shield lockup is shown on a Cambridge Blue tile.

sections.name: Guidelines
sections.notes: Colour, typography, photography, visual language and signage grouped under one nav item - present but one click deep.

sections.name: Content principles
sections.notes: Writing style and accessibility via a dedicated style guide; verbal identity handled as guidance, not just tone adjectives.

sections.name: Brand protection
sections.notes: Trademarks and enforcement, paired with the sidebar's report-unauthorised-use contact.

sections.name: Merchandise
sections.notes: Branded-product rules get their own top-level section - a real need for a university with colleges and shops.

sections.name: Get help / Report unauthorised use
sections.notes: Named team, email and physical address; the strongest governance sidebar in this batch.

needs: Visible foundations on the hub: no colour values (Cambridge Blue is shown but never specified) and no typeface names appear before clicking through
Pictured do/don't examples for the shield and lockups; the hub shows only correct usage
A brand-strategy layer - mission, positioning and personality are absent; the intro describes the institution, not the idea
Motion and video identity guidance alongside signage and photography
Accessibility contrast pairings for the palette, especially given the teal-on-dark hub design
A version number or last-updated date on the toolkit itself

principle.title: Answer who can use the brand before how
principle.explanation: In any organization where many semi-independent units share one mark - departments, franchises, partners - most brand damage comes from unauthorized or out-of-scope use, not bad kerning. Cambridge puts the permission model at the front door so every later rule lands on someone entitled to apply it.
principle.howToApply: Open the 35353 guide with a short eligibility section - who may use which assets (internal team, partners, press) and how to request access - before any visual rules, and pair it with a visible contact for reporting misuse.

entries.tagline: A brand center whose index cards are miniature specimens - the Color card is a swatch grid, the Typography card is Aa tiles - so the nav previews the system before you click.
entries.summary: The public face of Zoom's Brand Center: a deep-blue hero with 3D gradient shapes and floating chat/phone icons, top nav for Brand guidelines / Download assets / Partner branding / Help, and four 'Guideline quick links' cards (Color, Typography, Logo, Photography). It is honest that this is a teaser: the hero states 'Team members: Use the lock button in the lower left of the page to log in and view the entire site', and the capture ends shortly after the quick links. What is public is polished and on-brand, but the substance is gated - WebFetch returned nothing beyond the page title, and no values or rules are verifiable from outside.
whatWorks: Index-as-specimen quick links: the Color guide card is an actual swatch grid (blues, violet, magenta, green, orange, teal, olive), Typography shows layered 'Aa' tiles, Logo shows the wordmark on its blue tile, Photography shows a real portrait - each card demonstrates its section's content

Explicit audience signposting in the hero: 'Need help getting started? Check out our intro page under the help menu' for outsiders, and a separate instruction for team members to log in for the full site
'Download assets' and 'Partner branding' are top-level nav items, so the two most common visitor jobs are one click from anywhere
The hero itself performs the refreshed identity - dark blue field, luminous 3D gradient forms, product-shaped icons - rather than describing it
A persistent lock button (bottom-left) makes the public/internal boundary a visible, deliberate mechanism instead of a surprise 404

sections.name: Header navigation
sections.notes: Brand guidelines, Download assets, Partner branding and Help dropdowns plus search - a complete top-level map of the center.

sections.name: Welcome hero
sections.notes: 'Welcome to the Zoom Brand Center' with onboarding pointers for both outsiders and logged-in team members; visually the strongest brand statement on the page.

sections.name: Guideline quick links
sections.notes: Four preview cards - Color guide, Typography guide, Logo guide, Photography guide - each illustrated with its own content type.

sections.name: Need more help?
sections.notes: A support section begins at the capture's edge; content not visible.

sections.name: Login gate
sections.notes: Lock button lower-left; the full site is restricted to team members, which bounds what this public layer can teach.

needs: Public specs for anyone referencing Zoom: no hex values, typeface names, clearspace or minimum sizes are reachable without a team login
Usage rules and don'ts on the public layer - a partner or journalist cannot verify correct usage from what is visible
A verbal-identity presence - voice, tone or messaging never appears in the visible nav
Accessibility guidance such as approved contrast pairings for the saturated blue/magenta palette
A version number or last-updated date visible on the center
Clarity about what 'Partner branding' grants versus the gated internal guide, so outsiders know which rules apply to them

principle.title: Let the index preview the system
principle.explanation: Zoom's quick-link cards prove that navigation can carry identity: a swatch grid says 'color lives here' faster than a label, and the palette, type and photography are already teaching before the first click. Dead-text menus waste the guide's best storefront.
principle.howToApply: On the 35353 guide's landing page, build each section card out of its own content - the color card from real brand swatches, the type card from the actual display face, the photography card from an approved image - so the index doubles as a one-screen brand summary.

entries.tagline: A portfolio-level front door that routes you to per-brand guidelines and bakes the permission workflow (My Requests) right into the kit.
entries.summary: The landing hub of Meta's multi-brand asset center: a hero explaining the job ('Learn how to use brand assets and showcase content from Meta technologies and programs'), five brand cards (Meta, Facebook, Instagram, Threads, WhatsApp), and an 'Exceptions' block spelling out when you do and do not need permission. As a hub it does its routing job cleanly, but the captured page itself contains no actual identity rules - no logo diagrams, colors, or type - so everything of substance lives one click deeper.
whatWorks: Brand-first navigation: five clean cards (Meta, Facebook, Instagram, Threads, WhatsApp), each with its official mark, so you self-select the sub-brand before seeing a single rule

The 'Exceptions / More details' block states the permission model in plain language: advertising is reviewed by the Ad Policy team and 'does not require permission here'; all other marketing 'must use the officially provided assets and abide by the guidelines on this site'
A 'My Requests' link in the top nav turns the guide into a workflow tool - you can track approval requests without leaving the resource center
Sets a practical constraint up front: requests are processed in English only, which prevents dead-end submissions
Warm lifestyle hero photo of two people rather than abstract swatches - the portfolio brand leads with its human subject matter

sections.name: Hero / intro
sections.notes: Big 'Brand Resource Center' title with a one-line mission statement and a full-width lifestyle photograph; instantly communicates scope

sections.name: Brand directory
sections.notes: 'Explore how to use brand assets from Meta technologies and programs' - five cards with logos and arrow links to per-brand guideline microsites; the strongest part of the page

sections.name: Exceptions / More details
sections.notes: Two short paragraphs covering the advertising carve-out (Ad Policy team review) and the general rule that official assets plus on-site guidelines replace case-by-case permission

sections.name: My Requests
sections.notes: Persistent nav item for tracking asset-use requests - governance built into the interface rather than a buried email address

sections.name: Footer legal
sections.notes: About, Terms, Help, 'Our trademarks', Privacy, Cookies - trademark policy is one link away

needs: Any visible identity content at hub level - not one logo rule, color value, or clearspace diagram appears before you click into a sub-brand
Direct downloads: the hub routes but never lets you grab an asset kit from the landing page
Typography and voice guidance anywhere in the visible flow
A version number or last-updated date - nothing signals whether the guidance is current
Even one worked do/don't example at the portfolio level (e.g. how Meta and Instagram marks may sit together in co-branding)

principle.title: Build the approval workflow into the kit
principle.explanation: Most brand kits end with 'email us for anything else', which is where compliance dies. Meta puts a 'My Requests' tracker in the nav and states exactly which uses skip review (ads via Ad Policy, marketing that follows the guidelines), so the reader always knows their next step and its status.
principle.howToApply: When publishing brand assets for 35353 or a client, pair the rules with a lightweight request path: a form or tracked inbox, an explicit list of pre-approved uses that need no contact, and a stated turnaround. The guide should answer 'may I?' or route it - never strand the reader.

entries.tagline: A values-first guide: four named brand values open the page, and every asset that follows is framed as evidence of them.
entries.summary: Canonical's Ubuntu brand page leads with belief, not assets: 'Canonical and Ubuntu - Our brand values' names four values (Freedom, Reliable, Precise, Collaborative), each with a sentence of meaning, before any logo appears. Only then come 'Our brand guidelines' and a 'Brand assets' section with Logos and a six-swatch Colour palette card. The guide lives inside Canonical's broader design portal alongside Font, Vanilla (the design system) and Accessibility - a tidy structure, though the page itself is shallow on specifics and its footer still reads 2023.
whatWorks: Opens with four named brand values (Freedom, Reliable, Precise, Collaborative), each explained in one plain sentence
Frames the guidelines as a promise ('everything you need to create professional communication materials') tied to brand growth, giving the rules a why
Brand sits inside one design portal with Font, Vanilla (design system) and Accessibility as sibling nav items - identity and product system share a roof
Logos card states the logo's job in brand terms ('striking and clear... represents the brand's core values') rather than just offering a download
Colour palette is presented as an evolved, meaning-bearing system ('convey the correct meaning') with six swatches led by Ubuntu orange and aubergine

sections.name: Brand values
sections.notes: Four values in a clean four-column grid, each with a one-sentence definition - the philosophical base of everything below.

sections.name: Our brand guidelines
sections.notes: A short manifesto connecting consistent use of the guidelines to the brand's growth - rationale before rules.

sections.name: Brand assets - Logos
sections.notes: The Ubuntu wordmark + circle-of-friends mark with a statement of the logo's role; links to the logo section.

sections.name: Brand assets - Colour palette
sections.notes: Six swatches (orange, aubergine, black, greys) framed as a system for conveying 'the correct meaning'.

sections.name: Design portal nav
sections.notes: Brand / Font / Vanilla / Accessibility / Resources / Contribute - the brand layer is one wing of a complete open design site.

needs: Copyable color values - the palette shows swatches but no hex/RGB on this page
Typography rules on the brand page itself - the Ubuntu font family has a section but the brand page never states usage or hierarchy
Clearspace, minimum size and misuse examples for the logo
Imagery and photography direction - nothing visual beyond logo and palette
Real-world application examples (web, decks, packaging, events)
A version stamp and owner - the footer's 2023 copyright suggests staleness with no update trail

principle.title: State what the brand believes before what it looks like
principle.explanation: Ubuntu opens its guide with four named values and one-sentence meanings, so every rule that follows reads as a consequence of belief rather than an arbitrary restriction - the cheapest way to make a guide teach judgment, not just compliance.
principle.howToApply: Start any brand guide with 3-5 named values, each defined in a single plain sentence, then explicitly connect each later rule back to the value it serves ('the palette is restrained because we are Precise').

entries.tagline: A ruthlessly minimal two-card kit whose smartest move is shipping the integration use case - the 'Connect Supabase' OAuth button - as a downloadable asset.
entries.summary: One short page: a 'Brand assets' heading, a blanket trademark sentence, and exactly two cards - 'Supabase logos' (SVGs in light and dark theme, 'Download logo kit') and 'Supabase Integrations' (an official 'Connect Supabase' button kit for OAuth flows). This is a deliberately thin kit, and it is honest about that: it states one rule ('Do not use any other color for the wordmark'), points at the downloads, and stops. Effective for its narrow job, but everything beyond the logo is absent.
whatWorks: Anticipates the number-one real-world use: third-party developers embedding a 'Connect Supabase' OAuth button get an official, pre-built button kit instead of improvising one
One unambiguous rule stated on both cards: 'Do not use any other color for the wordmark' - the single highest-risk misuse is impossible to miss
Blanket protection sentence up front: 'All Supabase trademarks, logos, or other brand elements can never be modified or used for any other purpose other than to represent Supabase Inc.'
Logos ship as SVG in both light and dark theme - the two variants developers actually need, previewed on the page in a dark card exactly as they will be used
The page itself is on-brand: dark surface, green bolt mark, same layout language as the rest of supabase.com

sections.name: Intro / trademark statement
sections.notes: 'Brand assets - Download official Supabase logos' plus the one-sentence legal blanket; total reading time about ten seconds

sections.name: Supabase logos
sections.notes: Preview of the green-bolt wordmark on dark, notes SVGs in light and dark theme, the wordmark-color rule, and a 'Download logo kit' button

sections.name: Supabase Integrations
sections.notes: Live preview of the official 'Connect Supabase' button, instruction to use it 'to initiate the OAuth redirect', and a 'Download button kit' button - the standout module

sections.name: Marketing CTA
sections.notes: 'Build in a weekend, scale to millions' banner with Start-your-project buttons - product funnel, not brand content, sharing the page

needs: Color values: the brand green appears everywhere but no hex/RGB is published on the page
Clearspace and minimum-size diagrams for the mark and wordmark
Misuse examples - the one 'do not recolor' sentence is the entire don'ts section
Typography: nothing on typefaces, weights, or hierarchy
Guidance for the symbol used alone (favicon/app-icon contexts) versus the full wordmark
A version or last-updated date on the kit downloads

principle.title: Ship your most common third-party use case as a finished asset
principle.explanation: Most misuse happens when outsiders rebuild something themselves. Supabase noticed its ecosystem's top need - a Connect button in other people's apps - and shipped it as a downloadable, pre-approved component, converting a likely violation into a one-click correct outcome.
principle.howToApply: When building a brand-assets page, list the top three things outsiders actually do with the brand (embed a button, write a co-marketing header, drop a logo in a footer) and publish each as a ready-made kit. For 35353, that could be an official 'listing badge' or partner lockup shipped as SVG rather than described in rules.

entries.tagline: Specifies the marks all the way down to a Unicode codepoint and casing rules, so the brand survives even in plain text.
entries.summary: The 'Brands' page inside Vercel's Geist design system: one long, uniform treatment of the whole product family - Vercel, Next.js, Turbo, Turborepo, Turbopack, v0, eve, and AI SDK - each with light/dark logotypes, a symbol variant, spacing guidance, and a download link, capped by a 'General information' and 'Usage' section with explicit permitted and prohibited uses. It is a strong, engineering-grade brand layer; its gaps are everything non-logo (color, type, applications), which live elsewhere in Geist or nowhere.
whatWorks: Defines the Vercel symbol as a literal Unicode character (the black up-pointing triangle, U+25B2) under 'Symbol & unicode' - the mark has a specified plain-text fallback
Verbal precision per brand: 'Next.js spelling' allows 'Next' only after first mention with 'nextjs' in URLs, and 'eve spelling' mandates all-lowercase, always
Every sub-brand gets the identical anatomy - logotype in light and dark, symbol-only variant, download button - so the family reads as one system across eight brands
'Spacing considerations' ties clearspace to the mark itself: the safety area around the primary logo is defined by the height of its symbol, shown as diagrams
