'Usage' section gives copy-paste-able permitted statements ('Our website is hosted on the Vercel platform') plus a concrete misuse list (no business names, no implied endorsement, no merchandise, never more prominent than your own brand)
Ships the required trademark attribution line verbatim so partners can paste it: 'Vercel, the Vercel design, Next.js and related marks... are trademarks or registered trademarks of Vercel, Inc.'

sections.name: Vercel
sections.notes: Primary logotype on light and dark, 'Symbol & unicode' (U+25B2), 'Spacing considerations' diagrams, asset download - the template every other brand follows

sections.name: Next.js
sections.notes: Logotype, 'Next.js symbol' with same-line usage rule, and 'Next.js spelling' covering casing and URL form

sections.name: Turbo family (Turbo / Turborepo / Turbopack)
sections.notes: Three related marks each with logotype plus symbol sections; the shared treatment makes the sub-family legible at a glance

sections.name: v0 and eve
sections.notes: Newer product marks handled with the same rigor, including the all-lowercase 'eve spelling' rule

sections.name: AI SDK
sections.notes: Final product mark with logotype variants and downloads; completes full portfolio coverage

sections.name: General information
sections.notes: The exact trademark attribution sentence partners must include

sections.name: Usage / Misuse
sections.notes: Bulleted permitted uses with example sentences, followed by a prohibited list (modification, business names, endorsement implications, merchandise, prominence)

needs: Color: no palette or hex values on the page, despite logos shipping in light/dark - surface-behavior rules are implied, never stated
Typography guidance - the Geist typeface exists elsewhere in the design system but the brand layer never references it
Application examples: no mockups of the marks in real contexts (social avatars, co-branded headers, conference slides)
Visual don'ts - misuse is a text list with no pictured wrong examples
Co-branding / lockup rules for pairing Vercel with partner logos
A version number or changelog for the brand layer itself

principle.title: Specify the mark down to the character
principle.explanation: Brands now live in terminals, commit messages, package names, and URLs where no SVG can follow. Vercel gives its symbol a Unicode codepoint and each product an exact casing rule, so the identity stays correct even in plain text - a failure mode most guides never consider.
principle.howToApply: For any brand with a developer or text-heavy surface, add a 'plain text' spec: canonical casing (is it 35353 or 3-5-3-5-3?), URL slug form, an approved character or emoji fallback for the mark, and where abbreviations are allowed. Put it beside the logo rules, not in an appendix.

entries.tagline: Treats localized product screenshots as first-class brand assets, sitting equal to logos in a three-door press kit.
entries.summary: A compact press-facing kit with exactly three doors: 'Logos', 'Product screenshots', and the 'Slack brand center' (the full guide covering 'logos, color, typography, writing, illustration and more'). The screenshots card is the distinctive move - official high-res interface captures for desktop, mobile, and tablet in English, French, German, and Japanese. The page does its narrow media job well, but carries no actual rules beyond a legal paragraph; every specification is one click deeper in the Brand Center.
whatWorks: Elevates product screenshots to a named asset category: 'Get high-resolution assets of the Slack interface on desktop, mobile and tablet. Available in English, French, German and Japanese' - press never has to screengrab a stale UI

Defines the protected mark broadly and plainly: 'The Slack marks include the Slack name and logo, and any word, phrase, image, or other designation that identifies the source or origin of any of Slack's products'

Gives an unusually practical escalation path: uses not covered by the guidelines go to feedback@slack.com 'and include a visual mockup of intended use' - it asks for the artifact reviewers actually need
Three-card layout with clear jobs (Logos / Product screenshots / Brand center) means a journalist finds the right door in seconds
The page is visibly on-brand: aubergine panels, the multicolor octothorpe mark, and Slack's rounded display type in 'Try Slack with your team for free'

sections.name: Intro
sections.notes: 'Media Kit' heading with copy positioning the resources as usable 'without having to negotiate legal agreements', plus the mockup-required contact route

sections.name: Logos
sections.notes: Card with the wordmark on aubergine, the broad marks definition, and a 'View all' link to the logo library - definitions here, files one level down

sections.name: Product screenshots
sections.notes: Card previewing desktop and mobile UI captures; explicitly localized in four languages - the kit's standout offer

sections.name: Slack brand center
sections.notes: Gateway card to the comprehensive hub 'including logos, color, typography, writing, illustration and more' - honest signpost that the full guide lives elsewhere

sections.name: Legal strip
sections.notes: Gray band binding use of the marks to the guidelines and Terms of Service, with Slack reserving the right to 'cancel, modify, or change the permission... at any time at its sole discretion'

needs: Any on-page specifics: not a single color value, clearspace diagram, or minimum size appears in the kit itself
Direct downloads - each card routes to another page rather than offering a one-click zip
Visual do/don't examples for the logo, especially given how broadly the marks are defined
Boilerplate company description and press contact - standard media-kit items that are absent
A version or last-updated date; the legal reserve-the-right clause makes currency matter even more
Guidance on cropping or annotating the provided screenshots (what press may and may not alter)

principle.title: Package product screenshots as official brand assets
principle.explanation: For a software brand, the product UI appears in press more often than the logo does - and third parties will screenshot old, misconfigured, or fake-data versions unless you hand them better. Slack ships current, high-res, localized captures as a named kit category, controlling its most-reproduced surface.
principle.howToApply: For 35353 or any product brand, add a 'Product screenshots' section to the press kit: current UI on desktop and mobile, populated with approved demo data, exported at 2x, refreshed on each major release - and state whether cropping or annotation is allowed.

entries.tagline: A furniture site whose restraint is the sales argument — it sells things designed to outlive you, so nothing on the page looks like it will date.
entries.summary: Vitsœ has made Dieter Rams' 606 shelving since 1960, and the site is built on the same premise: buy once, add to it, take it with you. The homepage opens straight into three named products photographed in real, cluttered rooms — no slogan, no carousel, no hero video — then states four beliefs (Against obsolescence, Investing for life, Transcending fashion, Honest pricing) in plain four-column type. One neutral grotesque at three sizes, one blue link colour, and photography as the only imagery; the single decorative mark on the page is a small red pair of lips above the customer quote. Product pages replace discount mechanics with longevity maths — a $840–$3,875 range framed as about $2 a week — and put a free human planner in front of the buy step.
whatWorks: The nav IS the catalogue: Home / About us / 606 Universal Shelving System / 620 Chair Programme / 621 Table — products are named and numbered, never marketed at.
Each product opener is an asymmetric split: short left column (headline, two 2-line paragraphs, a blue "Learn more →") against one photograph of the product in a lived-in room.
Photography is honest and inhabited — real books, a child's drawing, an orange sofa, ordinary light — instead of white-sweep studio shots.
The "Why Vitsœ?" grid puts four beliefs in four equal columns of plain type, with "Discover our ethos →" right-aligned on the heading's baseline.
Service is designed into the page: a black-and-white photo of two planners at a table, "free planning" stated twice, a named relationship quoted — all before any checkout step.
Longevity replaces urgency: cost-per-week framing and "Honest pricing" where a competitor would put a countdown or a sale badge.
The customer quote is set at display size in the heading face, so social proof arrives as typography rather than as a testimonial widget.

sections.name: Header / nav
sections.notes: Wordmark locked up with "Design Dieter Rams" as a credential, then five text links named after the actual products. Utility (search, region, login, Contact us, Voice, Careers) sits above in small type. No mega-menu, no cart badge, no promo bar — the IA says "we make three things."

sections.name: Product openers — 606 / 620 / 621
sections.notes: Three stacked introductions instead of a hero. 606 gets the full-width treatment (text left, wide photo right); 620 and 621 share a two-up row. Copy is functional and rhythmic — "Start small. Add to it. Reconfigure it. Take it with you when you move…" — which is also literally how the product works.

sections.name: Why Vitsœ? — the belief grid
sections.notes: Four columns: Against obsolescence, Investing for life, Transcending fashion, Honest pricing. Each is one 3-line paragraph of body copy at the same size — no icons, no cards, no borders. "For 65 years we have stood up to a world that deliberately designs products to have a limited useful life" is the closest the page comes to a marketing line.

sections.name: Lifelong service
sections.notes: Text left, a wide documentary black-and-white photograph right: two planners working at a table inside a 606 system on a checkerboard floor. Sells the service layer (first system, moving it, reupholstering a decades-old chair) as part of the product, with "Meet our team of experts →" as the only ask.

sections.name: What our customers say
sections.notes: A single quote — "There's something quietly reassuring in buying something you can be certain will outlive you." — set at headline scale, paired with a small red lips illustration. One customer, one sentence, no star ratings or logo wall.

sections.name: Voice — editorial row
sections.notes: Four small cards linking to customer stories, a Counterprint Books founder profile, a recipe from the Vitsœ kitchen, and "A love letter to Vitsœ". Brand journalism that keeps a once-a-decade purchase warm without retargeting energy.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: "Keep in touch" with an honest promise — "You will only hear from us when we have something of interest to share" — an outlined Subscribe button, then four link columns (Company / Customer care / Professionals / Resources) that include CAD assets, brochures and prices. Ends on a plain © line and cookie links; no newsletter modal, no discount bribe.

principle.title: Let restraint carry the product argument
principle.explanation: When the claim is longevity, every page decision is evidence for or against it. A countdown timer, a gradient CTA or a trend-led layout quietly contradicts "this will outlive you"; one typeface, one accent colour, honest photography and calm pacing corroborate it. Restraint here isn't a style preference, it's the proof.
principle.howToApply: On a premium or long-life product page, cut carousels, urgency badges and decorative gradients, then replace them with: one full-width photograph of the thing genuinely in use, a four-column grid of plainly-worded beliefs, a cost-over-time figure instead of a discount, and a named human service step placed before the buy button.

site.name: Microsoft — LinkedIn single-image ad (1:1, Frontier Transformation Week)

entries.tagline: One word — "impact." — set roughly three times larger than anything else, and the whole square resolves in a glance.
entries.summary: A B2B event ad that behaves like a poster rather than a post. The left half is a type panel on near-white: a two-line sentence-case setup, then "impact." at display scale with a full stop, the event name and dates in caption type, and a black pill button. The right half is held by an iridescent ribbon graphic and a cut-out portrait looking down at a Surface. Pulled live from the LinkedIn Ad Library (advertiser Microsoft, paid for by Zenith UK), it also shows the platform frame at work: the creative carries the brand voice, LinkedIn's own headline bar and "Register" button carry the click. The body copy above it ("The gap between AI strategy and real-world execution is closing fast") is generic B2B — the craft is all in the unit.
entries.when: LinkedIn feed, running July 2026 (event: Frontier Transformation Week, September 14–17)
whatWorks: A ~3:1 type-scale jump inside a 1:1 frame: two modest setup lines, then one word at display size — hierarchy readable at feed-thumbnail size.
The full stop after "impact." turns a sentence fragment into a claim.
Vertical split: type owns the left half, image the right, so neither is cropped into nonsense when the square is scaled down.
What and when in two caption lines directly under the headline ("Frontier Transformation Week / September 14-17") — no separate detail block.
Two deliberately different CTAs: a black pill "Guarantee your spot" inside the creative for voice, LinkedIn's outlined "Register" in the frame for the actual click.
Small brand mark top-left: when the type is doing the shouting, the logo doesn't have to.
Palette held to three notes — off-white ground, black type, one iridescent gradient accent — so the graphic reads as energy, not noise.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The iridescent blue-violet ribbon curling behind a real person's head is the only saturated thing in a near-white square — colour, not contrast-shouting, is what stops the scroll. The subject is calm and mid-thought rather than grinning at camera, which reads as credible in a B2B feed.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: "It's time to turn your vision into real-world" runs at body scale across two lines, then "impact." drops in at roughly triple the size. The eye lands on the big word first and reads the setup second — the sentence works in either order. Event name and dates follow immediately in small plain type.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: The portrait is bottom-right, cut out over the same off-white as the type panel, eyeline angled down and left toward the tablet — and therefore back into the copy. The ribbon graphic bridges the two halves at the top so the composition doesn't split into two unrelated rectangles.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: Inside the creative: a compact black pill, "Guarantee your spot" — a promise, not a verb-noun label, and the only pure-black shape besides the type. In the LinkedIn frame beneath: "Jump ahead of your Industry's Curve" with an outlined "Register" button. The in-image button sets the tone; the platform button is the tap target.

principle.title: Make one word the whole ad
principle.explanation: A feed grants an ad about one word of real attention. If every line is set at a similar size, the viewer gets no word at all; if one word is set at display scale and everything else demoted to caption, the ad lands even at thumbnail size and even when scrolled past at speed.
principle.howToApply: For a 1:1 or portrait ad: pick the single word that IS the offer, set it ~3× the supporting line, put the event/date/detail beneath it at caption size, keep the image to one half of the frame, and let the platform's own CTA button do the converting while an in-creative button carries the brand voice.

entries.category: Book design → digital interface (MIT modernism to the screen)
entries.tagline: Took graphic design off the page and into the screen by refusing to separate designing from making.
entries.summary: Cooper joined MIT's Office of Publications in 1952 and became its first design director, drawing the MIT Press colophon — seven vertical bars abstracted from "mitp" and a stack of book spines — and redesigning the 1969 Bauhaus book in Helvetica on a strict grid. In 1973–74 she co-founded the Visible Language Workshop with Ron MacNeil, a room holding silkscreen, lithography and offset presses alongside computers; in 1985 it became a founding group of the MIT Media Lab. Her last decade produced "smart" typography that adapts to its background and the Information Landscape — text and data you fly through in three dimensions. She never learned to code, and got there anyway by sitting alongside programmers rather than briefing them.
whatWorks: Design in the production medium, not in a mockup of it — she put the presses and the computers in one room so students designed by running the machine.
The "Rotation System" drill: push the same sheet through the press again and again, changing inks each pass, and let the process reveal the form.
Train generalists, not specialists — rotate people through editorial, platemaking and digital work so nobody hands off blindly.
Build tools, not just artefacts: her group made type that reads its own background and re-pigments itself to stay legible — encode the rule instead of hand-fixing each instance.
Share the source: VLW code was passed down to each new intake, an open-source ethic before the phrase existed.
Get to new territory by collaborating with engineers as peers rather than writing specs at them.

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: With the material and the machine. First moves are production experiments — a press run, a screen, a piece of code — rather than sketches of a finished artefact. She described her own interest as "beginnings and process" rather than design theory, and treated the tools as the place where ideas are found, not where they get output.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: A shared workshop with instant feedback between thinking and making: design, produce, look, change, repeat, with every tool in the room and disciplines deliberately mixed (architecture, art, engineering, computer science). "Messages and Means", her oversubscribed class, gave students the means of production first and the brief second.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Making typography intelligent. Type that knows its context — when the background colour changes, it re-pigments to stay readable — extended into depth, motion and transparency, and finally into the Information Landscape, where hierarchy is expressed by position in 3D space instead of by point size on a page.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Judge work by whether it makes information clearer and more alive, not by whether it obeys a style. Assume the boundary between design tool and reproduction tool will dissolve once information is electronic, and that specialists will have to become generalists — so learn the next medium early, on purpose, while it is still awkward.

principle.title: Design in the medium, not about it
principle.explanation: A medium's real grammar — what it does easily, what it resists, what it does that nothing else can — only shows up when you produce in it. Designing a static picture of an interactive thing hides exactly the qualities worth designing with, which is why Cooper kept the presses and the computers in the same room and let students discover form by running them.
principle.howToApply: Before designing a screen, an animation or a print piece, spend the first 20 minutes making a crude version in the real medium — in the browser, in the actual app, on the actual paper — and let what the medium does cheaply shape the design. On the 35353 work, that means prototyping a section in live HTML/CSS before polishing it in Figma.

entries.category: Partner / co-marketing guidelines — the public layer of a gated brand portal
entries.tagline: A brand guide written for people who do not work at Uber — so its first rule is that your logo leads and Uber comes second.
entries.summary: brand.uber.com is mostly gated: the Identity system and creative assets sit behind sign-in. What is public is the partner layer — co-marketing guidelines for Uber and Uber Eats, plus a 309-asset logo library — and it is unusually strong on the two things partner guides normally fumble: hierarchy in a lockup, and words. Clear space is defined as the height of the letter U and drawn as a diagram; partner lockups specify order, a divider glyph and spacing measured in the same letter; and the messaging section gives a straight approved / not approved language table, including a ban on using "Uber" as a noun or a verb. Governance opens the page rather than closing it: everything using the wordmark goes to Brand Desk first, with a stated 3–5 business day turnaround.
whatWorks: States the brand hierarchy in one sentence — "Your brand should always take the visual lead in marketing that appears on your channels" — before any styling rule.
Encodes that hierarchy geometrically: partner logo first, line glyph between, spacing equal to the width of the "U", Uber second, in whichever of black or white contrasts more.
Clear space defined relative to the letterform (height of the U) and shown as a diagram over a tiled wordmark, so it needs no judgement to apply.
Approved vs Not approved language in two columns ("Request an Uber ride" / "Call an Uber"), plus fill-in-the-blank approved offer lines with [bracketed] slots.
Names what the company actually is — "a digital platform that connects people with independent contractors" — so partners describe the business correctly, not just spell it correctly.
Governance up front with an SLA: submit to Brand Desk, 3–5 business days, "revisions can add to that — so please plan ahead."
The Uber Eats parallel doc ships CTA badges and app icons in 15 languages, plus minimum sizes in both web pixels and print inches.

sections.name: Purpose + approval route
sections.notes: Opens by saying what the guide is for and that all partner materials, copy, press releases and sites using Uber wordmarks go to Brand Desk before launch — with a response time (3–5 business days) and a "Submit to Brand Desk" button right there. Governance as the first screen, not an appendix.

sections.name: Brand elements and logos
sections.notes: The hierarchy rule, then the wordmark shown black-on-light and white-on-dark as two side-by-side panels, three rider app icons (iOS, Android square, Android circle), and a "Download Uber logos" button. Every asset shown is also downloadable from the same page.

sections.name: Core colors
sections.notes: Two swatches, black and white, each with HEX, RGB, CMYK and PMS. Honest about its own scope: these are stated as the colours the logo and app icons are made of, not as a brand palette — which is also the gap (see needs).

sections.name: Logo guidance — clear space & lockups
sections.notes: Clear space = the height of the letter U, drawn as a diagram over a tiled Uber wordmark with blue guides. Then partnership lockups in both horizontal and vertical form, with a placeholder "Replace with logo here" box making the partner-first order unmissable.

sections.name: Messaging guidelines
sections.notes: The standout section. Defines the business, bans "Uber" as noun or verb ("your Uber is here", "Let's Uber to the show"), then two colour-coded columns of approved vs not-approved phrases, followed by approved offer-messaging templates. Verbal identity treated as a rule set with examples, not as adjectives.

sections.name: Uber Eats co-marketing (parallel document)
sections.notes: Same structure for the Eats brand: logo per background including on Eats green, CTA badge and app icons available in 15 languages, minimum sizes in web px and print inches, and branded extras — delivery bags, gift cards, GIPHY stickers — with "submit mocks to Brand Desk for approval" attached.

sections.name: Logo library (/logos)
sections.notes: 309 SVG assets in 14 collections, filterable by brand, language, product, colour format and orientation, with a strict naming convention (Logo_UberBlack_English_Stacked_White) and a date on every file. The asset layer is a searchable DAM, not a zip.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: A single "Last modified on …" timestamp on the document. Enough to prove the page is maintained, not enough to tell a partner what changed.

needs: A public typography section — no typeface, scale or licensing guidance outside the gate, so partners set Uber-adjacent copy in whatever they happen to own.
A real colour system — only black and white appear publicly; no brand palette, tints, or usage ratios.
Accessibility rules — nothing on contrast minimums, approved text/background pairings, or minimum type sizes for co-branded creative.
Photography and illustration direction — the page itself uses striking imagery but gives partners no yes/no examples for their own.
Logo misuse examples — the messaging section shows do/don't beautifully, while the logo section shows only correct usage; no stretched, recoloured, boxed or low-contrast counter-examples.
A version number and changelog, not just a modified date, so a partner knows whether their approved asset from last quarter is still current.
A worked end-to-end example — one finished co-branded ad or email annotated against every rule, which would settle most Brand Desk revisions before they happen.

principle.title: Rank the brands before you style anything
principle.explanation: In co-branded work almost every misuse is a hierarchy failure, not a colour failure — the partner makes your logo too big, puts it first, or gives it equal weight. Stating the rank in one sentence and then encoding it geometrically (order, divider, spacing tied to a letterform) removes the judgement call that causes the mistake.
principle.howToApply: In any partner, press or co-marketing section of a 35353 guide, write the rank rule as a sentence ("the partner brand leads; 35353 supports"), then specify it mechanically: which logo comes first, what glyph separates them, spacing measured off a letter of the wordmark, and which colourway to pick by contrast — and ship the lockups as finished files so the rule can be followed without redrawing it.

entries.tagline: A hotel group that runs its homepage as a magazine and keeps the entire booking engine compressed into one persistent utility bar.
entries.summary: Ace Hotel sells a scene rather than a room, and the homepage is built to argue exactly that. The whole reservation flow — location, dates, guests, promo code, Book Now — lives in a compact bar pinned to the header and is never repeated as a giant hero form; everything below it is editorial. A near-neutral shell of paper white, black and warm beige lets property photography supply all the colour, and dated live content (tonight's DJ set, Taco Tuesday in Kyoto, tarot readings in Palm Springs) sits on the homepage at the same weight as the offers. The trade-off is honest: the page is long, and a guest who arrived only to book has to trust the header rather than a big obvious form.
whatWorks: The entire booking engine is one compact header bar — location, date grid, guest stepper, promo code, Book Now — so the conversion path exists once instead of being restated as a hero form and repeated between every section
Each location card carries a one-line character line ("a mid-century desert oasis", "alongside the region's best beaches") instead of an amenity list — the property is sold by voice
Near-neutral shell (paper white, black, warm beige) means every ounce of colour in the page comes from the photography
Two type registers doing two jobs: serif display for anything editorial, sans for anything you operate (dates, filters, form labels)
The "Goings On" block lists real, dated, location-filtered events — a homepage carrying live content reads as a place that is genuinely open tonight
The Ace Reader block gives editorial (a city guide, an artist piece, an essay on queer belonging through books) the same visual weight as the rate offers
The dark footer is the only inverted band on the page, so it closes the document instead of bleeding into more content

sections.name: Booking / utility bar
sections.notes: Logo left; language selector, location chooser, check-in/out date grid, guest stepper, promo field and Book Now to the right. Kept small, sans-serif and functional — deliberately styled as an instrument rather than as brand. Keyboard-navigable date grid and an expandable guest dialog mean the whole reservation can be started without leaving the header.

sections.name: Welcome statement
sections.notes: A short centred paragraph on a light ground, no image: "a collection of international lifestyle hotels" holding "historical reverence hand-in-hand with considered, contemporary design." It positions before it sells, and its restraint sets the reading pace for the rest of the page.

sections.name: Locations grid
sections.notes: A 2–3 column card grid of eight properties, each a single strong photograph (Athens poolside, Brooklyn skyline, Kyoto architecture) with the city name as an h3 and one line of character copy below. Minimal overlay text, no rate badges — the picture and the sentence do the whole job, and "Fukuoka — coming soon" is left in place as a signal of momentum.

sections.name: Offers
sections.notes: Five rate offers (Ace Member Rate, Extra Credit, Make it Last, Pay Now and Save, Week Daze) as branded graphic cards with their own beige and animated backgrounds, each with a Book Now plus a View offer link. Named like editorial, not like discounts — the commercial section still speaks in the brand's voice.

sections.name: Goings On (events)
sections.notes: Curated event cards filterable by location, each with a real time, place and short description, illustrated with the actual flyer artwork. This is the section most hotel sites skip, and it is the one that proves the brand claim: the hotel is a venue, not just a bed.

sections.name: Ace Reader (editorial)
sections.notes: A featured article followed by a grid of recent pieces — local guides from named figures, artist spotlights, essays — each with a large photograph, location and date. Placed after the commercial blocks so it reads as substance rather than filler.

sections.name: A-List signup & footer
sections.notes: A full-width newsletter form with a plain incentive ("secret codes, special events, big news, and up to 15% off your next stay") and a real privacy checkbox, then the only dark band on the page: a multi-column footer with utility links, social icons, the Seibu Prince partnership mark and an atmospheric image with text overlay.

principle.title: Let the booking widget be a tool, not the identity
principle.explanation: On any site with a dominant conversion widget — a booking engine, a property search, a quote form — the default is to blow it up into the hero and then repeat it every few sections, which turns the whole page into an interface and leaves nothing to argue the brand. Ace compresses the entire reservation flow into one persistent header bar styled as an instrument, then spends the rest of the page on photography, live events and writing. Conversion stays one click away everywhere without ever becoming the design.
principle.howToApply: On a 35353 or client site with a search or enquiry widget, build it once as a compact sticky utility bar with its own tighter, more functional visual language (sans type, small controls, neutral chrome), and resist restating it as a full-width block between sections. Then design the body editorially — one honest photograph per place or product, a line of character copy instead of a feature list, and at least one dated, genuinely live section so the page proves the business is active.

entries.category: Meta carousel ad (4:5 cards, Facebook + Instagram feed)
entries.tagline: Five carousel cards shot as one object on one brown ground, with zero text burned into the creative — the swipe becomes a rotation, not a channel change.
entries.when: Meta feed (Facebook + Instagram), running from Jul 2, 2026 — Eliot Racer launch (Ad Library ID 2285312748942033)
entries.summary: Tracksmith’s Eliot Racer launch runs as a product carousel in which every card is a long-exposure macro of the same shoe, lit the same way, on the same warm brown ground. Nothing is written on the image — no headline, no price, no "NEW" flash — so the creative gets to be photography while the Meta text block carries the entire argument, including a specific lab claim. The palette is two colours (bone white and brass) against brown, matched to the brand’s hare mark, so the ad is recognisable as Tracksmith without a logo lockup anywhere in frame. The motion blur is not decoration: it states the product claim (speed, energy return) in the medium rather than in words.
whatWorks: Zero text baked into the creative — the copy lives in the platform’s own text block, freeing the image to be a photograph rather than a poster crammed with a headline and a badge
One ground colour, one light source and one palette across all five cards, so swiping reads as turning an object rather than flipping between separate ads
Long-exposure blur does the job a "FAST" headline would do — the claim is demonstrated in the photography instead of asserted in type
A strict two-colour product palette (bone + brass) tied to the brand’s gold hare, giving instant attribution with no logo lockup in frame
The card order is an argument: hero silhouette in motion → midsole and outsole macro → the drop-in insole lifted out — each card answers the objection the last one raises
Body copy earns the superlative with a measurable proof ("outperformed every other shoe in the lab with the highest energy return to softness ratio") rather than adjectives
The same headline and Shop Now sit under every card, so no swipe position is a dead end

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: A pale shoe streaking through warm brown darkness, shot at a shutter speed slow enough to smear the trailing edge. In a feed of flat white-background product shots and text-on-image promos, an almost abstract, moody macro is the pattern interrupt — it looks like editorial photography, which is exactly why it stops the scroll.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: All words sit in the Meta text block, above the creative: "Redefine race day with the all-new Eliot Racer. Maximum energy return meets next-level cushioning in an understated silhouette." Then the proof paragraph — drop-in midsole, carbon plate, and the lab result. Note the order: promise, mechanism, evidence. "Understated silhouette" is doing brand work too, telling a Tracksmith runner this is not a neon super-shoe.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Five 4:5 cards, each a macro of a different part of the same shoe on the identical brown ground. Card one is the silhouette in motion; card two crops hard into the midsole and gold outsole tread with the hare stamped on the foam; card three floats the drop-in insole out of the shoe with the Tracksmith script visible. The consistency is the craft — same ground, same key light, same blur language — so five images behave as one product study.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: Repeated verbatim on every card: TRACKSMITH.COM / "Men’s Tracksmith Eliot Racer" / Shop Now. Rendered in Meta’s native button chrome rather than a custom button drawn into the artwork, so it inherits the platform’s tap target and looks like the feed instead of like an ad pretending to be one.

principle.title: In a carousel, make the cards one object — not five ads
principle.explanation: Carousels fail when each card is designed independently: different backgrounds, different crops, a different headline burned into each one. Swiping then feels like channel-surfing and the viewer leaves at card two. Holding one ground colour, one light source and one palette across the whole set turns the swipe into a rotation around a single subject, and the card order stops being a gallery and becomes an argument.
principle.howToApply: For any multi-image ad, listing carousel or gallery block, lock the background, lighting and palette before shooting and produce the whole set in one session. Then order the cards as a case — establishing shot, the detail that proves the claim, the thing the buyer cannot see in a store — keep text out of the images so the copy block can carry it, and repeat one identical CTA under every card.

entries.tagline: The designer who invented information design by treating a trade catalogue as a navigation problem — and gave the world the parentheses around a phone area code.
entries.summary: Sutnar trained in Prague, taught at the State School of Graphic Arts and designed the Czechoslovak pavilion for the 1939 New York World’s Fair — then stayed, as the war closed the way home. From 1941 he spent nineteen years as art director of Sweet’s Catalog Service, the largest trade-information publisher in America, and with research director Knud Lönberg-Holm built the first systematic model of what the two of them named "information design." His grids, tabs, colour coding and cross-reference marks anticipated the navigational conventions of the web by about four decades, and his working maxim — "the designer must think first, work later" — is the most portable thing in this journal.
whatWorks: Sort the content before opening the design tool — Sutnar treated structuring the information as the design work and the layout as its visible consequence
Design the spread, not the element: he made the double-page spread (today, the viewport) the unit of design, because it is what the reader actually sees at once
Build the fixed framework first — grid, type, colour roles, index — then allow variety only inside it, so a system survives thousands of pages made by many hands
Add explicit navigation devices as designed objects: tabs, arrows, heavy rules, colour bars, oversized punctuation — so a reader can traverse without reading sequentially
Judge the work by behaviour, not by appearance: did the reader find the fact and take the action?
Design upward — he refused to pander to assumed public taste, holding that the job was to "uplift the public to an expert design level"

sections.name: How he begins
sections.notes: "The designer must think first, work later." Sutnar refused to draw until the data was sorted. He described himself as a Constructivist who liked to take a thing apart, find the right organising structure and rebuild it — so the first pass on any brief was analytical, not visual. An assistant recalled him untangling knotted balls of client data with apparent ease and then drawing, in one go, a layout that expressed the solution exactly. The single confident layout is the output of the thinking, never a substitute for it.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: He designed the system, not the page. At Sweet’s the unit of design was the dynamic double-page spread — what a reader takes in at a glance — and above that sat a fixed framework of grid, typographic hierarchy, colour coding and indexing that held constant across a catalogue of thousands of pages produced by many hands. Contemporaries described the indexing as a visual Dewey Decimal system: the framework was rigid so the content could vary without the whole becoming noise.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Navigational devices treated as first-class design elements. Enlarged punctuation — commas, colons, exclamation marks blown up to graphic scale — worked as what he called linguistic traffic signs; alongside them, thumb tabs, arrows, bold rules, colour bars and cross-reference marks let a reader jump into the middle of a document and orient instantly. The same instinct produced his best-known anonymous artefact: the parentheses around US telephone area codes, designed for Bell in the late 1950s so a dialler could see at a glance which digits were the prefix.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: His definition doubles as his test: information design is "the integration of meaning (content) and visualisation (format) into an entity that produces a desired action." The question is never whether a layout looks resolved but whether it produced the action — found, understood, dialled, ordered. Paired with that is a refusal to design down: taste should be raised toward expert level, not estimated and catered to. Consistency in the framework, variety within it.

principle.title: Sort the information before you design it
principle.explanation: Most pages that read as busy are not styling failures — they are unsorted content that got styled anyway. Sutnar’s "think first, work later" treats hierarchy, grouping and cross-reference as the actual design work; once those are settled the visual solution is close to forced, which is why he could draw a finished layout in one pass. It is also what lets a system scale: a framework decided in the analysis survives thousands of pages and many hands, while a framework improvised in the layout does not.
principle.howToApply: Before opening Figma on a page, brand guide or dashboard, write the content out as a plain text outline — every fact, grouped and ranked, with cross-references marked — and refuse to draw until that outline reads cleanly. Then design the navigation devices as real elements with their own specs (section labels, rules, colour coding, an index or jump list) rather than adding them as decoration afterwards, and test the result by task: can someone land mid-page and find one specific fact without reading from the top?

entries.category: Full brand guide — public marketing portal for a national operator
entries.tagline: A brand guide built for the people who actually break brands — it names a separate cut of the corporate typeface for print, for screen and for PowerPoint, and ships the files for each.
entries.summary: Deutsche Bahn’s Marketingportal is the public marketing and brand portal for a national rail operator, running from brand and naming strategy through logo, typography, colour, the proprietary "Puls" element, icons, imagery, motion branding and layout, and ending in real applications and legal terms. Its strongest quality is operational realism: it is written for thousands of staff, agencies and regional units who will make a poster, a station sign and a Word document in the same week, so the rules are specified by destination and shipped with the files. It is also unusually rigorous on accessibility — contrast ratios published per text size, a rule against colour as the sole carrier of meaning, and dark mode handled as a systematic transformation. The main caveat is that it explains almost none of its reasoning, and it is German-only.
whatWorks: DB Type ships as three named cuts mapped to where people actually work — DB Neo for print and vehicle lettering, DB Neo Screen for digital, DB Neo Office for Word and PowerPoint — with .otf, .ttf and .woff2 supplied so nobody has to fall back to Arial
One non-negotiable stated in a sentence: DB Red is always part of the design, and text is only ever black or white — which makes almost every palette decision decidable without a judgement call

Accessibility published as numbers per text size (4.5:1 small text, 3:1 large text and graphic elements, 1.3:1 decorative) plus a colour-blindness rule that bans colour as the only means of communicating relevant content

Dark mode as a system rule rather than a screenshot: secondary colours mirror across the scale (Blue 700 becomes Blue 200) and font weight drops one step to compensate for optical bulk on dark grounds
Naming and domain strategy sit inside the brand guide, so what a new product is called and which URL it takes are treated as brand decisions rather than marketing afterthoughts
The proprietary "Puls" graphic element and motion branding are documented as base elements alongside logo and colour — not relegated to an appendix
Rules carry scope, not just pictures: the rainbow logo variant is permitted only in LGBTQ+ related DB communication, which is a usage boundary rather than a swatch

sections.name: Strategie — Markenstrategie & Namingstrategie
sections.notes: Opens with positioning and how products appear under the DB brand, then naming and domain strategy. Rare and valuable: most guides never say who decides a product name or when a domain gets registered, so this closes a gap that usually leaks into ad-hoc sub-branding.

sections.name: Logo
sections.notes: The mark, its variants and downloads, with legal usage terms attached. Placement guidance is about distance from edges and other elements. The rainbow variant is documented with an explicit scope limit. Correct usage is well covered; counter-examples are not.

sections.name: Typografie
sections.notes: DB Type in three families — DB Neo (Adobe/print/vehicle lettering), DB Neo Screen (web and UI), DB Neo Office (MS Office and business documents) — plus DB Non Latin for other scripts. Free to use but only for Deutsche Bahn projects; installation instructions per platform; mixed case always; even the bullet glyph is specified (U+2022 in DB Red 500, with defined spacing). Presented as concise summaries plus an FAQ.

sections.name: Farbe
sections.notes: DB Red and white as the iconic pair, with values across CMYK, HEX, SCSS, RGB, NCS, RAL and Pantone. Rules for which combination applies on white grounds (red mark, black text in print, Cool Gray 700 digital) and on red grounds (white mark, white text). Twelve secondary base colours, each in eight shades from 100 to 800, explicitly for campaigns and illustration rather than decoration. Then the WCAG thresholds, the colour-blindness rule and dark-mode mirroring. This is the chapter that does show right/wrong pairs.

sections.name: Puls
sections.notes: The brand’s proprietary graphic accent, treated as a base element in its own right next to logo, colour and type — and folded into the colour rules (on white it is red; on red it is white), so the accent element and the palette are specified together rather than separately.

sections.name: Icons, Bildwelt & Motion Branding
sections.notes: Three distinct icon sets — functional, app and illustrative — rather than one undifferentiated library, which prevents UI icons and marketing spot illustrations being used interchangeably. Photography direction and motion principles sit beside them as first-class base elements.

sections.name: Layout, Best Practice / Anwendungen
sections.notes: Grid and composition rules, then a separate applications chapter showing the identity in the wild — BahnCards, station and OOH placements, digital screens. The applications chapter is dated separately (30.11.2022) from the base elements (20.01.2026), so a reader can see which parts have been refreshed.

sections.name: Rechtliches & contact
sections.notes: Impressum, terms of use, font licence terms and privacy, plus two named routes: marke@deutschebahn.com for brand questions and markenrecht@deutschebahn.com for trademark questions. Splitting the brand inbox from the legal inbox is a small thing that saves a lot of misrouted requests.

needs: Rationale. The typography chapter in particular is procedural how-to with almost no "why", so a team can obey the system but cannot extend it correctly to a surface the guide never anticipated.
Do/don’t examples for type the way the colour chapter has them — colour shows right and wrong pairs side by side; typography largely does not.

A verbal identity layer. A guide that covers strategy, naming, motion and iconography has essentially nothing on voice, tone or messaging pillars, so writing is the one part of the brand left ungoverned.
Logo misuse counter-examples — the stretched, recoloured, boxed, rotated and low-contrast set. Correct usage plus downloads is not the same as a misuse page.
A version number and changelog rather than a per-chapter modified date, so a partner can tell whether the asset they were approved to use last quarter is still current.
An English layer. For an operator whose agencies, suppliers and European partners are not all German-speaking, a German-only portal quietly limits who can comply with it.
One end-to-end worked example — a single campaign annotated against every rule at once — which would settle far more questions than any individual chapter.

principle.title: Name a typeface for every place people actually work
principle.explanation: Brand type systems almost never break in the studio — they break in the office. The licensed display cut cannot be installed in PowerPoint, will not render on a vehicle or in an email client, and has no web format, so people substitute Arial and the identity quietly leaks out of everything that is not a designed asset. DB solves it by shipping three cuts of one family, each named for its context and supplied in the file format that context needs, which turns a compliance problem into a download.
principle.howToApply: In any brand guide, list the type system by destination rather than by weight: which cut for print, which for screen and web (with woff2), which for Word, PowerPoint and email (with .ttf), and which fallback covers scripts you do not support — then attach the actual files to each line. Do the same for colour by naming the value systems the destinations need (HEX and a token name for digital, CMYK and Pantone for print) so nobody has to convert by eye.

entries.tagline: A full commerce homepage where type is never once set on top of a photograph.
entries.summary: Blue Bottle runs a long, hard-working e-commerce page - hero carousel, best sellers, four editorial bands, a collection grid, a subscription spec sheet, brew guides and dated reviews - without ever overlaying a headline on an image. Photographs run edge to edge and clean; every headline, subhead and button sits in a white or pale-sage panel beneath or beside them. Hierarchy comes almost entirely from case, letterspacing and vertical space in one grotesque, and the single accent colour (Blue Bottle blue) appears only in the mark and on the packaging itself. A caveat: several bands lazy-load their imagery, so a full-page capture catches a couple of empty panels.
whatWorks: The hero is an uncropped photograph of the cold-brew set on concrete with a hard raking shadow, and carries zero type; the headline 'THE NEW COLD STANDARD', a one-line subhead, the dark 'Explore Cold Collection' button and the 01/02/03 slide counter all sit in the white band beneath it.

Every section title - BEST SELLERS, SHOP BY COLLECTION, EXPLORE OUR BREW GUIDES - is set at nearly the same size in the same wide-tracked all-caps grotesque; hierarchy is carried by case, tracking and whitespace rather than by a big type scale.

One accent, used once: Blue Bottle blue only ever appears in the bottle glyph and on real packaging in the photography. Primary buttons are solid near-black, secondary buttons are hairline outlines, so the palette never competes with the product.

Product cards rank flavour above category - name in caps with the price on the same baseline, then the tasting notes ('Blackberry, Lemongrass, Golden Raisin'), then roast type in grey - with a single small corner chip for 'New' / 'Best Seller' / 'Bundle & Save'.

The subscription block is written as a spec sheet, not a pitch: three labelled groups (YOUR DAILY RITUAL / EXTRA SAVINGS / EXCLUSIVE ACCESS) split by hairline rules, with the actual discount code sitting in the bullet list.

Social proof is product-specific and dated - each review names the exact SKU ('THREE AFRICAS - 12OZ WHOLE BEAN'), shows a thumbnail, a first-name-plus-initial byline, a 'Verified Buyer' tag and a date - in a three-up arrow carousel instead of a star wall.

sections.name: Announcement bar + nav
sections.notes: A slim warm-white bar carries one offer sentence ('Free shipping on subscriptions and orders over $45') and a country selector. The nav below is tracked uppercase (SHOP / BEST SELLERS / SUBSCRIPTIONS / LOCATIONS) with the bottle glyph alone centred - no wordmark - and search / account / bag icons right. It reads as stationery, not chrome.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Full-bleed still life of the cold-brew kit in raking sunlight, then a text band under it: caps headline, one sentence of copy, a filled dark button, and the slide counter right-aligned on the headline's baseline. Because nothing sits on the image, contrast is never negotiated and both halves stay independently swappable.

sections.name: Best sellers
sections.notes: Four product cards on pale grey tiles with soft cast shadows, each with one small status chip, name + price on a shared baseline, tasting notes and roast. A centred hairline-outline 'Shop Best Sellers' button closes the block - the secondary CTA style is consistent everywhere it appears.

sections.name: Editorial split bands (Matcha, Craft Instant)
sections.notes: Two 50/50 bands alternate the text side: a pale sage panel with caps headline, two lines of voiced copy ('nobody has done instant quite like this (really, nobody)') and a ghost button, against a macro photograph on the other half. Same component, mirrored - which is why the page stays long without feeling padded.

sections.name: Shop by collection + membership
sections.notes: Four cutout product tiles on white, each with a caps name and a benefit line ('CRAFT INSTANT - Make Cafe-Quality Iced Lattes, Instantly'). The membership band uses an eyebrow ('EXPERIENCE KYOTO-STYLE ESPRESSO') above the headline plus its own 01-04 counter, so a second carousel reads as a different object from the hero.

sections.name: Subscriptions + brew guides
sections.notes: The subscription block trades persuasion for specification (three labelled groups, hairline rules, exact savings). Brew guides follow as two wide image-left / text-right cards with underlined 'Learn More' text links - a third, quieter CTA tier below filled and outlined buttons.

sections.name: Reviews + footer
sections.notes: Dated verified reviews per SKU, then a charcoal footer: the full lockup (wordmark plus glyph), four columns (COMPANY / LEARN / MORE / SUBSCRIBE AND STAY UPDATED), an underline-only email field with an arrow submit, and a legal row that includes an explicit 'YOUR PRIVACY CHOICES' control.

principle.title: Never set type on the photograph
principle.explanation: Overlaying a headline on an image forces three compromises at once: the photo gets cropped or darkened to protect legibility, the copy length becomes a function of the composition, and every future image swap risks breaking contrast. Blue Bottle proves a long commerce page can run entirely on adjacency - image in its own field, words in theirs - and the result reads more expensive, not less, because the photography is never scrimmed.
principle.howToApply: On the next 35353 or client page, build the hero and every editorial band as two stacked or side-by-side fields: an uncropped image field and a text field with the headline, one sentence, and one button. Set headlines in tracked caps at a modest size and let case plus space carry hierarchy, keep the brand accent for the mark alone, and use exactly three CTA tiers - filled, hairline-outline, underlined text link.

site.name: Chanel - wide display banner (Gabrielle Chanel Essence)

entries.tagline: The whole unit is graded into one amber-on-cream range so the only real contrast left is the type.
entries.summary: A 2000x550 banner split almost exactly in half: bottle left, type right. What makes it work is a colour decision - the perfume, the ribbon of chiffon around it and the background all sit inside one narrow warm-neutral range, so nothing in the image competes. The only high-contrast element in the frame is near-black type, which means the eye lands on 'GABRIELLE / CHANEL' first and the product second, exactly the order a launch needs.
whatWorks: One colour family for the entire image: amber liquid, amber fabric, cream ground - the composition has tonal depth but no colour contrast, so the type wins by default.
Two-line stacked wordmark with the house name set larger than the product name: 'GABRIELLE' reads first as the news, 'CHANEL' lands as the payoff.
A wide empty gutter down the centre holds the halves apart, and the ribbon's tail crosses it - the only thing stitching image to type.
One descriptor line only - 'THE NEW EAU DE PARFUM' - at caption size, tracked to roughly the width of the headline above it.
The CTA is a small-caps 'DISCOVER' with a single black rule under it: no button fill, no colour, no arrow. In a luxury unit the underline is enough of an affordance.
Nothing else: no price, no offer, no badge, no logo bug repeated in a corner - which is what lets a 550px-tall strip feel like a page rather than an ad slot.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: A single bottle suspended in a ribbon of warm chiffon, lit so the glass and the fabric share the same amber. There is no model, no scene and no motion - the stop comes from the tonal glow, not from an event.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'GABRIELLE' over 'CHANEL' in the house's tight caps grotesque, set flush left, with generous leading between the two lines and the second line noticeably larger. Product name first, brand as resolution - the reverse of most display ads.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Hard 50/50 split: image left, type right, with the bottle placed slightly left of its half's centre so the frame does not read as two boxes. The format's extreme width is used deliberately - the empty middle is the composition.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: 'DISCOVER' in tracked small caps with a hairline underline, positioned on the type column's left edge, well below the descriptor. It is the lowest-contrast CTA imaginable and still unmissable because it is the only underlined thing in the unit.

principle.title: Grade the image to one colour family, then let type be the only contrast
principle.explanation: Most banners fight themselves: a saturated product photo, a coloured headline and a bright CTA button all bid for the same attention inside a few hundred pixels of height. Pulling product, prop and background into a single hue range removes every competing bid, so a single near-black wordmark carries the whole hierarchy - and the unit reads as composed rather than assembled.
principle.howToApply: For a premium 35353 or listing-brand banner, pick one hue family for the photograph (warm stone, cool slate) and grade the subject, background and props into it, then place the type in near-black or near-white as the only high-contrast element. Cap the unit at a stacked two-line headline, one caption-size descriptor and an underlined text CTA - no filled button, no price, no badge - and let the empty middle of a wide format do the framing.

entries.category: Swiss / International Typographic Style - typographic education
entries.tagline: Turned typography into a curriculum of one-variable exercises - the plane, the line, the word, rhythm.
entries.summary: Ruder trained as a compositor before he taught, and it shows: he treated typography as a craft with testable properties rather than a style. From 1942 at the Allgemeine Gewerbeschule Basel, and from 1947 alongside Armin Hofmann, he built a programme whose courses had waiting lists by the mid-1960s, serialised its thinking in Typografische Monatsblätter as 'Wesentliches' (1957-59) under the headings The Plane, The Line, The Word and Rhythm, and distilled it into 'Typographie: A Manual of Design' (Niggli, 1967). His lasting contribution is a method: isolate one variable, run it as a series, judge the result by reading.
whatWorks: Isolate one variable and run it as a series - his teaching moved through the plane, then the line, then the word, then rhythm, with dozens of variants each, before any finished piece.

Enumerate the options instead of intuiting them: his nine-square grid demonstrations lay out the roughly two dozen positions and shapes a module allows, so composition becomes a choice from a known set.
Get contrast from a limited kit - one type family, few sizes, decisive weight and scale jumps - rather than from more typefaces.
Treat the unprinted surface as material you place. White is an element with a job, not the leftover after setting type.
Prefer asymmetry: an off-centre axis creates tension the eye can follow, where centring flattens sequence.
Judge by reading, not by looking - if the rhythm of the setting slows a reader down, the composition has failed regardless of how it photographs.

sections.name: How he begins
sections.notes: From the constraint, not the concept. Ruder starts with the properties of the material at hand - the plane he is placing on, the family he is allowed, the reading distance - and treats the brief as a communication problem with a plain duty: convey information in writing.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: The systematic series. One element is varied across many attempts, laid out side by side, and the range is inspected before a direction is chosen. This is why his teaching transferred - the method produces evidence a student can argue from, not a taste a student must absorb.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Contrast engineered inside one family, with white space as an active counter-form: extreme size jumps, a single sans (he championed Univers precisely because its numbered system made contrast systematic), asymmetric axes, and generous unprinted areas that give the setting rhythm.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Typography exists to be read, so the reading test outranks the visual one. Rhythm - the alternation of dense and open - is the quality he judges; ornament and centring are rejected not on ideology but because they interrupt sequence. A composition should be defensible from its own structure.

principle.title: Change one variable at a time, in a series you can see all at once
principle.explanation: Designing by iteration hides your options: each version replaces the last, so you compare a memory to a screen. Ruder's method makes the range visible - fix everything but one property, produce ten or twenty variants, and pin them together. You end up choosing from evidence, and you learn what that property actually does, which is the part that transfers to the next job.
principle.howToApply: Before committing a 35353 hero or a brand-guide spread, pick the single variable that is actually in question (headline weight jump, position of the block on the plane, word spacing, image-to-text ratio) and build 10-20 versions that change only that. Screenshot them into one board at the same scale, choose from the board, then run the reading test - read the winner aloud at real size before it goes into the layout.

entries.category: Full brand guide - public, enterprise / open source
entries.tagline: 'This is the source code of the Red Hat brand' - a guide that hands you pre-built colour collections instead of a swatch wall.
entries.summary: Red Hat publishes its whole rulebook openly, opens with a one-line thesis set in its own red, and routes you straight into the eight pages people actually need. Its strongest move is refusing to leave composition to chance: colour ships as seven named, pre-built collections rather than sixty loose values, the typefaces are open source and installed everywhere work happens, and the typographic rules are unusually decidable - sentence case always, flush left, never track manually, measure of 20-100 characters. Where it thins out is the why: the rules are stated with authority but rarely argued, and there is no verbal-identity layer behind the four personality words.
whatWorks: Opens in the brand's own voice, in Red Hat red: 'This is the source code of the Red Hat brand', followed by a plain answer to 'why does that matter?' and a 'Get started' grid of the eight most-used pages (logo, colour, fonts, icons, templates, co-branding, product logos, hybrid handbook).

Colour is delivered as seven pre-composed collections - Core light / dark / red, Expressive light / dark, Interface light / dark - so a designer picks a collection, not individual hexes, and off-brand combinations are structurally hard to make.

Exact values across systems for the core red (#ee0000, RGB 238/0/0, CMYK 0/98/85/0, Pantone 1788C) inside an 11-family palette numbered 10-80+ from light to dark, plus auxiliary sets separated by job (information colours; warm/cool people tones reserved for skin).

Typography rules are decidable rather than aspirational: sentence case even for headlines, flush left by default, default tracking never manually adjusted, one emphasis treatment only, no italics or underlines, line height 120-150% (110% above 150px), measure 20-100 characters.

The type system is open source (SIL) and distributed to every tool people actually use - Google Fonts, GitHub, Figma, Adobe CC, Google Workspace, Miro - with Noto Sans named as the non-Latin fallback, so font substitution stops being a brand risk.
Accessibility is numeric and dual-coded: 4.5:1 for text up to 17pt, 3:1 for 18pt-plus and informative graphics, and an explicit rule never to carry meaning with colour alone.
The logo chapter is treated as an architecture problem - product, universal, initiative, event and endorsement logos each get their own rules, alongside naming, trademarks and co-branding.

sections.name: Brand platform & personality
sections.notes: Strategy first: the platform ('No one innovates alone'), the company story, and four personality words - open, authentic, helpful, brave. Present and well written, but it stops at adjectives; nothing here tells a writer how to sound.

sections.name: The Hat & logo system
sections.notes: The mark is explained in plain language ('Our logo is a red hat with the words "Red Hat"'), with clear-space diagrams, then extended into a full architecture: product logos, universal, initiative, event and endorsement marks, plus naming and trademark rules and a co-branding page.

sections.name: Colour
sections.notes: The strongest chapter. Red Hat Red (red-50) as a mandatory ingredient - 'everything from Red Hat should include it' - inside 11 numbered families, seven pre-built collections, information and people auxiliary palettes, restraint guidance ('pops of red-50', no flooding), and flat prohibitions on off-palette colour, custom gradients and orphaned secondaries.

sections.name: Fonts & typography
sections.notes: Three cuts by job - Red Hat Display for large and bold, Red Hat Text for body and small sizes, Red Hat Mono for code - with Noto Sans for CJK and Cyrillic, open-source licensing, and a tight list of rules on case, alignment, tracking, emphasis, leading and measure.

sections.name: Photography & 3D illustration
sections.notes: Two named image languages with distinct jobs: documentary photography of people and places, and a house 3D illustration style for abstract or technical subjects - which keeps the brand from defaulting to stock whenever a subject cannot be photographed.

sections.name: Icons & digital badges
sections.notes: Separate technology and UI icon sets with construction guidance, plus digital badges (including employee resource groups) - the unglamorous assets that usually go undocumented and then drift.

sections.name: Hybrid style handbook, templates & what's new
sections.notes: A whole handbook for co-created work, split by who leads (Red Hat-led versus partner-led), plus downloadable templates and a 'What's new' feed - the closest thing here to a change log.

needs: A verbal identity: voice and tone with worked do/don't rewrites and per-channel calibration. Four personality adjectives are a brief for a writer, not a system.
Rationale beside the rules. 'Sentence case always' and 'never adjust tracking' are stated but not argued, so a team facing an unlisted case has nothing to reason from.
Motion principles - timing, easing, how the Hat behaves in animation and video - which is a real gap for a brand this heavily used in product and event media.
Approved contrast pairings shown as concrete combinations (which palette member on which surface), not only the WCAG thresholds.
A version number and a dated change log; a 'What's new' feed does not tell a reader which edition of the rules they are looking at.
Worked application mockups end to end - an ad, an email, a deck, a booth - assembled from a named collection, so the collections are proved rather than described.

principle.title: Ship pre-built colour collections, not a swatch wall
principle.explanation: A palette page with sixty values delegates the hardest decision - which of these actually go together, and in what roles - to whoever is in the biggest hurry. Naming a handful of complete collections (background, surface, text, accent, interactive, all locked together) makes the on-brand combination the path of least resistance and turns 'is this off-brand?' into a checkable question.
principle.howToApply: In the 35353 brand guide, define four to six named colourways - e.g. Core light, Core dark, Bold accent, Interface - each specifying page background, surface, body text, heading, accent and button colours as a locked set. Publish them as CSS custom-property sets and Figma variable modes with matching names, and write the instruction plainly: start from a collection, never from the palette.

entries.tagline: Three hand-drawn glyphs are the identity, the navigation and the archive filter - all at once.
entries.summary: A studio site with no hero copy: the first screen is a dark, near-monochrome shot of the studio's own printed matter, and the argument is made by the artefact. Below it, a dark band of five monoline-illustrated 'quick links' turns fonts, a poster shop, a workflow book and a workshop into one product family, and the newsletter sits inside that band at the same weight rather than as a popup. The main event is a five-column masonry archive of forty-plus projects - stamps, garments, chairs, app screens, posters - all shot on plain white or grey so wildly different work reads as one body. The one caveat for Natalie's taste: the category glyphs carry no visible labels, which needs accessible names to be usable.
whatWorks: Zero hero copy. A full-bleed, heavily desaturated photograph of their own fanned publications - colour bleeding in only at the edges - occupies the first screen, with no headline, tagline or CTA anywhere on it.

Three drawn glyphs (a cube, a folded sheet, a squiggle) are the entire taxonomy, and they appear twice: in the fixed header as identity and above the works grid as the filter control - so navigation and identity are literally the same object.

Every offer is drawn, not photographed: fonts, poster shop, workflow book, workshop and 'The No Book' each get a monoline illustration in one line weight, which holds five unrelated products together as a family.

The works grid is uniform-neutral - each project photographed or mocked on plain white or light grey at a consistent scale - so a neon poster, a black chair and an app screen sit in the same field without clashing.
The newsletter form lives inside the quick-links band at the same visual weight as the products: no modal, no sticky bar, no scroll trigger.

The footer is four short columns and one sentence of positioning ('Studio Feixen is a Swiss based design company that creates good looking stuff to make the world a better place.') plus address and drawn social icons - no sitemap, no repeated nav.
The archive uses infinite scroll with a visible 'Loading Projects' state, which frames the studio's output as ongoing rather than a curated top ten.

sections.name: Fixed header
sections.notes: A slim light-grey bar: wordmark left, the three category glyphs immediately beside it, then About / Shop / Talk and search, with a right-aligned 'Studio Feixen Fonts →' link. The commercial product gets the most prominent slot in the nav - the studio is telling you it sells something.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Full-bleed dark image of their own printed work, fanned so you read it as volume of output rather than a single piece. Desaturated to near-black with colour surviving only at the edges, which makes the bright works grid below land harder by contrast.

sections.name: Quick links + newsletter
sections.notes: A dark band of five illustrated cards, each with a monoline drawing, a name and two lines of plain description ('Do you have an empty white wall at home? Here you'll find some colors!'), with carousel arrows and two small colour dots as markers. The e-mail capture sits at the right of the same band, three fields and a Subscribe button.

sections.name: Works grid
sections.notes: The word 'Works' centred in a soft rounded display face, with 'Full Overview' and 'Filter' plus the three glyphs at left, then a five-column masonry of forty-plus thumbnails. Uniform neutral backgrounds and consistent scale do the unifying; no titles or hover chrome interrupt the scan.

sections.name: Infinite archive
sections.notes: The grid keeps loading with a visible spinner and label. Practically, it means the page has no 'end of work' moment - the depth of the archive is the credential, replacing the case-study and client-logo blocks most studio sites use.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Light grey, four small columns - About (one sentence), Follow us (icons drawn in the same monoline language), E-Mail, Address. It behaves like a business card: what, where, how to reach us, nothing else.

principle.title: Draw your taxonomy, then reuse it as the filter
principle.explanation: Most sites carry two separate systems: a visual identity, and a set of category labels bolted on for navigation. Feixen collapses them - a small set of custom drawn glyphs is the brand mark family and the archive's filter control, so every act of navigation reinforces the identity and the header needs no words. It also forces the useful discipline of deciding how few categories your work truly has.
principle.howToApply: For a 35353 or portfolio archive, name the three to five categories the work actually falls into, draw one glyph per category in a single stroke weight, and use that same set in the header and as the grid's filter. Then keep the grid uniform-neutral - one background, one scale - so varied work reads as one body. Non-negotiable fix on Feixen's version: give every glyph an accessible name and a visible label or tooltip, since an unlabelled icon filter is a usability failure on touch and for screen readers.

site.name: Zelle x Vox - co-branded native display banner

entries.category: Wide display banner - branded-content / native unit
entries.tagline: A bank ad that sells a lesson: publisher voice, collage illustration, and one lime button as the only saturated thing in the frame.
entries.summary: A 2000x697 co-branded unit for Zelle running in Vox's editorial environment, and it commits fully to the publisher's language rather than the bank's. The left half is a cut-paper collage - an acid-green 1980s brick phone, a mint speech bubble reading 'UNKNOWN CALLER' in halftone dots, a lime starburst full of dollar signs - on a flat olive-brown field. The right half is a numbered service headline in a high-contrast editorial serif. There is no app screenshot, no card, no product at all; the offer is knowledge, and the only saturated block in the unit is the CTA.
whatWorks: The joke is legible before the words: an ancient brick phone plus an 'UNKNOWN CALLER' bubble plus a starburst of dollar signs states 'phone scam' in one glance, so the headline confirms rather than explains.

The co-brand lockup ('Vox x Zelle', publisher first, multiplication glyph between) sits above the headline at small size - the partnership is disclosed before the pitch, which is what makes the editorial voice legitimate rather than borrowed.
The headline is written as service journalism, not advertising: '3 Simple Tricks to Help Spot a Scam' - a number, a promise of usefulness, no brand name in the sentence.
Type choice does the borrowing: a high-contrast editorial serif in white, tightly leaded over two lines, is the publisher's register, not a bank's sans.
One flat olive-brown field runs behind both halves, so the collage cutouts and the type share a single surface instead of sitting in two boxes.
The lime CTA rectangle is the only saturated block in the unit and is aligned to the headline's left edge - colour is spent on the click, and nowhere else.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The collage. Duotone-green vintage handset angled across the left half, with two paper-cut speech balloons - one mint with halftone 'UNKNOWN CALLER' lettering, one lime starburst of '$$$$'. Deliberately analogue and slightly ugly, which is why it stops a scroll inside an editorial feed of photographs.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: '3 Simple Tricks to Help Spot a Scam' in white editorial serif, flush left across two lines. The number front-loads the value, 'Help Spot' keeps the claim honest for a financial advertiser, and the brand is entirely absent from the sentence.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Roughly 50/50 split, collage left and type right, unified by a single flat olive-brown ground. No frame, no card, no product shot - unusual for a payments brand and the reason it does not read as an ad unit.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: A lime-filled rectangle with 'LEARN MORE' in tracked dark caps, placed under the headline on its left edge. It is the highest-chroma element in the frame and matches a colour already present in the collage, so it reads as part of the artwork rather than a pasted button.

principle.title: When trust is the product, make the ad the useful thing
principle.explanation: For categories where the purchase is really a trust decision - payments, insurance, mortgages, real estate - a product shot has nothing to prove. Offering a numbered piece of practical knowledge in the publisher's editorial voice buys credibility instead of attention, and the brand can stay in a small co-brand lockup because the usefulness is doing the selling.
principle.howToApply: For 35353, build a co-branded or native unit around one numbered piece of buyer/seller knowledge ('3 ways to spot a rental scam', '4 costs first-time buyers miss'), set it in an editorial serif on a single flat ground, illustrate it with one collage or cut-paper hook rather than a listing photo, keep the brand to a small lockup above the headline, and spend the only saturated colour in the unit on the button - pulled from a colour already in the artwork.

entries.tagline: Put a Japanese subject on a Swiss grid and build it from the fewest flat primitives that still name it.
entries.summary: Tanaka studied ancient Japanese art at Kyoto City University of Arts before he designed anything modern, and that order matters: he worked from tradition outward rather than importing a style. After textile design and a newspaper job in Osaka he moved to Tokyo in 1957, worked at Nippon Design Center, opened his Aoyama studio in 1963, made the graphics for Expo '70, became creative director of Seibu in 1975, and helped define Mujirushi Ryohin (MUJI) from 1980 - a brand whose identity is the deliberate absence of one. His posters reduce Noh masks, dancers and fans to flat circles, arcs and rectangles held on a strict grid, in three to five colours.
whatWorks: Study the source tradition first, formally. His Noh, Kabuki and Rinpa references are not motifs he sampled - he trained in them, which is why the reductions read as authoritative rather than decorative.
