Combine two systems on purpose: a Western modular grid to hold the composition, a Japanese subject to fill it. The tension between them is the work.
Build subjects from primitives - a face assembled out of arcs, circles and rectangles - so the image survives any scale and any medium.
Cap the palette hard (often three to five flat colours), with no gradients and no outlines, so colour reads as structure rather than shading.
Use vertical kanji columns as compositional rules: the text is a structural line that divides the plane, not a caption dropped on top of the image.
Let restraint be the identity - for MUJI, the rule that the goods, materials and process are shown and the mark stays quiet ('no brand') is a design decision about what NOT to add.

sections.name: How he begins
sections.notes: From the cultural source, reduced. He starts with a traditional subject - a Noh mask, a dancer, a fan, a Rinpa screen - and asks what its irreducible geometry is, before choosing a format or a palette. His formal training in ancient Japanese art is the front end of the process, not background colour.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Japanese subject on a modernist grid. The plane is divided first, then the motif is constructed to fit the modules; type - often vertical kanji - is placed as another structural element in the same grid. The result is legibly modern and unmistakably Japanese at the same time.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Flat geometric construction: shapes made only of circles, arcs and rectangles, filled with flat colour, no outlines, no gradients, no shading. A face becomes an arrangement of tones and curves that the eye completes - which is why his posters work at postage-stamp and billboard scale alike.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Balance is judged, not assumed: enough tradition to be rooted, enough abstraction to be current. And for a brand, the question is what to remove - MUJI's 'no-brand quality goods' position let material and process carry the identity, with graphics reduced to plain information.

principle.title: Rebuild the subject from the fewest primitives that still name it
principle.explanation: Reduction is a test, not an aesthetic. If a subject still reads when it is made only of circles, arcs and rectangles in flat colour, you have found its structure - and the result scales to a favicon or a facade, survives one-colour printing, and can be extended by someone else without your hand. If it stops reading, you have learned which feature was actually load-bearing.
principle.howToApply: For 35353's icons, illustrations or a listing-brand motif, redraw each subject on a grid using no more than six primitives, flat fills only, no strokes or gradients, and cap it at four colours. Test each one at 24px and at full-bleed hero size, and treat any shape that can be removed without breaking recognition as proof it should be. Where type belongs, run it as a structural column or rule that divides the plane rather than as a caption on the image.

site.name: Apple - App Store Marketing Resources & Identity Guidelines

entries.category: Third-party usage guidelines - partner / developer-facing identity rules
entries.tagline: The strictest third-party-use guide in tech: it legislates what must be inside your screenshot, not just where the badge goes.
entries.summary: This is not a brand guide for making things - it has no palette, no typeface and no grid. It is a compliance instrument for everyone outside Apple who shows Apple's marks, products and UI, and as that artifact it is close to definitive: every contestable rule is a number, a product-name spelling, or a flat prohibition. Its most unusual move is regulating the content of the screen you photograph - real running UI, full status indicators, no blank screens, fictional account data - which is the part most brands forget to specify at all. What it almost never does is explain why, so a partner facing an unlisted case has nothing to reason from.
whatWorks: Anything arguable is given a number: badge minimum height 10 mm in print and 40 px onscreen, clear space of one quarter the badge height (one tenth in very tight layouts), Apple device images no smaller than 25 mm or 200 px.

It specifies the screenshot's contents, not just the frame - show the app as it actually runs, full network / Wi-Fi / battery icons in the status bar, one push notification on the lock screen only, no blank screens, and no Home Screen unless you are showing your own widget.

Product names get a typographic spec table: iPhone's lowercase i and uppercase P, 'touch' always lowercase, Apple Watch and Apple Vision Pro as two and three words that must never break across lines and never take a preceding 'the'.
Naming grammar comes with counter-examples down to the URL level: 'App name for iPhone' not 'iPhone App name'; company.com/app/iphone is acceptable, iphoneapp.com is not.

Localization is solved for the partner rather than delegated: 50 localized badges are supplied, with the rule that the modifier ('Download on the', 'Pre-order on the') translates while 'App Store' never does.

The unauthorized-use list anticipates real abuse instead of speaking in principles - no 3D renders or illustrations of Apple hardware, no die-cut promos shaped like a device, no food packaging or disposables, no vehicle decals or bumper stickers, and no generic device drawings carrying Apple's distinctive details.
Hierarchy is stated plainly: one badge per layout or video, subordinate to the main message, black badge preferred and white only when a single badge needs to fit the layout's colours.

sections.name: App Store Badges
sections.notes: The core chapter: downloadable badge artwork for App Store, Mac App Store and Apple TV in download and pre-order variants, the preferred-black / alternative-white decision rule, one-badge-per-layout hierarchy, minimum size and clear space as numbers, no modifying / angling / animating, and a one-colour printing allowance if contrast holds.

sections.name: Product Images
sections.notes: Use current-generation devices your app supports, feature them alone, and use the supplied images 'as is' - no reflections, shadows, cropping, tilting, flipping, spinning or animating, copy beside the image rather than on it, correct relative scale between multiple products, plus the explicit list of unauthorized depictions.

sections.name: Screen content & device frames
sections.notes: The chapter that sets this guide apart. It governs what appears inside the screen: real running UI, latest OS, correct localized status-bar layer, the 5G icon only if the app is optimized for it, a single lock-screen notification that must open the app, Dock and menu-bar handling for Mac, and rights cleared for every asset shown with fictional rather than real personal data.

sections.name: Photography & Video
sections.notes: Custom photography is allowed but constrained: authentic interaction, straight-on shots preferred, no extreme angles or altered colour / shape / size, no fantastical treatment, the logo never obscured and never used for promotional value. Video adds motion rules - establishing shot before pan or zoom, simple fades and dissolves, no Apple interaction gestures as transitions, app's own sounds only, a 'sequences shortened' disclaimer where relevant.

sections.name: Messaging & Style
sections.notes: Product naming and typography: correct names over generic terms, always singular, Apple trademarks always set in English even in translated copy, a non-translatable list, the per-product casing table, approved 'works with' / 'compatible with' phrasing, and URL naming rules with acceptable and unacceptable examples.

sections.name: Legal Requirements
sections.notes: Trademark symbols on first mention in US body copy only (never in headlines or badge artwork), exact credit-line wordings for US and international use, a prohibition on implying association with Apple, and the full Marketing Artwork License Agreement - limited, non-exclusive, tied to Developer Program membership, terminable on 10 days' notice with a 30-day inventory depletion period.

needs: Any generative layer at all - no colour values, no typeface, no grid or spacing system - so a partner can comply but cannot design from it. Deliberate for this artifact type, but it means it must be paired with the partner's own guide.
Rationale next to the rules. 'Do not tilt the device' and 'no extreme angles' are stated without the brand reason, so an unlisted case (a new format, a new surface) has no principle to extend from.
Visual do / don't pairs. The prohibitions are described in prose far more than they are shown; a wall of annotated wrong examples beside the right ones would settle most disputes before they start.
Accessibility guidance - there is a black-versus-white badge decision rule based on visual weight, but no contrast requirement for badge-on-background or for copy set near it.
Coherent governance: the licence artwork carries a document stamp (EA0861, 08/15/17) while the guidelines themselves are undated and unversioned, so a reader cannot tell what changed or when.
Layout source files - a Figma or Illustrator template with badge clear-space and minimum-size guides built in - so compliance is a constraint in the file rather than a measurement task.

principle.title: Legislate the content of the screenshot, not just its frame
principle.explanation: Brands carefully specify logo clear space and then let anyone publish a screenshot of the product with a half-loaded state, an empty list, a fake-looking name, or three notification bubbles stacked for effect. Apple treats the inside of the screen as brand surface: what must be running, which indicators must be full, what must never appear, and whose data may be shown. It is the highest-leverage rule set for a product brand, because screenshots are where most people actually see the product.
principle.howToApply: Add a 'showing the product' page to the 35353 guide that governs screen contents, not just frames: which app or site state may be captured (populated, never empty or loading), the approved demo dataset and fictional names to use, required chrome (full status indicators, current release, correct locale), an explicit never list (blank screens, error states, real client or customer data, stacked notifications), plus export specs at 2x and a stated rule on cropping and annotation.

entries.tagline: A hardware brand whose store reads like a monochrome product index — the dot-matrix naming system '(3a)', 'phone (4a) pro' does the branding that other sites do with color.
entries.summary: Nothing sells phones and earbuds off a page that is almost entirely white space, product photography, and one eccentric typographic convention: every product name is set lowercase in parentheses. That single device — plus dot-matrix display type inherited from the hardware's Glyph lights — makes an otherwise austere grid unmistakably theirs. The page trusts the transparent-tech industrial design to be the color, and the copy stays to one benefit line per product, so the whole store scans like a well-set spec sheet rather than a campaign.
whatWorks: A naming convention as identity: 'ear (3a)', 'phone (4b)' set lowercase in parentheses — a typographic rule, not a logo, carries the brand through every card
One benefit line per product card ('Call for 46 hours with our biggest battery ever') — no paragraph ever competes with the photography
Near-total monochrome UI lets the transparent hardware and its red accents be the only color on the page
Two-column product grid with identical card anatomy (photo, name, line, 'Discover') — rhythm over variety, so new SKUs slot in without redesign
Dot-matrix/LED display type is used sparingly as an accent, echoing the physical Glyph interface — the site borrows its personality from the product, not from web trends

sections.name: Header / nav
sections.notes: Minimal black-on-white bar; the wordmark's registered-trademark '(R)' is styled as part of the identity joke. Offers and Learn links stay quiet — the nav never shouts over the grid.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: One oversized product photograph with generous negative space and a short launch line; the hero behaves like a magazine cover for whichever product is newest, and swaps without changing the page's structure.

sections.name: Product grid
sections.notes: Eight identical cards, two columns: photo on neutral ground, parenthetical name, a single concrete benefit ('Capture what you hear with Audio Snapshot'), and a 'Discover' link. Hierarchy is carried by image size and type weight alone.

sections.name: Community / Club Nothing
sections.notes: Community, Club Nothing and Playground links pull the ownership experience into the store — the brand treats buyers as members, which fits its drops-and-community sales model.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: A dense but tidy multi-column map (About, Community, Support, Business), newsletter signup, and store/language selector — the one place density is allowed, kept legible with strict column alignment.

principle.title: Let a typographic convention be the brand
principle.explanation: Nothing proves an identity can live in a rule rather than an asset: lowercase parenthetical product names and a dot-matrix accent face are cheaper than illustration systems and impossible to mistake once learned. Conventions scale to every new page and SKU automatically; logos and hero gradients don't.
principle.howToApply: Pick one enforceable typographic rule for a brand — a casing convention, a punctuation device, a numbering style — apply it everywhere names appear (nav, cards, invoices, ads), and strip back competing decoration until the rule is noticeable.

site.name: IKEA — 300×250 rich-media display banner (Smallest Store in the World)

entries.tagline: IKEA built a working store — 2,800 shoppable products, browsable by department — inside a single 300×250 banner, to prove any cramped space can be lived in.
entries.summary: Aimed at apartment hunters browsing real-estate listings, the unit turns the banner's own claustrophobic dimensions into the message: if IKEA can fit a whole store into 300×250 pixels, it can fit your studio flat. The creative is a mosaic of thousands of tiny product thumbnails that resolve into furniture silhouettes; hovering zooms into departments, clicking buys the real product. Placement did half the work — the tiny store sat exactly where people were shopping for tiny homes.
whatWorks: The format constraint IS the concept — a cramped banner selling solutions for cramped apartments, so the medium proves the claim before the copy does
Media placement completes the idea: it ran on real-estate sections, in front of people actively worrying about small space
The mosaic-of-products visual works at two scales — furniture silhouettes from a distance, individual buyable SKUs up close
Full purchase utility inside the unit (browse by department → click → buy) instead of a click-through promise
Unmistakably IKEA with almost no branding budget spent: flat blue and yellow plus the catalogue's own product photography

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: A whole IKEA store rendered at 'actual size' inside the ad slot — the absurd density of 2,800 products in 75,000 pixels stops the scroll on its own.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'Make the most of any space' — one line that reads simultaneously as product promise and as a description of the banner itself. No secondary copy needed.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Product-thumbnail mosaic forming furniture shapes: sofa, bed, cushion. The pixel-mosaic craft rewards a second look and turns browsing into play.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: The unit itself is the call to action — hover to enter a department, click a product to buy it on ikea.se. Utility replaces the 'Shop now' button.

principle.title: Make the format's constraint the concept
principle.explanation: The banner's tiny canvas is usually treated as a limitation to shout over. IKEA made the limitation the argument: the ad demonstrates space-efficiency instead of claiming it. When the medium itself proves the message, no copy has to.
principle.howToApply: Before designing any fixed-size unit, ask what the format's most annoying property is (small, skippable, muted, paused-over) and write one concept where that property demonstrates the product's benefit rather than fighting it.

entries.tagline: Co-founder of Push Pin Studios who fused illustration, typography and satire into a single voice — and proved a studio could market itself with its own publication.
entries.summary: Chwast (with Milton Glaser) built Push Pin Studios into the great counter-argument to Swiss rationalism: warm, witty, drawn-by-hand design that raided art history — Victorian woodtype, Art Deco, comics — and repurposed it with a satirist's timing. His anti-war poster 'End Bad Breath' and hundreds of covers, ads and typefaces share one engine: the idea is a visual pun first, and every craft decision exists to land the joke. The Push Pin Graphic, the studio's self-published periodical, doubled as its portfolio, lab and marketing for decades.
whatWorks: Concept as pun: he starts from a twist — two images fused into one meaning (Uncle Sam's mouth as a bomber run) — and only then chooses a style to serve it
A deliberately maintained style library: he collects historical vernaculars (woodtype, Deco, comics) and treats them as a palette to cast from per job, not influences to hide
Self-publishing as practice: The Push Pin Graphic gave the studio a deadline to experiment against and a promotional artifact, with no client's permission needed
Flat, bounded color and simplified contour drawing so the concept reads instantly at poster distance
Wit as a decision rule: if a sketch doesn't produce a smile or a wince, it isn't the sketch

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: With the twist, not the layout: Chwast hunts a double meaning — an object that can stand for two things at once — sketching small and fast in pen. The drawing style is chosen after the idea, from his shelf of historical vernaculars.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Illustration and typography designed as one unit. Lettering is drawn as part of the picture (or the picture behaves like lettering), so the piece can't be split into 'image plus caption' — this is the signature Push Pin fusion.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Historical pastiche with a modern punchline: borrow a period style the audience half-remembers, then break it with contemporary color or a satirical subject. The familiarity gets attention; the break carries the message.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Anti-purist: 'style' is a tool, not a religion, and humor is evidence the idea works. If the concept needs a paragraph to explain, it's dead; if it survives being redrawn crudely, it's strong.

principle.title: Publish your own periodical — give experiments a deadline and an audience
principle.explanation: Push Pin's influence came less from client work than from The Push Pin Graphic: a recurring, self-assigned publication that forced the studio to invent on schedule and mailed the proof directly to the people who hire. Self-initiated work with a recurring deadline compounds into both skill and reputation.
principle.howToApply: Start a small recurring artifact — a monthly one-page PDF, a printed mini-zine, a themed Instagram series — with a fixed ship date and a theme per issue; use it to test styles no client is asking for yet, and send it to the clients you want.

entries.tagline: A cycling-apparel store that alternates clean white commerce blocks with cinematic road-photography and genuine editorial, so the brand sells the sport as hard as the shorts.
entries.summary: Rapha's homepage runs two visual registers in strict alternation: flat, white, price-and-size product grids shot on consistent mannequin setups, and full-bleed lifestyle photography of riders on real roads in real weather. Editorial isn't a blog link in the footer — 'Latest Stories' tiles (films, route guides, racing coverage) sit in the main flow beside the sale grid, and the Rapha Cycling Club section sells membership like a product. The discipline is in the photography system: commerce shots are interchangeable and neutral; story shots are atmospheric and never asked to display a price.
whatWorks: Two photography systems with a hard wall between them: white-ground product shots for buying, cinematic ride photography for believing — neither is asked to do the other's job
Editorial in the shop flow: five 'Latest Stories' tiles (2:3 image, headline, dek) sit mid-page, giving the brand a magazine's authority without leaving commerce
Category tiles use lifestyle imagery while product cards stay clinical — navigation seduces, purchase informs
Membership (RCC) merchandised as a flagship product with its own confident claim — 'The best cycling club in the world' — rather than hidden in the nav
A text-only service band (returns, crash repair, guarantee) placed before the footer converts trust at exactly the moment of hesitation

sections.name: Promo bar + nav
sections.notes: Stacked promotional headers (sale, new collection) above a spare horizontal nav split by Men/Women/Accessories/Club. Urgency lives in the thin bars, never inside the brand photography.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Full-width sale hero with centered overlay type and dual gendered CTAs — one image, two clear exits, no carousel.

sections.name: Best of Sale grid
sections.notes: Four product cards with price, colorways and inline size selectors on white — buying mechanics exposed right on the card to shorten the path from browse to basket.

sections.name: Category + LIGHTSPEED feature
sections.notes: Three 2:3 lifestyle category tiles, then a full-width collection feature with USA Cycling co-branding — the page breathes between grid density and single-image drama.

sections.name: Rapha Cycling Club
sections.notes: Membership pitched with club imagery and editorial copy; the brand's community moat is sold with the same craft as its jackets.

sections.name: Latest Stories
sections.notes: Five editorial tiles — races, routes, a Merckx film — each 2:3 photo plus headline and dek. This is the section that makes the prices upstream feel justified.

sections.name: Service band + footer
sections.notes: Four plain-text trust statements (free returns, crash repair, quality guarantee), then a conventional multi-column footer with region selector.

principle.title: Separate the photography that sells from the photography that convinces
principle.explanation: Rapha never asks one image to both romanticize the sport and display the product's five colorways. Splitting the two jobs into two rigid systems — atmospheric full-bleed vs. neutral catalog — lets each be excellent, and the alternation itself gives the page rhythm.
principle.howToApply: For any commerce or portfolio build, define two named image specs up front (evocative: full-bleed, graded, no UI overlays; catalog: fixed ground, fixed crop, price-safe) and enforce that every image on the page belongs to exactly one spec.

site.name: Adidas Originals ZX Flux — retailer display banner (Pixelllo)

entries.category: Display banner (wide retail unit) — portfolio/spec work
entries.tagline: A retail sneaker banner that gets the e-commerce hierarchy exactly right: product at heroic angle, price set as the biggest type on the unit, one boxed CTA.
entries.when: Retailer web ad set for Pixelllo (UAE), Behance portfolio, 2018
entries.summary: A designer-published retail unit for the Adidas Originals ZX Flux (from a Behance banner set for UAE retailer Pixelllo — portfolio work, labeled as such). It's a textbook of the price-led retail banner: the shoe is cut out and flown at a dynamic diagonal with a soft echo copy behind it, the background is graded to the product's own coral pink, and the right column stacks name → 'AED 199' at display size → reversed 'SHOP NOW' box. Nothing competes with the two things a deal shopper needs: what it is and what it costs.
whatWorks: Price as the headline — 'AED 199' is the largest type on the unit, because in retail prospecting the price IS the creative
Monochromatic color strategy: background, floating 3D shapes and product all live in one coral family, so the white price and CTA are the only contrast
The product is duplicated — sharp foreground shoe plus blurred echo — creating depth and motion without animation
Strict right-column information stack (product name, price, boxed CTA) keeps the reading order unambiguous at a glance
Floating brand-adjacent geometry (extruded squares) fills negative space with energy while staying quieter than the product

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: A cut-out sneaker at a steep diagonal, twice normal display size, against a field graded to the shoe's own color — motion implied by angle and the blurred second shoe.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'ADIDAS ORIGINALS ZX FLUX PINK UNISEX' in compact caps — pure identification, deliberately subordinate to the price line below it.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Studio product photography with clean masking; the white sole gives the composition its one bright anchor and separates product from the tonal background.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: 'SHOP NOW' reversed out in a white keyline box, bottom-right — last in the reading order, exactly where the eye lands after the price.

principle.title: When price is the offer, set it like a headline
principle.explanation: Retail units fail when the price is a footnote under brand theater. If the deal is the reason the ad exists, the number deserves display-type treatment and the sole contrast color — everything else (name, imagery, geometry) should rank below it.
principle.howToApply: In any promo unit or sale card, size-test the price at 2–3× the product name, pull all supporting elements into the product's own hue family, and reserve white (or the one accent) for the price and the CTA box alone.

entries.tagline: Co-founder of Emigre who designed typefaces FOR the coarse screens and printers everyone else designed around — and turned a type foundry into a magazine-powered movement.
entries.summary: When the 1984 Macintosh's 72-dpi screen made traditional faces fall apart, Licko designed bitmap faces (Emperor, Oakland, Emigre) that treated the pixel grid as a medium instead of a defect. With Rudy VanderLans she built Emigre into the first great digital type foundry, its magazine acting as specimen book, manifesto and distribution channel at once. Her later Mrs Eaves — a revival of Baskerville named for Sarah Eaves — showed the same method pointed backward: re-examine the source's constraints (letterpress ink gain) and design for today's medium rather than tracing the past. (Image: her Mrs Eaves specimen — no free portrait exists on Commons.)
whatWorks: Design for the actual output device: her bitmap faces embraced 72-dpi coarseness rather than approximating high-resolution forms that the screen would mangle
Tool-driven form-finding: she works from what the current tech does natively (pixel grids, early font editors) and lets aesthetics emerge from those rules
The foundry-plus-magazine loop: Emigre magazine set new faces in real editorial use, which sold licenses, which funded new faces
Revivals as arguments, not tracings: Mrs Eaves reinterprets Baskerville's letterpress 'gain' for offset printing instead of copying outlines
Naming and voice as part of the product — faces named with history and wit (Mrs Eaves, Filosofia) that give licensees a story to retell

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: From the constraint inventory: what can this output device actually render? Licko starts by cataloguing the medium's hard limits (pixels per em, printer dots, ink spread) and treats that list as the brief.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Systematic variation within self-imposed rules: fix a coarse grid or modular parameter set, generate families by varying one parameter at a time, and keep only variants that stay legible in real text settings.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Low-resolution modularity — building letterforms from repeatable units so a face scales across sizes and devices coherently; later applied conceptually in ornament systems (Whirligig) and pattern fonts.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: 'You read best what you read most' — legibility is habituation, not an eternal standard, so new forms deserve time rather than dismissal. Ship faces into real use (the magazine) and let reading, not taste panels, judge them.

principle.title: Design for the resolution you actually have
principle.explanation: Licko's breakthrough came from refusing to pretend the medium was better than it was. Designing to the true constraints of the current device — instead of degrading an ideal form — produces work that looks intentional today and reads as visionary later.
principle.howToApply: Start each project by writing down the real delivery constraints (smallest viewport, email-client CSS, 1x screens, print at 85 lpi) and design primary assets natively at those limits first — then scale up, never the reverse.

entries.tagline: A dark, code-first email-API site that pitches with a copy-pasteable SDK snippet in the hero and treats documentation surface area as the main sales argument.
entries.summary: Resend sells email infrastructure to developers by behaving like the product: the hero pairs a one-line promise ('Email for developers') with real SDK code you could paste into a project, and the rest of the page is proof — SDKs in nine languages, machine-readable docs (append .md to any URL), OpenAPI specs, CLI and MCP tooling for AI agents. The visual language is late-night-terminal: near-black ground, thin keylines, restrained neon accents and monospaced type doing the illustration work. It reads as a tool made by people who use it, which is the entire trust argument for infrastructure.
whatWorks: Code in the hero: a real, runnable SDK snippet is the first 'image' on the page — the product demo and the headline are the same element
Dark UI with monospace-as-illustration: code blocks, JSON and terminal frames provide the visuals, so decoration never outruns substance
Breadth as proof: nine official SDKs, OpenAPI specs and markdown-mirrored docs are presented as features, arguing reliability by thoroughness
Developer-ergonomics flexes ('append .md to any URL', CLI, MCP server) signal the team optimizes for the buyer's actual workflow
Restrained accent palette on near-black keeps focus on text and code, and makes the few gradient moments feel like earned brand, not wallpaper

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: One-line category claim plus a live code sample and install command — the visitor's first interaction is reading the integration they'd actually write.

sections.name: Integrations & tooling
sections.notes: CLI, MCP server and agent-oriented tooling presented early; the page targets both the developer and the developer's AI tools, which is a 2026-native move.

sections.name: Docs & specs
sections.notes: Documentation, OpenAPI YAML/JSON and markdown mirrors of every page offered as first-class content — the docs are merchandised, not hidden in the nav.

sections.name: SDK wall
sections.notes: Nine language libraries in a uniform grid of framed cards — repetition of identical card anatomy communicates platform maturity at a glance.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Deep sitemap-style footer (blog, changelog, handbook, customers, security) that doubles as a credibility index — every link is another artifact of a functioning company.

principle.title: Make the integration the hero image
principle.explanation: For technical products the buyer's real first question is 'what does it take to wire this in?' Resend answers it in the hero with actual code instead of a screenshot or abstraction, collapsing evaluation time and signaling confidence — you only lead with code when the code is nice.
principle.howToApply: When building a page for any API-ish product, replace the hero illustration with the smallest complete working example (real endpoints, real field names, copy button), and keep it under ten lines so it reads at a glance.

entries.tagline: An ad designed to appear only when the viewer pauses Netflix — the paused episode stays on screen while KitKat claims the break it just created.
entries.when: Concept project by Jorge Sánchez, Behance, August 2025
entries.summary: A concept for Netflix's pause-ad format (portfolio work, labeled as such): when the viewer pauses Stranger Things, the frame splits — the show's paused card stays live on the left with episode metadata and time remaining, while the right two-thirds becomes a KitKat set piece: the bar snapping over a film-studio scene, a 'break' clapperboard, and the line 'Tus pausas necesitan un break, y nosotros también.' The genius is contextual: the brand whose entire equity is 'have a break' buys the exact moment a break begins, and the QR code gives the paused, phone-in-hand viewer something to do.
whatWorks: Perfect moment-message fit: KitKat's 40-year 'break' platform mapped onto the literal pause state — the context does the persuasion
The show is respected, not covered: the paused episode remains visible with its metadata, so the ad feels like part of the UI rather than an interruption
One brand color floods the unit — KitKat red bridges seamlessly from Netflix's dark UI, and the chocolate provides the only texture contrast
The film-set art direction (softboxes, clapperboard, camera) ties the candy to the streaming context instead of a generic product-on-red shot
QR + 'scan for a break' CTA suits the actual viewing posture: TV paused, phone already in hand

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The pause itself triggers the unit — zero fight for attention because the viewer just voluntarily stopped; the split-screen reveal reads as a native UI behavior.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'Tus pausas necesitan un break, y nosotros también' — one line that names the moment, lands the brand platform, and winks at the ad's own presence.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: A snapped KitKat on a red podium staged as a film set, with wafer crumbs mid-air; production-design metaphor keeps it in Netflix's world.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: A QR panel styled like a phone ('Escanea y date un break') plus a discreet 'Ad' tag — conversion routed to the second screen, where the paused viewer's attention actually is.

principle.title: Buy the moment your brand already owns
principle.explanation: The strongest media placement is one where the user's current state restates the brand promise — KitKat in the pause, not in the pre-roll. When context and platform agree, the creative only has to acknowledge the moment, not manufacture one.
principle.howToApply: For any campaign, list the micro-moments in the product or platform journey (pause, loading, empty state, delivery wait, checkout success) and match the brand's core promise to the one moment that literally enacts it — then design the unit to feel native to that state's UI.

entries.category: Legendary studio / experimental identity & self-initiated work
entries.tagline: A two-partner, ~25-person studio that ran self-initiated experiments — 40 Days of Dating, The Happy Film, Beauty — as its loudest marketing and its R&D lab at once.
entries.summary: When Stefan Sagmeister made 25-year-old Jessica Walsh a name partner in 2012, the studio doubled down on a rare operating model: stay deliberately small, keep client identity work (Function) funded and famous through headline-grabbing personal projects (Beauty — from the 'Beauty = Function' debate they publicly staged). 40 Days of Dating, Walsh's blog-turned-phenomenon, brought tens of millions of visitors and client calls without a single pitch. The studio treated craft experimentation — hand lettering, staged photography, early CGI — as content, publishing process openly and hiring through a famously competitive internship pipeline. (Image: co-founder Jessica Walsh; Stefan Sagmeister's individual practice is profiled separately, 2026-06-23.)
whatWorks: Self-initiated projects as business development: 40 Days of Dating and The Happy Film generated global press and inbound clients — marketing spend of zero, credibility of an art practice
Deliberate smallness: two partners and a compact team meant a partner's hands touched every job, which WAS the product being sold
Publish the process: sketches, experiments and behind-the-scenes work went public continuously, turning the studio's learning into its content channel
Craft maximalism as differentiation: hand-lettering, physical sets and staged photography in an era of flat digital — the studio zigged materially
A named debate as a filter: the 'beauty vs. function' argument gave the studio an intellectual position clients could hire, not just a style

sections.name: How it's structured
sections.notes: Two name partners with distinct energies (Sagmeister: sabbatical-driven conceptualist; Walsh: prolific, social-native maker) over a small permanent team plus a competitive intern pipeline — small enough that authorship stays real.

sections.name: How it takes on work
sections.notes: Client identity and campaign work is accepted selectively and priced on the studio's fame; the fame itself is manufactured by self-initiated projects the studio fully owns. Roughly: personal work buys attention, client work buys rent.

sections.name: Signature method
sections.notes: Make the experiment public and personal — diaries, films, dating blogs, staged tableaux. The studio's inner life is the campaign; craft (lettering, set-building, photography) is executed to gallery standard so the press writes about the work, not the stunt.

sections.name: What holds it together
sections.notes: An explicit intellectual platform (beauty as function) plus ruthless documentation habits. When Walsh spun off &Walsh in 2019, the model — small, loud, self-initiated — carried on, proving it was an operating system, not one partner's charisma.

principle.title: Run self-initiated projects as your loudest marketing
principle.explanation: S&W never out-spent bigger agencies; they out-published them. A personal project you fully control can demonstrate exactly the kind of work you want to be hired for, generate press no pitch deck can, and double as R&D — the studio model works at any scale, including a team of one.
principle.howToApply: Budget real hours (not leftovers) each quarter for one self-owned project scoped like client work — brief, deadline, launch plan — designed to showcase the exact service you want more of, and publish its process, not just its result.

entries.title: Sink a headline behind a mountain with a layer mask
entries.skill: Non-destructive masking — placing type behind a photographed subject with a duplicated layer + layer mask, and refining the mask edge
entries.brief: Create the classic 'text behind subject' effect: set the word ALTITUDE across the sky of a mountain photo, then mask a duplicate of the peak back over the letterforms so the summit overlaps the type.
steps: Open the reference image and set the headline in a heavy geometric sans (Archivo Black or similar), white, tracking +50, sized so the peak will overlap the lower third of the letters
Duplicate the photo layer, drag the copy ABOVE the type layer, and add a black (hide-all) layer mask to the copy
With a hard white brush at 100%, paint on the mask only where the summit ridge should cover the letters — zoom to 200% and follow the rock edge precisely
Switch to a 30%-flow soft brush for the atmospheric edges (snow haze) so the transition isn't a hard cut
Toggle the mask (Shift+click) and view at 100% and 25% to check the illusion reads at both sizes; nudge type opacity to ~92% so it sits IN the scene
Flatten to a copy and export a 1600px JPEG

assets.label: Reference image (Everest from Kala Patthar, CC BY-SA — Wikimedia Commons)
assets.note: Download full size; the ridge line against the sky is the masking edge to trace

assets.label: Spec
assets.value: Canvas 1920×1080 · type overlaps the peak by roughly one-third of cap height · no drop shadows, the mask alone sells the depth

entries.successLooksLike: At full-screen the word reads instantly as sitting BEHIND the summit — the rock edge cutting the letters is pixel-clean at 200%, the hazy snow edges are soft, and nothing was erased destructively (toggling the mask restores the intact photo).
entries.stretch: Add a second, smaller line ('8,848 M') tucked behind a nearer ridge, and grade the whole composite with a single Curves layer clipped to a group so photo and type accept the same tone.

entries.tagline: A deliberately tiny assets page whose best move is publishing the FAKE logo next to the real one, annotated with the tell.
entries.summary: The WordPress project keeps one short public page for its marks: six official lockups, each in vector PDF plus two PNG finishes, and a trademark-policy link. Its standout section, "Fight the fake logo (fauxgo)", puts the wrong W beside the right one with cap-height and serif-shape guides drawn over both and captions "Bad. (short & squat)" / "Good! (tall & graceful)" — teaching the silhouette rule that community redraws actually break. The page is itself on-brand, set in the project's serif with "Code is poetry" in the footer, and it closes by naming the trademark owner. It is a press kit, not a brand guide, and it does not pretend otherwise — which is also where its gaps sit.
whatWorks: Six named lockups (all-versions source, standard, vertical, word mark, W mark, simplified) so people pick a variant instead of inventing one
Every variant offered as vector PDF plus PNG in BaseGray and white, i.e. one asset per real background situation
Editable source files (Illustrator CS5+, Sketch) published openly, acknowledging that an open-source community will rebuild the mark anyway
The "fauxgo" pair: the counterfeit is shown, not just prohibited, with construction guides over the letterform
A crowd-sourced enforcement route — "if you see one of these in the wild, please suggest a change"
Trademark ownership stated plainly in the footer, with the policy one click away

sections.name: Official WordPress logo
sections.notes: One paragraph: use one of the following, and only in accordance with the trademark policy. Rules live in the linked policy rather than on the page — fine for a press kit, but it means the page alone cannot answer "may I do this?"

sections.name: Downloads
sections.notes: A 3x2 grid of six logo variants, each captioned with its role (Standard / Alternative, vertical arrangement / Word Mark / W Mark / Simplified) and three download links. The grid IS the logo system: variants are shown together at one scale so relationships are legible.

sections.name: Fight the fake logo (fauxgo)
sections.notes: The page's real contribution: two large Ws side by side with SERIF SHAPE and CAP HEIGHT guides ruled across them, labelled Bad (short & squat) vs Good (tall & graceful). It names the failure mode by silhouette, which is how counterfeits are actually spotted at a glance.

sections.name: Page craft / footer
sections.notes: The page is set in the project's editorial serif with generous measure and a "Code is poetry" footer, so the artifact demonstrates the brand while dispensing it. Legal line: the WordPress trademark is the intellectual property of the WordPress Foundation.

needs: Clearspace and minimum-size diagrams — the two rules a press kit exists to enforce, and both are absent
Colour values: no hex, RGB, CMYK or Pantone anywhere, so "BaseGray" is a filename rather than a specification
A typography line — even one sentence naming the wordmark face and an approved pairing for partner materials
Do/don't pairs beyond the fauxgo (recolouring, drop shadows, rotation, placing the mark on busy photography)
Application examples: avatar and social crops, favicon/app icon, co-branding lockups with plugin and host partners
A version number, date and owner on the page itself, plus a changelog — currently the only date signal is the trademark line

principle.title: Publish the counterfeit, not just the correct artwork
principle.explanation: People rarely misuse a logo because they lack the file; they misuse it because they rebuild it from memory and get the proportions wrong. Showing the wrong version beside the right one — with the construction guide drawn over both and the error named in plain words ("short & squat") — teaches the silhouette rule, which is the only rule an untrained eye can actually apply in the wild.
principle.howToApply: Add a "wrong marks in circulation" board to the 35353 brand guide: collect the real bad versions already out there (stretched wordmark, re-typed number, recoloured badge, mark on a busy photo), place each beside the correct art at identical size, rule one construction guide across both, and caption each with the specific tell rather than a generic "do not distort".

entries.category: Design-system brand layer (public system, SSO-gated Brand World)
entries.tagline: Colour defined by surface role and layer order rather than by swatch — so day/night, elevation and status all fall out of the naming.
entries.summary: Backpack is Skyscanner's public design system, and its brand-relevant value sits in Foundations rather than in a brand book: colour is published as canvas / surface / elevated-sheet roles instead of a palette wall, status colour splits into Spot (icons) and Fill (surfaces), and the core brand accents are explicitly a last resort "if there isn't any other appropriate semantic colour". Content, Accessibility and Localisation are top-level sections, not appendices, and every page carries a "last updated" timestamp. The catch is the brand layer itself: "Brand world — a journey into how we look, act and feel across every touchpoint" is SSO-gated for employees, leaving outsiders a logo Terms & Conditions page and downloadable marks. It is a strong product-facing brand layer with a locked front door.
whatWorks: Colour named by role and layer (Canvas, Canvas Contrast, Surface, Surface Contrast, Elevated sheet) so composition decisions are made by the system, not per screen
One stated structural rule — "there can only be one canvas per screen" — which makes wrong layouts diagnosable
Day/Night handled as behaviour rather than a second palette: elevation is shadow in Day mode and an Elevated Sheet token in Night mode; Text on Dark/Light deliberately do not shift
Status colour split by where it lands: Spot colours for icons, Fill colours for surfaces
Brand accents demoted — Sky Blue and friends are for when no semantic colour applies, which protects the semantic layer from decoration
Icons documented per platform (Web, iOS, Android, Compose) plus accessibility and a contribution route, so the set stays one set
Every page stamped with a last-updated date and time; Contributing is a first-class section

sections.name: Welcome / IA
sections.notes: A shortcut grid that doubles as a table of contents — Foundations, Layout primitives, Icons, Components, Content, Accessibility, Localisation, Brand world — each with a one-line description of what it governs. Icons are characterised in words ("simple, modern, friendly, and sometimes quirky"), which is brand personality smuggled usefully into a component page.

sections.name: Brand ↗ (Brand world + Logo T&Cs)
sections.notes: Two children only. Brand world is the actual identity guide and is SSO-gated: "Skyscanner employees can sign in via SSO". Logo T&Cs is public and purely legal — permitted purpose (promoting partnership), downloaded form only, a required trademark-attribution sentence, no denigration or confusingly similar marks, and permission revocable at any time with immediate effect.

sections.name: Foundations
sections.notes: Twelve foundations: Animation, Blur, Border, Colours, Focus indicator, Grids, Icons, Layout, Typography, Radius, Shadow, Spacing. Notable that Blur and Focus indicator are foundations at all — the system specifies the effects and states that usually get improvised.

sections.name: Colours — Overview / Usage / Code
sections.notes: The strongest page. Text styles per surface; status colour as Spot vs Fill; Canvas (one per screen, Default vs Contrast for card-heavy screens); Surfaces stacked above canvas with Surface Contrast for emphasis; Elevated sheet as the top layer; "other elements" reserved for dividing lines and scrims; core brand accents last. Each colour ships with a usage tab and a code tab, so designers and engineers read the same rule.

sections.name: Content / Accessibility / Localisation
sections.notes: Verbal identity ("how we use words to bring designs and interfaces to life"), accessibility, and internationalisation sit at the top level beside components — for a travel product where dates, currencies and scripts change per market, this is the right IA, and the localisation card shows the same booking card in English and Arabic.

sections.name: Governance
sections.notes: Per-page "Page last updated on <date>, <time>" stamps, a Contributing section with a route for product design, and a versioned URL space (/latest/...). Living, if not formally versioned.

needs: A public brand layer: partners, agencies and press cannot see logo construction, palette values, typeface or photography direction at all — only the legal T&Cs
Clearspace and minimum-size diagrams for the sunrise mark alongside the downloadable files
Semantic HEX/RGB values visible on the Usage page rather than only inside the Code tab, so non-engineers can specify a colour
Print, OOH and merchandise guidance — the system is product-only, yet the brand appears on airport signage and campaign media
Explicit semantic version numbers plus a changelog, not just last-updated timestamps
The WHY: the rules are decidable but largely unexplained, so a team outside Skyscanner can copy the taxonomy without understanding when to break it

principle.title: Name colours by surface role and layer order, not by palette
principle.explanation: A swatch wall makes every screen a fresh negotiation: which blue is the background, which is the card, which is the button. Naming colour by role and stacking order — one canvas per screen, surfaces above it, elevated sheet on top, status as spot vs fill, brand accents last — turns those negotiations into lookups, and makes dark mode a transformation of roles rather than a second palette.
principle.howToApply: Restructure the 35353 colour page around roles instead of brand colours: define canvas (default and contrast), surface (default and contrast), elevated sheet, text-on-light / text-on-dark that never shift, status spot vs fill, and a short "brand accent — only when no semantic role fits" note. Publish each role as a token with light and dark values side by side, state the one-canvas-per-screen rule, and keep the raw palette on a separate reference page.

entries.tagline: A colour is not specified until every surface it must survive has a value — hex, CMYK, Pantone, RAL paint, vinyl film and reflective foil.
entries.summary: Amsterdam publishes its entire house style openly as "Stijlweb": four pillars (the brand, the ground rules, the applications, the language policy) over an A–Z index of about thirty topics, from icons and colour to podcasts, PowerPoint, forms, email signatures and construction-nuisance communication. Its two outstanding pages are colour and typography. Colour is three base values (white, red, black — white and red leading), eight full supplementary colours with no tints or gradients allowed, and three greys, each specified in CMYK, Pantone, hex, RGB, RAL lacquer, 3M film, Avery film and Oracal — including reflective foil codes for vehicles and signage, and silver reserved for ceremonial print. Then it does what almost no guide does: publishes a legibility matrix stating, per background colour, which heading and body-text colours are permitted.
whatWorks: Colour values given per production medium — screen, print, paint, vinyl and reflective foil — so a van, a sign and a website are the same red by specification, not by eye
A stated non-negotiable: use full colours only, never rasterised tints and never gradients
A text-on-background matrix (per background: which heading colour, which body colour, and what to do on white) instead of "ensure sufficient contrast"
Named exceptions with thresholds: white headings on orange or light green are print-only and only from 40pt Amsterdam Sans ExtraBold
Campaign latitude with a test attached — coloured text on colour is allowed if you run an accessibility check online and an audience test offline
Typography specified by destination: print, façade lettering and wayfinding, online, MS Office, Arabic — with a request form for the licensed Amsterdam Sans
Applications reach the unglamorous surfaces most guides skip: workwear, email signatures, forms, charts and maps, podcasts, PowerPoint, social

sections.name: Four pillars (Over het merk / Uitgangspunten / Middelen / Taalbeleid)
sections.notes: The whole guide is framed as brand and brand rights (the Andreas crosses, the city arms) → ground rules for logo, colour, icons, typography and imagery → applications from workwear to every online channel → language policy (the Schrijfwijzer, clear naming, use of other languages). Strategy, visual, applied and verbal in one sentence each.

sections.name: Alle onderwerpen (A–Z index)
sections.notes: About thirty topic links in four columns, alphabetical rather than hierarchical: colours, logo, typography, icons, photography, image policy, campaigns, theme design, charts/tables/maps, clear naming, film and animation, forms, email signature, podcasts, PowerPoint, social media, websites and apps, core values, colophon. An index beats a hierarchy when the audience is thousands of municipal employees looking for one answer.

sections.name: Kleuren (colour)
sections.notes: Three base colours, eight supplementary for background planes, headings and accents, three functional greys for infographics and maps. A full table gives CMYK, PMS, hex, RGB, RAL lacquer, 3M film, Avery film and Oracal per colour — Amsterdam red is #ec0000 / 0-100-100-0 / PMS 2035 / RAL 3020 / 3M 100-13 with reflective 580-72. Silver exists only for ceremonial print of the mayor and aldermen.

sections.name: Leesbaarheid (legibility matrix)
sections.notes: Per background colour, the permitted heading and body-text colours plus what to do on white: on red, headings black or white and body white; on yellow and orange, black only; on purple and dark blue, white only; on blue and dark green, black body with black-or-white headings. Print uses the same combinations, with rgb for online PDFs.

sections.name: Typografie (Amsterdam Sans)
sections.notes: One family as the image-defining typeface, chosen to sit with the Andreas crosses and to read equally offline and online. Licensing is explicit: city staff, amsterdam&partners and their suppliers only, via a request form. Rules then split by destination — print, façade lettering and wayfinding, online, MS Office, Arabic.

sections.name: Governance
sections.notes: A named owner ("Contact team huisstijl"), colophon, proclaimer and a web archive of superseded guidance; even the print vendors are named, with the required ISO colour profile for one of them. The guide is written for the people who actually break brands — and tells them who to email.

needs: Rationale: the rules are exhaustively specified but rarely explained, so external teams can obey the system without being able to extend it
Contrast published as numbers per text size (4.5:1, 3:1) alongside the colour-pair matrix, and a rule that colour alone never carries meaning
Dark-mode and digital-surface behaviour as a transformation rule — the palette is designed for print, paint and light backgrounds
Version number, date and changelog per page; the web archive implies versioning but pages are not stamped
Developer-ready distribution: the colour table as downloadable tokens (CSS/JSON/Figma variables), not a table to retype
An English edition and a licensed fallback typeface for external partners who cannot receive Amsterdam Sans
Shown do/don't pairs for photography and campaign layouts, rather than policy prose

principle.title: A colour is only specified once every surface it must survive has a value
principle.explanation: Brand drift almost never starts on screen; it starts when someone has to make the brand red on a van wrap, a painted door, a reflective sign or an embroidered jacket and has only a hex code. Publishing CMYK, Pantone, RAL, vinyl-film and reflective-foil codes for every colour — plus a matrix of which text colours are legible on each background — removes the moment of improvisation where the identity actually breaks.
principle.howToApply: Extend the 35353 colour page from hex/RGB to a per-medium table: screen (hex, token name), print (CMYK, Pantone), signage/vehicle (RAL and a named vinyl film), plus an explicit "no tints, no gradients" line. Then add a legibility matrix — for every background colour, the permitted heading colour, body colour and the treatment on white — and state the one print-only exception with its minimum size, so the guide answers the question at the moment it is asked.

entries.tagline: A studio homepage built from ONE repeated module — kicker, headline, arrow — so films, vinyl, podcasts and merch read as a single catalogue instead of five different card systems.
entries.summary: A24's site refuses almost every convention of an entertainment homepage: no nav bar, no hero button, no cards. The header is three glyphs (MENU, the serif A24 wordmark, search) floating in white over a full-bleed film still, and the hero is pure type — six upcoming titles stacked in a big grotesque with tiny superscript years, hierarchy carried by tone rather than size. Below it the whole page is one editorial module repeated: a one-word all-caps kicker (SHOP / PODCAST / WATCH), a large headline, an arrow plus a micro-CTA, and an image half that alternates left and right — punctuated every few beats by an edge-to-edge film still with the title set small in the corner. Two honest caveats: a black newsletter panel lands on top of the hero on first visit, and the feed loops back to the top forever, so the footer is only reachable from the menu.
whatWorks: Chrome reduced to three glyphs — menu, wordmark, search — in white over full-bleed imagery, so nothing ever competes with a film still
Hero as a type stack: six titles at the same size with 2026 in superscript, the active one white and the rest dimmed — hierarchy by VALUE, not by scale
One module for everything: kicker + headline + arrow-link, so a Blu-ray, a podcast and a soundtrack LP need no badges, cards or borders to be told apart
The single all-caps kicker word does all the labelling a card system would have needed
Every product — book, vinyl, crewneck, Blu-ray — is photographed on the same light-grey stage panel, so merch and media sit in one visual family
Arrow + tracked micro-label (SHOP NOW / LISTEN NOW) instead of filled buttons: the link reads editorial, not e-commerce
Talent and podcast portraits are black-and-white, keeping film colour the only colour on the page
Full-bleed stills interrupt the two-column rhythm every few modules — a cadence rather than a template

sections.name: Header
sections.notes: No navigation bar at all: hamburger + 'MENU' at far left, the serif A24 wordmark centred, a search glyph at far right — all white, all sitting directly on the hero image with no background plate. It never fights the picture, and it tells you the site's only two jobs are browse and find.

sections.name: Hero — the title stack
sections.notes: A full-viewport, softly out-of-focus film still (olive/gold) with six upcoming titles set left-aligned in a large neutral grotesque, each trailed by a small superscript '2026'. The active title is white, the others drop to a muted tint — so the hero is a live index, not a poster, and the whole slate is legible in one look. A down-arrow bottom-right is the only affordance. A black 'WANT MORE A24?' email panel overlays the centre on first load.

sections.name: The repeated editorial module
sections.notes: The body is one component reused down the page: tiny tracked all-caps kicker (SHOP / PODCAST / WATCH), a two-to-four-line headline in the same grotesque at ~48px, then an arrow with a tracked micro-CTA. The image side is a flat light-grey panel holding either a product shot or a black-and-white portrait, and it alternates left/right module to module. No card, no border, no shadow — the grey panel IS the container.

sections.name: Full-bleed film bands
sections.notes: Every few modules the two-column rhythm breaks for an edge-to-edge still ('The Death of Robin Hood', 'Mother Mary') with a barely-visible WATCH kicker and the film title in white at the lower left — no button, no synopsis. These bands are the page's punctuation and the only place the imagery is allowed to go loud.

sections.name: Commerce, treated as editorial
sections.notes: Shop items get exactly the same module as a podcast episode: 'AAA24 Membership' with a chrome 3D logotype, the Sing Sing screenplay in its orange book cover, The Invite soundtrack as a yellow vinyl half-out of its sleeve, an ASYNC crewneck flat-lay. Because the ground and scale are constant, a $30 book and a $200 membership read as one shelf.

sections.name: Infinite loop instead of an ending
sections.notes: The feed doesn't terminate — it restarts from the hero, framing the studio's output as ongoing rather than a curated top ten. The trade-off is real: the footer (three link groups, a second email capture, social icons on dark) is effectively menu-only, so anything a visitor needs must live in the menu.

principle.title: Build one module and let the pictures do the varying
principle.explanation: A mixed feed — films, products, podcasts, articles — usually collects a card system per content type, and each new type adds chrome: badges, borders, differently-sized tiles. A24 does the opposite: one module (kicker word, headline, arrow) carries every type, and all the variety comes from the photography inside it. The page stays quiet, the components stay few, and a new content type costs one word instead of one design.
principle.howToApply: For a mixed 35353 feed (new listings, market notes, neighbourhood guides, team news), design a single row: tracked all-caps kicker that names the type, a headline at one size, an arrow + micro-CTA, and an image panel on a fixed neutral ground that alternates side. Add a full-bleed photo band every third or fourth row as punctuation. Resist adding a second card style when a new content type appears — add a new kicker word instead.

site.name: Everlane — Meta feed ad (4:5, Luxe Italian Leather Crossbody)

entries.category: Meta feed ad (4:5 portrait, zero baked-in type)
entries.tagline: A 480×600 creative with not one word set on it — the product is the whole image, and every piece of copy is left to the platform's own chrome.
entries.when: Meta feed — Facebook, Instagram, Messenger and Threads; running since 1 June 2026
entries.summary: Pulled live from the Meta Ad Library, this is the plainest kind of well-made feed ad: a cognac leather crossbody tote shot dead straight-on, centred, on a bone ground tuned to the leather's warmth, with a soft floor shadow and generous margin. There is no headline, no logo lockup, no price flash, no sale badge — the creative contains zero type. All the words live in Meta's own chrome: the Everlane avatar and 'Sponsored' label, one line of primary text ('Discover why everyone is obsessing over these pieces.'), the link caption naming the exact SKU ('Everlane Luxe Italian Leather Crossbody In Cognac'), and a grey Shop Now button. The result is an asset that cannot break when it's re-cropped to square, story or Marketplace — and one that doubles as a catalogue image.
whatWorks: 4:5 portrait, not 1:1 — roughly 25% more vertical feed height for the same scroll
Ground colour tuned to the subject (bone against cognac) so the silhouette separates at thumbnail size, before any detail is legible
One object, straight-on, centred, with real margin — it reads as a shape first and a product second
Zero baked-in type: nothing to clip, re-flow or fail translation when the same asset is cropped into other placements
The full product name is the link caption, so the promise is a specific SKU rather than the brand
The primary text does the persuading in a single line; the creative's only job is stopping the scroll
Colour is doing the branding — no logo needed inside the frame, because the account name is already in the unit

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: A tall, near-empty warm field with one object in it. In a feed of busy, text-stacked creative, emptiness is the pattern interrupt — the eye resolves the bag shape instantly because there is nothing else to parse.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: Deliberately absent from the image. Meta's chrome supplies it: 'Discover why everyone is obsessing over these pieces.' — social proof phrased as curiosity, one line, no exclamation, no price. Because the platform renders it, it's live text: selectable, translatable, and rendered at the platform's own accessible size.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: 480×600. Cognac full-grain leather, handles up, strap draped across the body of the bag to show it's a crossbody, tiny debossed wordmark visible on the front panel, soft contact shadow implying a real surface. It's honest catalogue photography, not a styled lifestyle scene — the same frame that would sit on the PDP.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: Meta's own grey 'Shop Now' button, sitting under the link caption block (EVERLANE.COM → product name → brand boilerplate). Nothing in the creative competes with it, so the only clickable-looking element in the whole unit is the real one.

principle.title: Put no type in the creative — let the platform draw the words
principle.explanation: Baked-in headlines are the first thing to break when one asset has to serve feed, story, Reels, Marketplace and dynamic placements: text gets cropped, shrunk under the legibility threshold, or stranded in one language. A creative that is only subject-on-ground survives every crop, and the platform's chrome already renders the copy as live, translatable, accessibly-sized text next to a real button. The trade is honest — you lose the headline when someone screenshots or shares the image alone — so the first line of primary text has to carry the argument.
principle.howToApply: For 35353 paid social, ship creatives as one subject on a ground colour sampled from the subject, 4:5, ~15% margin, no type and no logo inside the frame; put every word in the ad copy fields and make the link caption the specific thing (address, neighbourhood, price band) rather than the brand. Keep baked type for formats with no chrome to borrow — display banners, OOH, email headers.

entries.tagline: Designs books as three-dimensional objects — and starts every one by building five to seven tiny paper models before a single page is laid out.
entries.summary: Irma Boom is the most decorated book designer alive — youngest-ever winner of the Gutenberg Prize (2001), a Yale critic since 1992, with work held at MoMA — and her method is almost entirely physical. She begins each project by making miniature 3D models of the book, typically five to seven of them, which she describes as filters for her ideas; she has accumulated hundreds, and eventually published them as a book of their own, 'The Architecture of the Book' (2010). Structure comes out of content, not style: the 2,136-page SHV Thinkbook took three and a half years of research and shipped with no index, reversed chronology and an untreated white cover designed to soil with handling.
whatWorks: Build five to seven small physical models before designing anything — and treat them as filters for ideas, not as presentations
Design the object, not the pages: thickness, weight, page edges and material are part of the composition
Let the content dictate the structure, even when that means breaking a convention (no index, reversed chronology)
Front-load research so form arrives out of the material rather than out of a style choice
Rename the relationship you need: she works for 'commissioners', not clients — equal collaborators, with trust and freedom stated up front
Let the artefact age on purpose — a cover that dirties with use makes wear part of the design
Be selective; she takes few projects, which is what makes the depth of research possible

sections.name: How she begins
sections.notes: With the content, and at miniature scale. Before layout, she builds tiny three-dimensional models of the whole book — five to seven per project — to think about sequence, proportion, thickness and where the reader enters. The dummies are working tools ('filters for her ideas'), so decisions about structure get made while they are still cheap to change. Research runs first and runs long: the SHV Thinkbook meant three and a half years in archives across Amsterdam, Paris, London and Vienna.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Iterate in the object rather than on the screen. A book is a physical volume, so the maquette is the drawing — she keeps making small versions until the structure is inevitable, then scales up. Hundreds of these models exist; the collection itself became 'Irma Boom: The Architecture of the Book' (2010), which is the clearest statement of the method: the archive of prototypes IS the portfolio.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Designing the entire landscape of the book, including the parts most designers ignore. Page edges are a surface to print on; paper choice, embossing, die-cuts and finishing each carry logic rather than decoration. The SHV Thinkbook has 2,136 pages, no index and an anti-chronological order, with a white cover meant to dirty as it's used. The Chanel N°5 book is 300 pages of white embossing — an almost inkless, semi-invisible narrative — inside a black box. Weaving as Metaphor (2006) has deliberately ragged edges echoing textile selvedges.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: The book must be an object of beauty with quality and permanence, not a container for information — her explicit answer to the idea that print is obsolete. She refuses the word 'client' in favour of 'commissioner', on the grounds that the relationship has to be equal and built on trust for anything unconventional to survive; and she stays very selective, since depth is only possible on few projects. A decision is judged by whether it helps the reader understand the content, not by whether it looks designed.

principle.title: Make it small before you make it right
principle.explanation: Structural decisions — sequence, proportion, rhythm, where the eye enters — are the expensive ones, and they're the ones a full-size layout hides behind detail. Building the whole thing at a quarter scale, several times over, forces those decisions while they cost nothing and makes the shape of the whole visible at once. The prototype is a filter: most of the five to seven versions exist to be rejected.
principle.howToApply: Before designing a 35353 page, brochure or listing package, put the entire thing on one sheet at ~25% — thumbnails of every section in order, real proportions, no type detail — and make five variants that change only the sequence and the proportions. Judge rhythm and entry point from the board, print it, keep the one that survives, and only then design at full size. For print pieces, fold a physical dummy at the real paper weight before choosing anything else.

entries.category: Public brand portal (post-refresh identity + writing guide)
entries.tagline: A public brand portal with only two top-level sections — Identity and Brand Writing — so the verbal system gets equal billing, including a 'Writing with AI' chapter that says what a model may and may not write.
entries.summary: Zalando published its brand refresh as an open, dark-mode portal that splits into exactly two halves: Identity (identity system, logo, typography, colour, layout, motion, visual assets) and Brand Writing (writing at Zalando, brand voice, inclusive language, writing with AI, localisation, style manual, glossary). Giving writing half the navigation is unusual and the content earns it — the voice traits are named in the brand's own subject language ('Relaxed basics', 'Contrasting patterns', 'Unexpected details', 'Flexing our voice'), and the AI chapter draws a genuinely decidable line rather than a warning. The visual side is rule-led too: the brand mark is always orange, the word mark only ever black or white, text only black or white. Its one real weakness is that a public guide never publishes an actual colour value.
whatWorks: Two top-level sections only — Identity and Brand Writing — so the verbal system is structurally half the brand, not an appendix

Each design principle is joined by a rule line to the outcome it buys: Simple → a system that's easy to use; Dynamic → distinct assets that build recognition; Consistent → clarity of brand role; Flexible → future-proof for new channels
Voice traits named in the brand's own vocabulary — 'Relaxed basics', 'Contrasting patterns', 'Unexpected details' — so a fashion company's voice system reads on-brand as you learn it

A 'Writing with AI' chapter with a usable split: AI may analyse and re-angle what you wrote; it may not originate on-brand copy, strategy or localisation — and its output is reviewed 'the way you'd review something written by a junior colleague'
Colour written as roles, not swatches: brand mark always orange on any background, word mark only black or white and never orange, text only black or white with greys for small details
One variable typeface with a leash — Zalando Sans runs Condensed Extra Light to Expanded Black, but the instruction is to 'stick to the pre-defined styles for your category' on a 4/8-point size scale
Motion treated as a real discipline: its own introduction, choreography, core assets, a grid system for motion, motion typography and application examples
Inclusive language and localisation sit inside the writing section as standard chapters rather than as a compliance note

sections.name: Our refreshed brand (hero)
sections.notes: A dark portal opening with the orange brand mark animating as video, plus a short paragraph on WHY the refresh happened — a start-up grown into a fashion and lifestyle platform that needed to evolve. Rationale before assets, in two sentences.

sections.name: Visual identity (six cards)
sections.notes: Logo system, Typography, Colour, Layout, Motion and Visual assets as a 2×3 grid of thumbnails, each with a single-line summary and its own subtree. The card previews are real artwork — the wordmark, a 'Superfamily' type specimen, the actual colour table, a photograph on a live grid — so the grid doubles as a specimen sheet.

sections.name: Brand positioning, identity and design principles
sections.notes: 'BOLD / Fun / Welcoming' set over campaign photography, the positioning line ('the go-to destination for quality fashion and lifestyle shopping'), a short identity narrative ending on 'A New Style of Entertainment', then the four design principles — Simple, Dynamic, Consistent, Flexible — each ruled across to the consequence it produces. This is the guide's strongest page: principles with their payoffs attached.

sections.name: Colour (primary / secondary)
sections.notes: Orange as the hero colour tied to heritage, black and white as the foundation. The rules are decidable: the brand mark is always orange regardless of background or motif; the word mark exists only in black or white and never in orange; text is only ever black or white, with grey permitted for small details. Don'ts name the specific failures — white on orange, orange on white, mixed text colours, low contrast on imagery. What's missing is any actual value.

sections.name: Typography (Zalando Sans)
sections.notes: One variable superfamily spanning Condensed Extra Light to Expanded Black, Latin and Latin Extended-A, downloadable from the portal. Then the leash: use the pre-defined styles for your category, and size on 4- and/or 8-point increments. A guide that hands over a wide range plus an instruction not to roam it.

sections.name: Brand Writing
sections.notes: Seven chapters — Writing at Zalando, Our brand voice (We speak Zalando → Relaxed basics → Contrasting patterns → Unexpected details → Flexing our voice → Voice examples), Inclusive language, Writing with AI, Localisation, Writing style manual, Glossary. The voice model is built as clothing vocabulary: 'basics' are the clear, friendly, informal elements used everywhere; 'contrasting patterns' is being to the point with energy and without judgement; 'unexpected details' is refusing the obvious word.

sections.name: Bringing our identity to life + governance
sections.notes: An applications gallery of the identity in the wild — a street-level digital screen, packaging tape, print, the heart glyph — followed by a two-column index of every page, a named contact (brand-refresh@zalando.de) and 'Made with love in Berlin, Dublin, Hamburg & Helsinki'. There's a route to a human, but no version number and no date.

needs: Actual colour values — Zalando orange is specified by name and by rule but published with no hex, RGB, CMYK or Pantone, so no external partner can match it
Numeric contrast pairings instead of 'WCAG standard combinations are recommended' — which ratio, at which text size, on which background
Logo clearspace and minimum-size diagrams, plus shown misuse pairs; the logo section describes mechanics in prose
A version number, date and changelog — the portal documents a refresh without stamping itself, so nobody can tell whether they're reading the current rules
Machine-readable distribution: colour and type as tokens (CSS/JSON/Figma variables) next to the font download, not values to retype
Light/dark surface behaviour as a transformation rule — the portal itself is dark, but nothing states how the palette flips between surfaces
A print and packaging layer: applications are shown photographically but there are no specs for the physical surfaces a retailer actually ships

principle.title: A 2026 brand guide needs an AI clause — say what a model may write and what it may never originate
principle.explanation: Voice now breaks where nobody is looking: in generated first drafts, at scale, across every team with a prompt box. A guide that only lists voice adjectives leaves that decision to whoever is prompting. Zalando's answer is a split anyone can apply without judgement calls — AI may analyse and re-angle copy you already wrote, and is good at binary choices; it may not originate copy meant to sound on-brand, invent strategy or creative concepts, or handle localisation. Output is then reviewed like a junior colleague's draft: every word read, not skimmed.
principle.howToApply: Add a one-page 'Writing with AI' section to the 35353 brand guide with three lists. Green: tighten a paragraph you already wrote, generate options for a binary choice, check a draft against the voice traits.
